title: AMARJIT SINGH v. STATE OF PUNJAB
text: The Supreme Court upheld the conviction of Amarjit Singh under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code for murdering his grandfather Mehar Singh. The court relied on the evidence of Mangat Singh and Hazara Singh, who testified that the appellant had attacked Mehar Singh with a Kirpan. The court also noted that the blood-stained Kirpan was recovered from the appellant's possession and that human blood was found on it. Additionally, the court accepted the testimony of Dr. Jasbir Singh, who conducted the post-mortem examination and opined that all the injuries were caused by a sharp-edged weapon like a Kirpan. Citations: 1995 SCC Supl. (3) 390; JT 1995 (5) 529; 1995 SCALE (4)555 Legal tags: Criminal Law; Murder Case; Indian Penal Code; Section 302 IPC; Terrorist Affected Areas (Special Courts) Act, 1984; Special Court; Additional Judge; Investigating Officer; Prosecution Evidence; Defence Witnesses; Motive and Proof; Evidence Law; Appellate Jurisdiction; Supreme Court of India; Judgment and Order

title: DOSA SATYANARAYANAMURTY ETC. v. THE ANDHRA PRADESH STATE ROADTRANSPORT CORPORATION
text: The Supreme Court dismissed the petitions, affirming the constitutional validity of Chapter IVA of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939, as amended by Act 100 of 1956. It held that the provisions of Chapter IVA were not ultra vires Parliament's powers, did not infringe Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution (as saved by Article 19(6)(ii) which permits complete or partial exclusion of citizens for state-run services), and did not contravene Article 14 by discriminating between State Transport Undertakings and private operators, as the classification had a reasonable nexus to the object of providing efficient public transport. The Court also found no established personal bias against the Minister in charge of transport. The seven schemes for nationalization in West Godavari District were deemed valid, with the Court clarifying that piecemeal implementation observations from a previous case did not apply as these were distinct schemes to be implemented in their entirety. It was also affirmed that the Chief Executive Officer was competent to publish the proposed schemes as a ministerial act, and that the schemes, as modified by the Minister to specify vehicle numbers per route, complied with Rule 4 of the Andhra Pradesh Motor Vehicles Rules. However, Rule 5 of the Andhra Pradesh Motor Vehicles Rules, which conferred power on the State Transport Undertaking to vary the frequency of services without following the procedure under Section 68E of the Act, was declared void, and the corresponding note appended to the schemes was directed to be deleted, as it amounted to a substantial modification. The Court also held that Section 68C empowered the State Transport Undertaking to include new routes in a scheme. Consequently, the petitions were dismissed with costs, save for the deletion of the note regarding service frequency. Citations: H. C. Narayanappa v. The State of Mysore, [1960] 3 S.C.R. 742; Gullapalli Nageswara Rao v. Andhra Pradesh Road Transport Corporation, [1959] SUPP. 1 S.C.R. 319; Saghir Ahmad v. The State of U. P., [1955] 1 S.C.R. 707; Gullapalli Nageswara Rao v. The State of Andhra Pradesh, [1960] 1 S.C.R. 580; Srinivasa Reddy v. The State of Mysore, [1960] 2 S.C.R 130 Legal tags: Motor Vehicles Act, 1939; Chapter IVA; Nationalisation of Road Transport Services; Constitutional Validity; Article 19(1)(g); Article 19(6)(ii); Article 14; State Transport Undertaking; Private Operators; Andhra Pradesh Motor Vehicles Rules; Rule 5; Section 68C; Section 68D; Section 68E; Bias; Quasi-judicial Procedure; Road Transport Corporations Act, 1950; Ministerial Act; Scheme Modification; Frequency of Services; New Routes; Fundamental Rights; Equality Clause

title: OARAMJIT KAUR v. STATE OF PUNJAB & ORS.
text: The Supreme Court clarified its order dated 12th December, 1996, in Writ Petitions (Criminal) Nos. 447 and 497 of 1995, regarding the National Human Rights Commission's (NHRC) role in examining flagrant human rights violations in Punjab. The Court affirmed the NHRC's findings on preliminary issues: 1) The NHRC, when acting under the Supreme Court's remit in exercise of its plenitude of jurisdiction under Article 32 of the Constitution, functions as a *sui generis* body, not strictly limited by the provisions of the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993, including the one-year limitation under Section 36(2). 2) Consequently, the NHRC's powers in carrying out this mandate are not curtailed by Section 36(2) or other limiting provisions of the Act. 3) The NHRC's adjudications on compensation, subject to the Supreme Court's approval, do not constitute an impermissible delegation of judicial power. 4) The NHRC can establish adjudicatory mechanisms, including appointing officers with judicial experience (e.g., enquiry-commissioners, claims-commissioners) to record evidence and recommend compensation, subject to its final endorsement, with special administrative and financial allocations to be provided by the Union of India and the State of Punjab. The Court emphasized that its powers under Article 32 are unfettered and the NHRC acts in aid of the Supreme Court's constitutional powers, rather than acquiring a new jurisdiction. The Court disapproved of the obstructive attitude of parties causing delays in the proceedings. The petition for clarification was disposed of accordingly, and an intervention petition was rejected. Citations: Article 32; Section 36(2); Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993; Antulay's case; Section 17; Section 18 Legal tags: National Human Rights Commission; NHRC; Supreme Court of India; Article 32; Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993; Section 36(2); Human Rights Violations; Sui Generis Body; Jurisdiction; Limitation Period; Compensation; Punjab; Central Bureau of Investigation; CBI; Mass Cremations; Kidnapping; Disappearances; Judicial Powers; Constitutional Law; Writ Petition (Criminal); Clarification Petition

title: UNION OF INDIA & ORS. v. M/S. SANJEEV WOOLLEN MILLS
text: The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal filed by the Union of India & Ors. against the orders of the Delhi High Court dated July 15, 1996, and March 19, 1997. The High Court had directed the release of goods imported by M/s. Sanjeev Woollen Mills under four Bills of Entry without recovery of any demurrage or container charges, holding the Customs Department responsible for the inordinate delay in releasing the goods, which was attributed to the conduct of the Customs authorities and alleged demands for illegal gratification. The Supreme Court found that the High Court's orders were passed in special circumstances due to the Customs authority's conduct, including not releasing the goods even after an order of unconditional release by their own Chief Commissioner. The court noted that the respondent's complaint of mala fides against Customs officers was under investigation. The Supreme Court held that the High Court's order did not require intervention for the period prior to April 5, 1997, and directed the appellants to file a progress report on the departmental inquiry by November 30, 1998. The court clarified that the order was not to be considered a precedent but was meant to do justice in the specific facts and circumstances of the case. title: NANIK AWATRAI CHAINANI v. UNION OF INDIA
text: The appellant, a licensee of railway stalls, was considered a railway servant under Section 3(7) read with Section 148(2) of the Indian Railways Act, 1890. The agreements for the stalls, which allowed extensive power to the Railway administration for directing and regulating the appellant's work, were terminable by one month's notice without assigning any reason. The appellant committed irregularities, failed to pay a fine imposed as per the agreements, and consequently, the agreements were terminated. Possession was sought under Section 138 of the Indian Railways Act. The Supreme Court held that while the appellant was a railway servant, he was not entitled to the protection of Article 311 of the Constitution as he was neither a member of the civil service nor dismissed, removed, or reduced in rank in a manner attracting the Article. His rights were confined to the terms of the written agreements, and any wrongful termination could be challenged in civil courts. The Court found no legal infirmity in the lower courts' orders and dismissed the appeal, stating that the appellant's status as a licensee did not grant him rights beyond the contractual terms, even if the stalls were initially allotted for rehabilitation purposes. Citations: A.I.R. 1937 Lahore 547; A.I.R. 1959 Cal. 64 Legal tags: Indian Railways Act; Licensee of Railway stall; Railway servant; Termination of agreement; Rights of licensee; Article 311 of the Constitution; Master and servant relationship; Dispute resolution; Contractual rights; Bare licensee; Rehabilitation; Malice; Criminal Procedure Code; Civil Procedure Code; Landlord-Tenant Law; Administrative Law; Constitutional Law; Property Law; Contract Law

title: Vatticherukuri Village Panchayat v. Nori Vnkatarama Deekshithulu & Ors.
text: The Court has held that the jurisdiction of the civil court to take cognizance of suits relating to land reform laws stands excluded by necessary implication. The Act concerned extinguishes pre-existing rights and creates new rights under the Act, and requires Tribunals to enquire into rival claims. A form of appeal has been provided against the order of the primary authority. Therefore, the right and remedy made conclusive under the Act are given finality by the orders passed under the Act. title: SHRI SHIVJI v. SHRI RAGHUNATH (DEAD) BY L.RS. & ORS.
text: The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal by special leave, upholding the High Court's decision. The appellant, a subsequent purchaser, had argued that the agreement for sale was fraudulent and void due to the rule against perpetuities. However, the Court found that the agreement was valid and enforceable. The Court referenced the case of Rambaran v. Ram Mohit, stating that a mere contract for sale of immovable property does not create an interest in the property, and thus the rule against perpetuities does not apply to a covenant of pre-emption. The Court clarified that the agreement constituted a fetter on the seller's right to deal with her share of the property and created a pre-emptive right enforceable when an attempt is made to alienate the land to third parties. The appellant, having purchased with notice of the agreement, was bound by it. Citations: [(1967) 1 SCR 293] Legal tags: Specific Performance; Agreement for Sale; Subsequent Purchaser; Fraud; Rule Against Perpetuities; Transfer of Property Act; Section 14; Section 40; Section 54; Pre-emption; Co-owner; Alienation; Notice; Enforceability; Special Leave Appeal; High Court Judgment; Property Law; Contract Law

title: THE GOVERNMENT OF TAMIL NADU & ANR. v. K. JAYARAMAN
text: The Supreme Court held that the Government order providing for pensionary benefits upon completion of 25 years of qualifying service cannot be given retrospective effect. The respondent, who voluntarily retired on March 20, 1970, before the amendment came into force on March 1, 1972, was not entitled to pension under the amended rules. However, considering the respondent had rendered two years of temporary service and had a shortfall of three years for pension computation, the Government was directed to consider his eligibility for pensionary benefits or relaxation thereof, and pass appropriate orders within four months. title: GHAZIABAD DEVELOPMENT AUTHORITY v. JAN KALUAN SAMITI,SHEOPURI, GHAZIABAD & ANR.
text: The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the High Court's order that had quashed the notification under Section 4(1) and the declaration under Section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. The Court held that the High Court erred in its conclusion regarding the validity of simultaneous publication of the Section 4(1) notification and Section 6 declaration, and the invocation of Section 17(4). The Court noted that a local amendment to Section 4 of the Act dispensed with the mandatory requirement of local publication in newspapers when the inquiry under Section 5A was dispensed with under Section 17(4). Furthermore, a proviso inserted into Section 17(4) by the UP Amendment Act, specifically concerning the period between September 24, 1984, and January 11, 1989, allowed for the simultaneous publication of the Section 4(1) notification and the Section 6 declaration. Therefore, the acquisition proceedings were deemed valid, and the appeal was allowed without costs. title: COMMISSIONER OF CENTRAL EXCISE & CUSTOMS v. M/S VENUS CASTINGS (P) LTD.
text: The Supreme Court held that manufacturers who have opted for the procedure under Rule 96ZO(3) or Rule 96ZP(3) of the Central Excise Rules for payment of duty cannot claim the benefit of determination of production capacity under Section 3A(4) of the Central Excise Act, 1944. The Court reasoned that the schemes under Section 3A(4) and Rule 96ZO(3)/96ZP(3) are alternative procedures, and an assessee cannot adopt a hybrid procedure. The Court found the view taken by the Andhra Pradesh High Court and a division bench of the Allahabad High Court to be reasonable and correct, while overruling the contrary view of another bench of the Allahabad High Court. The appeals were allowed, and the matter was remitted to the Tribunal to bring its orders in conformity with the Supreme Court's decision. title: OBERAI FORWARDING AGENCY v. NEW INDIA ASSURANCE CO. LTD. & ANR.
text: The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the judgment and order of the lower court, and dismissed the complaint filed by the respondents. The Court held that the insurance company (first respondent) was not a consumer under the Consumer Protection Act, 1986, as it had merely been assigned the right to recover compensation for the loss of goods and was not a beneficiary of the service hired. The Court clarified that the document executed by the second respondent in favour of the first respondent constituted an assignment of rights, not merely subrogation, allowing the first respondent to pursue the claim in its own name. However, this assignment did not make the first respondent a consumer. Consequently, the complaint filed under the Consumer Protection Act was not maintainable, even with the second respondent added as a co-complainant, as the second respondent had effectively transferred all its recovery rights. Citations: 1972 (2) SCC 877; 1997 (6) SCC 383; AIR 1965 Madras 159; AIR 1986 Andhra Pradesh 32; 1992 (2) CPJ 349; 1998 (2) CPJ 16 Legal tags: Insurance Law; Consumer Protection Act; Subrogation; Assignment of Rights; Consumer Status; Maintainability of Complaint; Contract Law; Transportation Law; Civil Procedure; Supreme Court of India; Appeal; Indemnity; Loss of Goods; Consignment; Jurisdiction

title: UNION OF INDIA AND OTHERS v. SADHA SINGH
text: The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, quashing and setting aside the judgment and order of the High Court of Punjab & Haryana which had directed the immediate release of the respondent, Sadha Singh, a life convict from General Court Martial. The High Court had erred by concluding that the respondent, having served 15 years 8 months and 29 days including remissions, was entitled to release. Reaffirming its Constitution Bench decision in Maru Ram v. Union of India & Anr., the Supreme Court held that Section 433A Cr.P.C. mandates a minimum of 14 years of actual imprisonment for life convicts, particularly for offences where death is a possible punishment. This provision overrides any special or local laws, including remission schemes, as Section 433A is a specific provision that prevails over such laws by virtue of Section 5 Cr.P.C.'s 'specific provision to the contrary' clause. It was clarified that remissions do not confer a right to release unless the remaining sentence is remitted by the Government. The Court further held that the Army Act, 1950, despite being a special act, does not contain any specific or contrary provision covering the area of Section 433A, thereby making Section 433A Cr.P.C. applicable to convictions under the Army Act. The decision in Ajit Kumar etc. v. Union of India was distinguished as it pertained to the applicability of Section 428 Cr.P.C. (set-off for pre-trial custody) and not Section 433A. Since the respondent had not completed 14 years of actual imprisonment, his immediate release was impermissible. Citations: 1987 Supp. SCC 493; (1981) 1 S.C.R. 1196 Legal tags: Life Imprisonment; Actual Imprisonment; Remissions; Section 433A Cr.P.C.; Section 5 Cr.P.C.; Army Act, 1950; General Court Martial; Murder; Supreme Court of India; Maru Ram v. Union of India & Anr.; Ajit Kumar etc. v. Union of India; Criminal Law; Statutory Interpretation; Overriding Provisions; Special vs. General Law

title: Airports Authority of India v. Unknown
text: The Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in its judgement dated 23rd April, 1999 allowed the application made by the Airports Authority of India to set up Hot Mix Plants for resurfacing the runways at IGI Airport, New Delhi. The court directed that the plants shall be set up at a safe distance of at least 3 kms from populated areas and that the vehicles transporting the resurfacing material shall be loaded and unloaded in the presence of security staff who shall constantly escort these vehicles to and fro from the Hot Mix Plants to the work site at IGI Airport. The court also directed that the Hot Mix Plants shall be operated for a period of one year from the date on which they are installed or till the resurfacing of the runways is completed, whichever is earlier. title: MANOJ v. STATE OF MADHYA PRADESH
text: The Supreme Court allowed the appeal and ordered the release of the accused person on bail. The Court held that the detention of the accused beyond 24 hours without a magistrate's order was unlawful. The Court also relied on the proviso to Section 167(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which mandates the release of an accused person on bail if they are detained in custody for more than 90 days. The Court noted that the accused had been arrested in connection with two cases, one in Rajasthan and one in Madhya Pradesh, but was not produced before a magistrate within 24 hours of his arrest in the MP case. The Court therefore held that the detention of the accused beyond 24 hours was unlawful and ordered his release on bail. title: VIJATABAI & ORS. v. SHRIRAM TUKARAM & ORS.
text: The Supreme Court held that the Tahsildar's suo motu proceeding under Section 49B of the Bombay Tenancy and Agriculture Lands (Vidarbha Region) Act, 1958, after a lapse of 11 years, was without jurisdiction and unsustainable in law. The Court found that the issue of whether respondent No. 1 was a tenant had already been conclusively decided in a prior proceeding under Section 8 of the same Act, where respondent No. 1's name was deleted from the list of tenants based on a compromise admitting he was never a tenant. This earlier order had become final as no appeal was preferred. Therefore, the Tahsildar could not reopen this concluded issue, nor could he set aside the previous order under Section 49B. The Court also noted that the compromise was acted upon by respondent No. 1 purchasing a portion of the land. The findings of the Collector, Maharashtra Revenue Tribunal, and the High Court in favour of respondent No. 1 were set aside. The appeal was allowed, and the findings against the appellants in the proceedings under Section 49B were quashed. title: SHRI D.M.DESHPANDE & ORS. v. SHRI JANARDHAN KASHINATH KADAM (DEAD) BY LRS.
text: The appellants, trustees of a public trust, sought possession of trust land (Survey No. 14) from the respondents. The second respondent, a former trustee, and the first respondent, claiming to be a tenant, were directed to hand over possession under a settled scheme and its subsequent amendment. The respondents' claim of tenancy was rejected by the Executing Court, the District Judge, and the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court held that the High Court erred in directing the issue of tenancy to be referred to the Tehsildar and in ordering the trust to hand over possession to the first respondent. The court emphasized that a vague plea of tenancy, lacking material particulars regarding its creation, time, and terms, is insufficient to raise an issue or warrant a reference to the Tehsildar. The Supreme Court allowed the appeals, setting aside the High Court's order regarding the tenancy issue and the handover of possession, thereby upholding the trust's right to recover its property. title: DELHI ADMINISTRATION v. STATE OF HARYANA & ORS.
text: The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal filed by the Delhi Administration. The Court held that the conditions attached to the grant of a permit under Section 48(3)(xiv) read with Section 63(2) of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1959, did not restrict a permit holder from plying vehicles beyond the specified inter-State route if done under another valid permit. The Court interpreted the counter-signature conditions, which stated that tickets would be issued for destinations between Delhi and Karnal, as positive instructions to issue tickets for that route and exhibit destination boards, but not as a prohibition against plying beyond Karnal or issuing tickets for stations beyond Karnal. The Court also held that operating beyond the inter-State route under valid separate permits did not constitute an "extension" of the route prohibited by the Act, as it did not involve an application for variation of the existing permit under Section 57(8). The Court acknowledged the potential for misuse where long-distance passengers might be preferred over those traveling on the inter-State route, but stated that if such preference violated a peremptory condition of the counter-signature, the Delhi State would be entitled to take action under the law. title: SEN (A.K.) v. THE STATE OF WEST BENGAL AND ANR.
text: The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal by certificate, upholding the High Court's decision. The court held that in execution sales, the crucial aspect is to ascertain what right, title, and interest were intended to be sold. Any misapprehension by the court or purchaser does not alter the legal effect of the sale. In this case, the sale intended to convey only the materials of the structures (structures simpliciter) and not the land underneath or the permanent tenancy rights associated with it. The sale certificate did not confer any right, title, or interest on the appellant concerning the permanent tenancy rights in the suit land. The High Court was correct in decreeing the plaintiff's claim. Citations: L.R. 14 I.A. 84 @ 85 Legal tags: Civil Procedure Code; Order XXI Rule 94; Certificate to purchaser; Sale in execution of money decree; Scope of sale; Structures vs. Land; Permanent tenancy rights; Title suit; Recovery of possession; Declaration of title; Mesne profits; Appeal by certificate; Misapprehension of court; Purchaser's understanding; Evidence in case; Execution of decree; Attachment and sale of property; Prohibitory order; Confirmation of sale; Sale certificate; Application under Section 47 CPC; Second appeal; Injunction; Notice under Section 80 CPC; Vindication of title; Suit for eviction; Auction sale; Valuation of property; Sale price; Legal effect of sale; Property rights; Landlord-tenant law

title: S. P. WATEL AND OTHERS v. STATE OF U.P.(with connected appeals)
text: The Supreme Court allowed the writ petition, quashing the Government notification dated June 16, 1964, concerning the disputed land under Section 8 of the U.P. Urban Areas Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1956. The Court directed a fresh inquiry to determine if the land was an 'agricultural area' on the relevant date. If found to be an agricultural area used for agriculture or horticulture, the Government could issue a notification under Section 8. Otherwise, no such notification should be issued. The Court also allowed the appeals, setting aside the High Court's order abating the suits and appeals. The High Court was directed to restore the cases and decide them on merits, considering the fresh determination of the land's status. Parties were to bear their own costs. title: JAGDISH CHANDER CHATTERJEE & ORS. v. SRI KISHAN & ANR.
text: The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal filed by the legal representatives of the deceased statutory tenant, B. N. Chatterji, affirming the High Court's decision. The Court held that the contractual tenancy had been duly terminated by notice, a fact not contested during the trial, thus negating the need for a remand on this issue. Crucially, the Court reiterated that the protection under Section 13 of the Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950, pertaining to the landlord's bona fide and reasonable requirement, was personal to the statutory tenant. Upon the death of the statutory tenant, this personal right does not devolve upon his heirs or legal representatives in the absence of a specific statutory provision to that effect. Furthermore, the Court rejected the contention that the heirs became 'tenants' under Section 3(vii) of the Act merely by paying rent during the pendency of the proceedings, clarifying that such payments were received without prejudice to the landlord's rights. Consequently, the legal representatives could only advance contentions appropriate to their representative character, not those personal to the deceased statutory tenant. Citations: 1972 AIR 2526; 1973 SCR (1) 850 Legal tags: Supreme Court of India; Civil Appeal; Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act 1950; Section 13; Section 3(vii); Statutory Tenant; Contractual Tenancy; Termination of Tenancy; Ejectment Suit; Landlord-Tenant Dispute; Personal Right; Heirs and Legal Representatives; Bona Fide Requirement; Rent Control Legislation; Appeal Dismissed; Order 22 Rule 4 Civil Procedure Code; Definition of Tenant

title: C.A.P. ANDIAPPAN v. C.I.T. MADRAS & ANR
text: The appellant, a resident of India carrying on business in Ceylon, was assessed for income tax in India for the years 1959-60 and 1960-61 on income earned solely in Ceylon. The Indian Income-tax authorities computed the tax under Indian law and provided an abatement equivalent to the tax paid in Ceylon, as per the India-Ceylon Agreement for the Avoidance of Double Taxation. The appellant contended that he was not liable to be taxed in India at all, or alternatively, that the abatement should have been the full tax leviable in Ceylon as a non-resident. The Supreme Court held that: (1) Under Article 3 of the Agreement, India was empowered to make an assessment in the ordinary way under its own laws, thus the appellant was liable to be taxed in India. (2) The phrase 'attributable to' in Article 3, read with item 8 of the Schedule, means the tax ultimately levied on the assessee in the other country, considering all provisions of the taxing statute including exemptions and allowances. Therefore, the abatement allowed should be the actual tax paid in Ceylon, not the hypothetical tax that would have been payable as a non-resident. The appeals were dismissed, affirming the High Court's decision. Citations: 55 I.T.R. 699 Legal tags: Income Tax; Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement; India-Ceylon Agreement; Tax Liability; Abatement; Resident in India; Business in Ceylon; Assessment; Income Tax Ordinance 1932; Indian Income-tax Act 1922; Article 3 of Agreement; Schedule to Agreement; Ramesh B. title: Government of India v. Shri Ram Prasad Ghosh
text: The Appellate Authority was justified in using the second report made by the police, even though it had not been placed into the hands of the parties. The only effect of the report was that many of the objections raised against the suitability of the appellant had been withdrawn by the police on further consideration of their records. Therefore, there was nothing to be met in relation to this report. Citations: AIR 1954 SC 255; 1954 SCR 1057 Legal tags: judgement

title: HINDUSTAN WIRES PRODUCTS LIMITED v. COMMISSIONER OF INCOME-TAX, PATIALA
text: The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals filed by Hindustan Wires Products Limited, affirming the High Court's decision in favour of the Revenue. The Court held that the insulated copper wires manufactured by the assessee, specifically winding wires used in electrical gadgets and for transmission (employed in coils, armatures, etc.), do not qualify as "cables" within the meaning of Item 7 of the Fifth and Sixth Schedules of the Income Tax Act, 1961. The Court clarified that Item 7, when read in conjunction with Item 24, refers to complete self-contained units of machinery or equipment for the generation and transmission of electricity, not merely components or parts of components. Consequently, the assessee was not entitled to the benefits of development rebate and deduction in respect of profits and gains as a "priority industry" under sections 33(1)(iii)(c)(A), 80E, 33(1)(b)(B)(i), and 80-I of the Income Tax Act, 1961, for the assessment years 1966-67 to 1971-72. The High Court was deemed correct in concluding that the Appellate Tribunal had erred in overlooking fresh evidence indicating the specific nature of the wires manufactured by the assessee. title: The Petitioner v. The Regional Transport Authority and The Government of Bombay
text: The case revolves around a dispute between the petitioner and the Regional Transport Authority regarding the rejection of their application for renewal of permits. The authority had approved a scheme submitted by the Provincial Transport Services, which excluded the petitioner from operating on certain routes. The petitioner argued that the rejection was unlawful and that the scheme suffered from discrimination. However, the court held that the Regional Transport Authority had the power to reject the applications under Section 68F(2) of the Act, as it was necessary to give effect to the approved scheme. The court also rejected the argument that the Chief Minister's decision was based on extraneous considerations not covered by the Act. Ultimately, the petition was dismissed without any costs being awarded to the respondents. Citations: AIR 1966 SC 1649 (1) Legal tags: petition; dismissed

title: PRATIBHA PROCESSORS & ORS. v. UNION OF INDIA & ORS.
text: The Supreme Court held that the importers are not liable to pay interest on warehoused goods if such goods are exempt from duty at the time of clearance. The Court reasoned that interest is compensatory in nature and is linked to the principal amount of duty payable. Since the principal amount (duty) was nil due to exemption, the interest payable was also nil. The Court distinguished this case from previous rulings where duty was payable, clarifying that interest is only chargeable when there is a delay in paying the actual duty amount. The Bombay High Court's judgment, which held the importers liable for interest, was reversed, and all appeals were allowed with costs. title: appellant v. respondent
text: The industrial tribunals have consistently refused to entertain claims for housing accommodation or special house rent allowance against employers, considering that such an obligation would be inexpedient and potentially detrimental to the national economy. The Planning Commission's report on the Second Five Year Plan emphasizes the need for sustained efforts from both the States and industries to address the problem of housing shortage. title: Personal Manager,SBI &Anr v. Krishna Grameena Bank Employees Union & Anr
text: The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the judgment of the Division Bench of the Karnataka High Court. It was held that employees of Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) are entitled to a special allowance of Rs.189/- per month for the post of "Cashier-in-charge of cash" as per the NABARD Circular dated 21.4.1992, issued with the prior approval of the Ministry of Finance (Banking Division), Government of India. The Court clarified that the National Industrial Tribunal (NIT) Award applied the principle of 'parity' in pay scales and allowances with sponsor banks, but did not establish 'functional similarity' or examine posts specifically. It was noted that the post of "Joint Custodian of Keys" as understood by the RRBs, entailing an allowance of Rs.380/-, does not have a comparable equivalent in the State Bank of India (sponsor bank) where a higher allowance is paid as an officiating allowance for performing Cash Officer functions, not as a 'keys allowance'. The Court directed that no amount shall be recovered for the period from 1.1.1991 to 21.10.1991, and any amounts already paid for this period shall not be recovered. The appeal was allowed with no order as to costs. Citations: 2001(1) SCC 353; 2000 (2) SCC 455; 1993 AIR SCW 2214; AIR 1987 SC 2342; AIR 1959 SC 1217 Legal tags: Regional Rural Banks (RRBs); State Bank of India (SBI); Sponsor Bank; Pay Scales; Allowances; Special Allowance; Cashier-in-charge of cash; Joint Custodian of Keys; National Industrial Tribunal (NIT) Award; Parity Principle; Functional Similarity; Equation Committee; Bipartite Settlement; NABARD Circular; Government of India; Writ Petition; Writ Appeal; Supreme Court of India; Karnataka High Court; Andhra Pradesh High Court; Recovery of Excess Payment; Industrial Dispute

title: Narcotics Control Bureau, Jodhpur v. Murlidhar Soni & Ors.
text: The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's decision to set aside the conviction and sentence of the respondent and his father under Section 21 of the NDPS Act. The Court agreed with the High Court's finding that the statements of the accused, purportedly recorded under Section 67 of the Act, were obtained under duress, citing medical reports and doctor's testimonies indicating injuries sustained by the accused, including a fractured rib. Furthermore, the Court noted that the prosecution failed to establish conscious possession of the contraband by the respondent, as the bag containing the narcotics was carried by his father, and there was no evidence to suggest the respondent's knowledge of its contents. Consequently, the appeal filed by the Narcotics Control Bureau was dismissed. title: D.C. Aggarwal (Dead) by LRs. v. State Bank of India and another
text: The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals, upholding the High Court's decision. The court found no substance in the appellant's claims for extension of service and promotion. Regarding promotion, the court held that the appellant was correctly assessed under the 1984 policy, which mandated a structured interview, and his poor performance in the interview justified the rejection of his promotion to TEGS VII. The court also rejected the argument of institutional bias, stating it was a resurrection of a previously settled issue. Regarding extension of service, the court affirmed that the appellant had no legal right to an extension, and the bank's decision not to extend his service was in the bank's interest and not subject to interference. The court cited the precedent in State Bank of Bikaner and Jaipur v. Jag Mohan Lal, stating that extensions are for the bank's benefit, not employee entitlement. Finally, the court held that even if the appellant had succeeded, the outcome would have been a reconsideration of his case, not an automatic grant of promotion or extension, thus denying any claim for monetary benefits to his legal heirs. Both contentions regarding extension and promotion were found unsustainable. title: AVISHEK RAJA & ORS. v. SANJAY GUPTA
text: The Supreme Court disposed of numerous Contempt Petitions (Civil) and Writ Petitions (Civil) concerning the implementation of the Majithia Wage Board Award for working journalists and non-journalist newspaper employees under the Working Journalists and Other Newspaper Employees (Conditions of Service) and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1955. The Court, while reiterating its judgment dated 07.02.2014 upholding the validity of the Majithia Wage Board recommendations, found that newspaper establishments' partial or non-implementation stemmed from a misunderstanding of the Award's scope, rather than wilful disobedience, thus not attracting civil contempt liability under Section 2(b) of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971. The Court clarified several contentious issues: (i) Clause 20(j) and Section 16 of the Act mean that wages notified under Section 12 supersede existing contracts, and while more favourable benefits can be agreed upon, an option to receive less than the notified wage, if involuntary, is to be resolved under Section 17 of the Act, applying the principle that minimum wages are non-negotiable as per Bijay Cotton Mills Ltd. and Ors. vs. State of Ajmer; (ii) the benefits of the Award are not restricted to regular employees but extend to contractual employees, based on the definitions under the Act; (iii) 'variable pay' is an integral part of the Award, intended to ensure equitable treatment; and (iv) 'heavy cash losses' as a ground for exemption from arrears must be distinct from mere financial difficulties and consistent over the stipulated period. Henceforth, all complaints regarding non-implementation are to be resolved through the mechanism provided under Section 17 of the Act. The writ petitions seeking interference with transfers/terminations were also disposed of, with directions that such service condition-related questions should be adjudicated by appropriate authorities under the Act or cognate laws like the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, rather than through Article 32 jurisdiction. title: THE STATE OF PUNJAB & ORS. v. BAKSHISH SINGH
text: The respondent, a police constable, was dismissed from service for unauthorized absence. The trial court set aside the dismissal, finding that the absence period was regularized as leave without pay and that the respondent was not given a proper opportunity of personal hearing, with his signatures obtained under duress. The lower appellate court confirmed that the charge of absence did not survive after regularization but remanded the case for reconsideration of punishment. The High Court summarily dismissed the appeal against this remand order. The Supreme Court, observing that the trial court's findings on regularization and lack of proper hearing were not set aside by the lower appellate court, held that the remand was unjustified. Citing Order XLI Rule 33 and Section 107 of the CPC, the Court asserted its power to pass orders for complete justice. Consequently, the Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the orders of the lower appellate court (remanding the case) and the High Court, and upheld the trial court's judgment and decree, thus reinstating the respondent. Citations: AIR 1998 SC 1895; AIR 1969 SC 1349 Legal tags: Dismissal from service; Unauthorized absence; Departmental enquiry; Regularization of absence; Leave without pay; Opportunity of personal hearing; Duress; Misconduct; Proportionality of punishment; Remand of case; Second appeal; Order XLI Rule 33 CPC; Section 107 CPC; Article 142 of the Constitution; Complete justice; Trial court judgment; Lower appellate court judgment; High Court judgment; Police constable; Punjab Police

title: THE PRAKASH COTTON MILLS (PRIVATE) LTD.  AND OTHERS v. THE STATE OF BOMBAY (NOW MAHARASHTRA)
text: The notification dated July 31, 1956, issued under section 114(2) of the Bombay Industrial Relations Act, 1946, directing the enforcement of an award for bonus payment against the appellant mill, was held to be beyond the powers conferred on the State Government by the said section. The Court found that the State Government's power under section 114(2) is limited by the subject-matter of the agreement or award, must conform to industrial law laid down by the Full Bench of the Industrial Court and Supreme Court decisions, and is co-terminus with the power of an adjudicator. Since the notification directed the enforcement of an agreement, which included a clause for minimum bonus payment even in cases of loss, and the appellant mill had not signed this agreement and had been making losses, the Court held that the State Government could not do what an adjudicator could not do, which was to enforce such an agreement against a non-consenting party in a loss-making scenario. Therefore, the notification was struck down. The Court clarified that this decision would not prejudice pending or future references regarding bonus payments. title: Shri Vimal Kishor Shah & Ors. v. Mr. Jayesh Dinesh Shah & Ors.
text: The Supreme Court allowed the Civil Appeal, thereby setting aside the final judgment and order of the High Court of Judicature at Bombay, which had allowed an arbitration application under Section 11 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, and appointed a sole Arbitrator. The Court held that a clause in a Trust Deed, providing for dispute resolution through arbitration, does not constitute an 'arbitration agreement' within the meaning of Sections 2(b) and 2(h) read with Section 7 of the Act. This is primarily because the beneficiaries, not being signatories to the Trust Deed, cannot be considered 'parties' to an arbitration agreement. The Court affirmed that a Trust Deed, much like a Will, is a unilateral document executed by the settlor, and mere acceptance of the Trust's terms by beneficiaries does not create an arbitration agreement among them. Furthermore, the Court ruled that disputes relating to Trust, trustees, and beneficiaries arising out of the Trust Deed and the Indian Trust Act, 1882, are not capable of being decided by an arbitrator. The Indian Trust Act, 1882, is deemed a complete and exhaustive code providing specific remedies and conferring jurisdiction on Civil Courts for such matters, thus creating an implied bar to the applicability of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act. The Court added 'cases arising out of Trust Deed and the Trust Act' as a seventh category to the list of non-arbitrable disputes established in Booz Allen & Hamilton Inc. v. SBI Home Finance Ltd. & Ors. Consequently, the application filed by the respondents under Section 11 of the Act was dismissed as not maintainable, with parties retaining the liberty to pursue other available legal remedies. Citations: 2010 (2) SCC 486; AIR 1965 Calcutta 628; (2011) 5 SCC 532; AIR 1969 SC 78; AIR 1975 SC 2238; (1970) 1 SCC 658 Legal tags: Civil Appeal; Supreme Court of India; Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996; Section 11; Arbitration Agreement; Trust Deed; Beneficiaries; Settlor; Trustees; Maintainability of Application; Indian Trust Act, 1882; Implied Bar of Jurisdiction; Non-arbitrable Disputes; Civil Court Jurisdiction; Contract Law; Definition of Party; Definition of Arbitration Agreement; Legal Interpretation; Judicial Precedent

title:
JAYA GOKUL EDUCATIONAL TRUST v. COMMNR. & SECY. GOVERNMENT HIGHER EDUCATION DEPTT. THIRUVANANTHAPURAM,
KERALA STATE AND ANR.
text: The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the judgment of the Division Bench of the High Court and upholding the reasoning of the learned Single Judge. The Court held that the AICTE Act, 1987, being a Central Act under Entry 66 of List I of the Constitution, occupies the field of granting approval for establishing technical institutions. Consequently, any State law or University statute requiring the ‘approval’ of the State Government for establishing such institutions would be repugnant to the AICTE Act and void to that extent, as established in State of Tamil Nadu & Another v. Adhiyaman Educational & Research Institute & Others. It was clarified that the Kerala University First Statute 9(7) merely required ascertaining the ‘views’ of the State Government for affiliation, which does not amount to ‘approval’. The State Government’s refusal to grant permission, based on its ‘policy’ against self-financing colleges or any other reasons mentioned in its counter-affidavit, was deemed illegal and void as there was no statutory power vested in the State for such approval, and even if there were, it would be overridden by the AICTE Act. The Court also held that the University’s decision not to grant final or further affiliation to the appellant without the State Government’s approval was erroneous, especially since the AICTE had already granted conditional approval after due consultation with relevant agencies including the State and University. The learned Single Judge’s order quashing the State Government’s letter dated 16.8.1996 and directing the Mahatama Gandhi University to consider the appellant’s application for final or continuance of affiliation on the basis of AICTE approval dated 30.4.1995, and other relevant factors not inconsistent with the AICTE Act or its Regulations, was confirmed. The appeal was allowed without an order as to costs. A separate Special Leave Petition filed by a petitioner not a party in the High Court was dismissed as premature. title: Jaswinder Singh v. State of Punjab
text: The appeal filed by the appellant, Jaswinder Singh, against his conviction by the trial court and affirmation by the High Court under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (IPC) and Section 307 IPC has been dismissed. The Supreme Court found the testimony of the sole eyewitness, Jasprit Singh (PW-1), to be convincing, reliable, and trustworthy, supported by medical evidence. The court rejected the appellant's contentions regarding his identification, noting that PW-1 had ample opportunity to observe the appellant during the incident, including opening the door, escorting the accused, and the appellant firing upon him, resulting in injuries. The court also dismissed the argument that the Test Identification Parade (TIP) was invalid, stating that PW-1's prior exposure to the appellant was permissible given the circumstances. Consequently, the appeal was dismissed. title: Pattu Rajan v. The State of Tamil Nadu
text: The Supreme Court dismissed the criminal appeals, affirming the judgment of the High Court of Judicature at Madras, which had convicted the accused-appellants for the abduction and murder of Santhakumar. The High Court had modified the Trial Court's conviction from Section 304 Part I IPC to Section 302 IPC, while retaining convictions under Sections 364 and 201 IPC. The Court rejected the argument that the FIR for murder was an impermissible second FIR, holding that the abduction and murder were distinct incidents with different intentions, thus justifying separate investigations. The prosecution's case, based entirely on circumstantial evidence, was found to be proven beyond reasonable doubt, with the chain of circumstances being complete. Key aspects affirmed include the establishment of motive (Accused No.1's desire to marry PW1), the 'last seen' circumstance (deceased with accused), recovery of the dead body based on Accused No.2's confession and identification by PW1, as well as corroborative evidence from post-mortem reports (homicidal death due to throttling) and forensic experts (superimposition test for identification, handwriting analysis, and petrol bill records). The absence of a DNA test was not deemed fatal given the other reliable evidence. The non-explanation by the accused regarding the 'last seen' circumstance under Section 313 Cr.P.C. was also considered an additional link in the chain of circumstances. The Court concluded that the evidence presented was overwhelming, consistent, cogent, and reliable, leading solely to the guilt of the accused. Citations: State of A.P. v. title: PAWAN KUMAR GUPTA v. STATE OF NCT OF DELHI
text: The Supreme Court of India dismissed the writ petition filed by Pawan Kumar Gupta challenging the rejection of his mercy petition by the President of India. The petitioner contended that his plea of juvenility was not finally determined and that he had been subjected to torture in prison. The Court found no merit in these contentions, noting that the plea of juvenility had been previously considered and rejected by the courts. The Court also held that alleged torture in prison could not be a ground for judicial review of the executive order rejecting the mercy petition. The Court referred to previous judgments in Epuru Sudhakar and Shatrughan Chauhan, reiterating that judicial review of the President's decision on mercy petitions is very limited and can only be exercised on specific grounds such as lack of application of mind, mala fide actions, consideration of extraneous factors, or exclusion of relevant materials. The Court concluded that it could not entertain the writ petition as there were no grounds warranting judicial review of the President's order. Citations: Article 32 of the Constitution of India; (2006) 8 SCC 161; (2014) 3 SCC 1; Mukesh Kumar v. Union of India Writ Petition (Crl.) No..40 of 2020 (29.01.2020); Vinay Kumar Sharma v. text: The Supreme Court held that the income received in British India cannot be said to wholly arise in India within the meaning of section 4A(c)(b) of the Income-tax Act, 1922. Therefore, there should be an allocation of the income between the various business operations of the assessee company, demarcating the income arising in the taxable territories in the particular year from the income arising without the taxable territories in that year for the purposes of section 4A(c)(b) of the Act. The Court allowed the appeal, stating that the answer to question No. 1 was in the negative and the answer to question No. 2 was as detailed above. Each party was to bear its own costs. title: KRISHNA MOCHI & ORS. v. STATE OF BIHAR
text: The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal and accepted the death reference, thereby confirming the death penalty awarded against the appellants, Krishna Mochi, Dharmendra Singh @ Dharu Singh, Nanhe Lal Mochi, and Bir Kuer Paswan @ Beer Kuer Dusadh. The appellants were convicted under Sections 302/149 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, and Section 3(1) of the Terrorist and Disruptive Activities (Prevention) Act, 1987, for their involvement in a gruesome carnage where 35 members of a particular community were massacred in Bihar. The Court, after reviewing the credible evidence from multiple witnesses for each appellant, found their participation in the crime to be unequivocally proven. The Court rejected arguments regarding the number of witnesses, non-disclosure in confessional statements, non-examination of the informant or investigating officer, absence of material recovery, and identification issues at night, emphasizing that the quality of evidence, not merely the quantity, is paramount. Applying the 'rarest of the rare' doctrine, the Court concluded that the crime, executed by a militant group (M.C.C.) through a conspiracy to annihilate a community, involving extreme brutality, tying victims, slitting throats, and causing 35 casualties, constituted extreme depravity, justifying the imposition of the death penalty as an 'exception' to life imprisonment. title: Vinay Shukla v. Union of India & Ors
text: The Supreme Court of India, comprising G.P. Mathur and Lokeshwar Singh Panta, in Writ Petition (Civil) No. 205 of 2006, dismissed the petition filed by Vinay Shukla under Article 32 of the Constitution. The petitioner, an IAS officer, had sought directions for proper investigation into allegations of abduction, harassment, illegal detention, and other serious criminal offences by high officials, punishment of wrongdoers under the Indian Penal Code, adequate compensation for illegal confinement and humiliation causing impairment of fundamental rights under Articles 14 and 21, and disciplinary action against erring officials of the Local Administration of District Gwalior. The Court observed that the alleged abduction and wrongful confinement occurred between September 21, 2006, and September 22, 2006, and the petitioner was not in any form of detention or unlawful restraint at the time the writ petition was filed. Consequently, the Court was not inclined to entertain the writ petition under Article 32 of the Constitution. Regarding the prayer for damages for illegal abduction and confinement, the Court held that such allegations are entirely factual in nature, requiring the recording of oral evidence for establishment. Therefore, the petitioner was granted liberty to seek appropriate legal remedies available in law for claiming such damages, and the writ petition was dismissed. title: BURMAH SHELL OIL STORAGE  &DISTRIBUTING CO.  INDIA LTD. v. THE BELGAUM BOROUGH MUNICIPALITY
text: The Supreme Court held that the company was liable to pay octroi tax on goods brought into the local area for consumption by itself or for sale to consumers directly, or for sale to dealers who subsequently sold the goods to consumers within the municipal area, irrespective of whether those consumers used the goods within or outside the municipal area. The company was not liable for octroi on goods that were brought into the local area and subsequently re-exported. The Court also noted that the term "consumption" can have a wider meaning in legal contexts, not necessarily implying complete destruction or usage of the commodity. The Court clarified the distinction between octroi and terminal tax, stating that octrois are leviable on goods brought into a municipal area for consumption, use, or sale, while terminal taxes are connected with the traffic of goods, whether imported or exported. The Court dismissed the appeal. Citations: 1963 AIR 906; 1963 SCR Supl. title: STATE OF GUJARAT ETC. v. VAKHTSINGHJI SURSINGHJI VAGHELA & ORS. ETC.
text: The taluqdari estates were liable to payment of jama, which was generally 60% of the survey assessment as a concession. However, taluqdars had no legal right to claim this concession upon expiry of their current settlements, and the government had the right to withdraw it at the next revisional settlement. The enhanced assessment did not affect any contractual or statutory right, nor did it amount to transference to public ownership. Thus, the claim for compensation for the difference between the jama and full assessment was rightly rejected by the Collector, Revenue Tribunal, and High Court. Regarding solatium, taluqdars are entitled to a 15% solatium on the market value of their extinguished rights under Section 7(1)(b) read with Section 11 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, subject to conditions in sub-clauses (i), (ii), and (iii) of Section 7(1)(b). The High Court's ruling on solatium was modified to reflect this. For irrigational bunds, tanks, and wells, compensation should be based on market value derived from income, not reinstatement value, as the latter is only applicable if bona fide reinstatement is intended. The High Court correctly rejected the reinstatement method and adopted the yield basis, directing further inquiries for accurate yield assessment. Regarding river and river beds, taluqdars had no property in running water, and submerged river beds were valueless. They could claim compensation only for 'Bhathas' (cultivable areas) formed in the river beds. The High Court's broader ruling on river beds was set aside, and a direction was issued for the Special Deputy Collector to inquire into claims for 'Bhathas'. The High Court's jurisdiction under Article 227 of the Constitution to superintend subordinate tribunals and ensure they obey the law was affirmed, allowing it to revise decisions where tribunals misread provisions. Citations: 1968 AIR 1481; 1968 SCR (3) 692 Legal tags: Bombay Taluqdari Abolition Act, 1949; Section 7; Section 14; Compensation; Jama; Land Revenue; Concession; Revisional Settlement; Solatium; Market Value; Land Acquisition Act, 1894; Section 11; Section 23; Section 24; Irrigation bunds; Tanks; Wells; Reinstatement Value; Yield Basis; River beds; Bhathas; Constitution of India; Article 227; High Court's power of superintendence; Revenue Tribunal; Collector's award; Agrarian Reform; Taluqdari Tenure; Extinguishment of rights; Transference to public ownership; Gujarat Taluqdars' Act, 1888

title: AVISHEK RAJA & ORS. v. SANJAY GUPTA
text:
The Supreme Court disposed of numerous contempt petitions and writ petitions, clarifying the implementation of the Majithia Wage Board Award. While acknowledging the non-implementation or partial implementation of the Award by various newspaper establishments, the Court found that such defaults stemmed from a 'wrong understanding' of the Award, rather than wilful disobedience, thus not attracting civil contempt liability under Section 2(b) of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971. However, the Court unequivocally directed that the Majithia Wage Board Award, having been upheld by its judgment dated 07.02.2014, must be implemented in full, granting establishments one more opportunity to comply. The Court clarified key ambiguities:
1.  **Clause 20(j) and Section 16:** Wages notified under Section 12 of the Working Journalists and Other Newspaper Employees (Conditions of Service) and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1955 (the Act) supersede all existing contracts. An employee cannot agree to terms less favourable than those in the Award; such undertakings, if alleged to be involuntary, raise a dispute to be resolved under Section 17 of the Act, aligning with the non-negotiability principle of minimum wages as laid down in *Bijay Cotton Mills Ltd. and Ors. vs. State of Ajmer*.
2.  **Applicability to Contractual Employees:** The benefits of the Award are not restricted to regular employees but extend to all 'newspaper employees' as defined in the Act, including contractual employees.
3.  **Variable Pay:** The 'variable pay' recommended by the Majithia Wage Board must be included for the purpose of calculating other allowances, as it was incorporated to ensure equitable treatment for employees.
4.  **Heavy Cash Losses:** Exemption from payment of arrears due to 'heavy cash losses' under Clause 21 of the Award must signify crippling and consistent losses over the three preceding accounting years, distinct from mere financial difficulties, and this is a question of fact to be determined case by case.
Henceforth, all complaints regarding non-implementation of the Majithia Wage Board Award shall be dealt with through the mechanism provided under Section 17 of the Act. The writ petitions concerning transfer/termination, being matters related to service conditions, are to be adjudicated by appropriate authorities under the Act or cognate laws like the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, rather than through the Supreme Court's writ jurisdiction under Article 32 of the Constitution. Citations: WP (C) NO.246 OF 2011; CONTEMPT PETITION (CIVIL) NO. 411 OF 2014; WP (C) NO.264 OF 2012; WP (C) NO.510 OF 2011; WP (C) NO.998 OF 2016; WP (C) NO.148 OF 2017; WP (C) NO.299 OF 2017 Legal tags: Contempt Petition; Writ Petition; Majithia Wage Board Award; Working Journalists and Other Newspaper Employees (Conditions of Service) and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1955; Wage Fixation; Wage Revision; Newspaper Employees; Working Journalists; Non-Journalist Employees; Section 12 of the Act; Section 16 of the Act; Section 17 of the Act; Civil Contempt; Wilful Disobedience; Statutory Compliance; Employee Wages; Allowances; Contractual Employees; Variable Pay; Arrears Payment; Financial Constraints; Heavy Cash Losses; Minimum Wages Principle; Article 32 of the Constitution; Industrial Disputes Act, 1947; Labour Law; Service Conditions; Transfer of Employees; Termination of Employment; Judicial Interpretation; Supreme Court of India

title: VINODAN T. & ORS. v. UNIVERSITY OF CALICUT & ORS.
text: The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals, thereby affirming the cancellation of the 1995 rank list prepared by the University of Calicut for Assistant Grade-II posts and rejecting the appellants' prayer for regularisation of their services. The Court held that persons merely selected for a post do not acquire an absolute right to be appointed, and an appointing authority can scrap a panel of selected candidates for well-founded reasons. The reasons cited by the University for cancelling the rank list, namely, the statutory ban on appointment of non-teaching staff for three years under the Pre-Degree Course (Abolition) Ordinance, 1997 (later Act 3 of 1998), and the creation of Kannur University leading to surplus staff, were deemed sufficient, just, and non-arbitrary. The Court distinguished the appellants' claim for regularisation from the principles laid down in *State of Haryana v. Piara Singh*, noting the existence of a complete statutory ban on appointments during the relevant period, the provisional nature of their daily wage appointments made pursuant to interim court orders, the absence of any University scheme for regularisation, and the potential violation of merit order and reservation rules if regularisation were granted. Consequently, the appellants could not obstruct the appointment of candidates from the subsequent 2001 selection process. The interim order was vacated without any order as to costs. title: BABY SAKSHI GREOLA v. MANZOOR AHMAD SIMON AND ANOTHER
text: The Supreme Court, hearing a Civil Appeal arising from SLP(C) No.10996 of 2018, quashed and set aside the High Court of Delhi's judgment dated 7th November 2017 in MAC. APP. 1107/2011, thereby allowing the appellant's appeal for enhancement of compensation. The Motor Accident Claims Tribunal had initially awarded Rs. 5,90,750/- with 7.5% interest, which the High Court enhanced to Rs. 11,51,000/- with 9% interest. The Supreme Court, upon detailed consideration of the grievous injuries (75% disability, treated as 100% for practical purposes due to moderate mental retardation, severe apathy, and urinary incontinence) suffered by the appellant in a motor vehicle accident, significantly enhanced the compensation. The Court revised the compensation under various heads: Loss of Earning Capacity due to Disability was enhanced to Rs. 13,18,000/- (considering minimum wages of a skilled workman with 40% addition for future prospects and a multiplier of 18); Pain and Suffering was increased to Rs. 15,00,000/-; Future Treatment was enhanced to Rs. 5,00,000/-; Attendant Charges were increased to Rs. 9,42,000/- (for a full-time skilled attendant); and Loss of Marriage Prospects was enhanced to Rs. 5,00,000/-. Other heads such as Medicines and Medical Treatment, Loss of Amenities of Life, Loss of Future Prospect, Special Education Expenditure, and Conveyance and Special Diet remained at Rs. 32,000/-, Rs. 1,00,000/-, Rs. 1,00,000/-, Rs. 75,000/-, and Rs. 20,000/- respectively. The total revised compensation awarded by the Supreme Court is Rs. 50,87,000/-. The interest rate of 9% per annum from the date of filing the claim petition till realization, as decided by the High Court, was maintained. The Insurance Company (Respondent No. 2) was directed to disburse the compensation within eight weeks, adjusting any amount already paid, while the inter-se liability between the driver-cum-owner and the insurance company is to be decided in accordance with law. Recognizing the appellant was a minor at the time of the accident, the Court directed Rs. 10,00,000/- to be disbursed to the father as guardian, and the rest of the amount to be invested in long-term Fixed Deposit Receipts to attract maximum interest, with monthly interest payments to the guardian. title: Union of India & others etc. v. Bombay India International Ltd. etc.
text: This case relates to valuation under the Excise Law. The key issues involved are (1) whether the activity of 'repacking' amounts to 'manufacture', and if so, what is the assessable value of the bulk packs cleared by the appellants? (2) whether there was suppression on the part of the appellants, and if so, how does it affect the valuation? (3) whether the amendment introduced vide Finance Bill, 1994 has any bearing on the assessment. The Commissioner found that IED, Kanpur was an extended arm of the appellants and that the activity of 'repacking' did amount to manufacture at the relevant time. He also found suppression on the part of the appellants in manipulating the price of the goods. However, when the matter came before the Tribunal, it failed to address these issues and remitted the matter for fresh decision. The Supreme Court has now allowed the civil appeal filed by the assessees and set aside the impugned judgment of the Tribunal. It has also directed the Tribunal to pass a fresh order in accordance with the principles enunciated by the Supreme Court. Citations: 1984 (2) RCR 103 Legal tags: valuation; excise law; manufacture; suppression; amendment; Finance Bill, 1994

title: T.C. MATHAI & ANR. v. THE DISTRICT & SESSIONS JUDGE, THIRUVANANTHAPURAM, KERALA.
text: The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, affirming the decisions of the Sessions Court and the High Court which had denied permission to the appellant, a power of attorney holder, to appear and plead on behalf of the respondent-couple in a criminal revision petition. The Court held that while Section 303 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (CrPC) entitles a person to be defended by a pleader, and Section 2(q) of the CrPC defines 'pleader' to include a person authorised by law to practise or any other person appointed with court permission, a power of attorney holder who is not an enrolled advocate cannot automatically become a pleader. Permission from the court is a condition precedent for a non-advocate to act as a pleader, and such permission must be sought by the party itself. Section 2 of the Power of Attorney Act, 1882, cannot override specific statutory provisions like those in the CrPC, which require particular acts to be done by a party in person or through a duly appointed pleader. While personal attendance of an accused can be dispensed with under Section 205 CrPC and they can appear through a pleader, appearance cannot be made through a power of attorney holder who is not a qualified pleader appointed with the court's permission. In the present case, the respondent-couple had not even moved for such permission. The Court emphasized that court work is a serious function requiring proper assistance from legally qualified persons or those explicitly permitted by the court, after due verification of their capability, to ensure the administration of justice. The appellant's contention based on the power of attorney instrument was deemed of no avail. title: Y.P. Sarabhai v. Union Bank of India & Anr.
text: The Supreme Court of India dismisses the appeal filed by Y.P. Sarabhai, a former security officer of Union Bank of India, against his dismissal from service in 1998 for alleged misconduct. The court upholds the findings of the Disciplinary Authority, Appellate Authority, and High Court that Sarabhai's absence from duty was due to his reluctance to carry out his transfer order to Chennai, and not due to genuine illness. The court notes that Sarabhai had initially represented that he was ill, but later produced a different medical certificate, and also failed to attend court proceedings on several occasions. The court holds that the dismissal of Sarabhai from service was justified and that he is not entitled to any relief. However, considering the peculiar facts and circumstances of the case, the court directs the Bank to pay a sum of Rs.1,50,000/- as a full and final settlement of all claims between both parties. title: Sri Nilanjan Bhattacharya v. The State of Karnataka and Others
text: The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the conditions imposed by the High Court regarding repatriation of the child. The conditions (a) and (b) of paragraph 18 of the High Court's order, which required certificates from Indian and US health authorities concerning the COVID-19 pandemic, were deemed unenforceable and set aside. The Court accepted the appellant's undertaking to comply with all prevailing regulations for international travel. The Court affirmed the High Court's direction to allow the appellant to take the child to the US, considering it to be in the child's best interest, given the child was born and raised in the US and the appellant's active involvement in the child's upbringing. The Court established arrangements for the child's communication and visitation with the mother, including video conferencing, annual visits to the US at the appellant's expense, and annual visits to India. These arrangements are to remain in place until modified by a competent court regarding custody. title: State of Gujarat & Ors. v. Mirzapur Moti Kureshi Kassab Jamat & Ors.
text: The Supreme Court, in this judgment, has set aside the Gujarat High Court's decision and upheld the constitutional validity of the Bombay Animal Preservation (Gujarat Amendment) Act, 1994. The Court found that the ban on the slaughter of cow progeny, including bulls and bullocks, is a reasonable restriction in the interest of the general public and aligns with the Directive Principles of State Policy, specifically Article 48, which aims to organize agriculture and animal husbandry and prohibit the slaughter of cows and calves and other milch and draught cattle. The Court also considered the amended Articles 48-A and 51-A(g) concerning environmental protection and compassion for living creatures. The Court re-evaluated the earlier judgment in Mohd. Hanif Quareshi v. State of Bihar, finding that the factual and societal conditions have changed significantly since 1958. The Court emphasized the crucial role of cow progeny in India's agrarian economy, their continued utility for agricultural operations, as a source of organic manure and biogas, and their value even after ceasing to be 'milch' or 'draught' animals. The Court concluded that the ban does not amount to an unreasonable restriction on the fundamental right to practice a trade or business under Article 19(1)(g) and that the ban serves a larger public interest, thus holding the Act to be intra vires the Constitution. title: DAULAT RAM v. SAROOP RAM & ANR.
text: The Supreme Court of India dismisses the appeal by special leave, holding that the appellant (Daulat Ram) has not proved that he alone redeemed the mortgage and is in continuous possession of the suit land. The court relies on documentary evidence showing that all three brothers (Sarup Ram, Daulat Ram, and Room Singh) jointly redeemed the property, making it a joint property of the brothers. As such, the appellant can no longer claim to be a mortgagee. The appeal is dismissed without costs. title: Godrej & Boyce Mfg. Co. Ltd. & Anr. v. The State of Maharashtra & Ors.
text: The Supreme Court allowed the appeals, setting aside the Bombay High Court's order. The court held that the mere issuance of a notice under Section 35(3) of the Indian Forest Act, 1927, is not sufficient for land to be declared a 'private forest' under the Maharashtra Private Forests (Acquisition) Act, 1975, unless the notice was served and acted upon within a reasonable time. The court emphasized that a literal interpretation of 'issued' in Section 2(f)(iii) of the Maharashtra Private Forests (Acquisition) Act, 1975, is not appropriate; rather, it requires a broader interpretation considering the context and the scheme of Section 35 of the Indian Forest Act, 1927, which includes the necessity of service and opportunity for the owner to show cause. Given the decades-long inaction by the state and the subsequent developments including construction and permissions granted by various authorities, the court found it unreasonable and unfair to declare the lands as private forests. The court also held that if substantial constructions have been made over a long period with the state's tacit or explicit approval, demolition may not be a practical or just remedy. The court quashed the stop-work notices and related mutations in revenue records. title: HARI RAM & ORS. v. STATE OF RAJASTHAN
text: The Supreme Court upheld the Rajasthan High Court's decision, which overturned the acquittal by the District & Sessions Judge, Bikaner. The High Court convicted the appellants (Hari Ram & Ors.) under Section 302/34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced them to life imprisonment. The Supreme Court found that the Sessions Judge's reasoning for discarding the testimony of key eye-witnesses (PWs 6 and 7) was perverse and based on conjecture. The Supreme Court re-appreciated the evidence and agreed with the High Court's conclusion that the testimony of PWs 6 and 7 was trustworthy and corroborated by medical evidence (26 ante-mortem injuries). The appeal was consequently dismissed. title: Alok Kumar Singh & Others v. State of U.P. & Others
text: The Supreme Court of India has decided a batch of appeals concerning the recruitment process for 4010 posts of Sub-Inspectors and Platoon Commanders in Uttar Pradesh. The Court addressed challenges related to the use of whitener/blade in examinations, the carry-forward of vacancies, and the 'rounding of percentage' for marks.  The Court upheld the High Court's decision in negating the submission regarding the interpretation of 'such vacancies shall be carried forward for further selection' in Rule 15(j). However, considering the complexities and the significant number of vacancies (607) arising from candidates discontinuing training or failing medical/character verification, the Court directed that these vacancies be offered within the current selection process, prioritizing merit and adherence to the 50% mark criteria. Similarly, 226 posts earmarked for dependents of freedom fighters, which could not be filled due to non-availability, were also directed to be made available in the present selection, noting that future selections would accommodate such reserved categories. Consequently, a total of 833 posts (607 + 226) were to be filled in the present selection, strictly based on merit, reservation principles, and preference, in addition to any other directions previously issued. Matters concerning promotion from Constable to Sub-Inspector were segregated and directed to be listed before the appropriate Bench. All appeals, writ petitions, and transferred cases were disposed of accordingly, with no order as to costs. title: ANZ Grindlays Bank Ltd @ Standard Chartered Grindlays Bank Ltd v. Union of India and others
text: The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the judgments and orders of the learned single Judge dated 29.2.2000 and the Division Bench of the High Court dated 19.6.2000. Consequently, the reference made by the Central Government to the Industrial Tribunal on 29.12.1997 was quashed. The Court held that the bipartite settlement dated 18.8.1996, entered into between ANZ Grindlays Bank Limited and the All India Grindlays Bank Employees Association, was an agreement under Section 18(1) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, and thus binding only upon the parties to the agreement. As the All India Grindlays Bank Employees Federation (second respondent) was not a party to this settlement, its rights were not affected, and the settlement was not binding upon it. The Bank's action of requiring a receipt from non-member employees desiring to avail benefits was deemed perfectly justified to protect its interests. The Court concluded that no 'industrial dispute' within the meaning of Section 2(k) of the Act existed or was apprehended between the appellant-Bank and the Federation, making the Central Government's reference under Section 10(1) of the Act wholly redundant, uncalled for, and futile. It was further noted that the settlement had already worked itself out and was superseded by a fresh settlement, rendering any potential award ineffective and causing severe injury to the Bank. The Court affirmed that a High Court has jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution to entertain a writ petition against an order of reference if no industrial dispute exists, as it pertains to the Industrial Tribunal's jurisdiction and can be demonstrated from a bare reading of the terms without further evidence. title: National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Kaushalaya Devi & Ors.
text: The Supreme Court, upholding the High Court's decision, ruled that the owner of the truck alone was liable to pay compensation for the death of Kishan Lal. This determination was based on two primary findings: firstly, that the driver of the truck did not possess a valid and effective driving licence for a heavy goods vehicle at the time of the accident, as the endorsement for such a vehicle was found to be ante-dated; and secondly, that the deceased was traveling as an unauthorized/gratuitous passenger in a goods carriage, specifically for collecting empty vegetable boxes, which does not fall under the purview of statutory insurance coverage for passengers in goods vehicles as per the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988. Citing precedents including *National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Swaran Singh & Ors.*, *National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Laxmi Narain Dhut*, and *New India Assurance Co. Ltd. v. Asha Rani & Ors.*, the Court reiterated that the insurer is not statutorily liable for passengers in goods vehicles and that such breaches are not inconsequential deviations. Consequently, the Civil Appeal filed by the National Insurance Co. Ltd. was allowed, and the Civil Appeal filed by the owner of the vehicle was dismissed. The insurance company was granted liberty to recover any compensation amount already disbursed to the claimant from the owner, or if not yet withdrawn, to have the deposited amount refunded and initiate recovery proceedings against the owner. title: Syndicate Bank v. New Look Rubbers (P) Ltd & Ors
text: The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the High Court's order in the Civil Revision. The Court held that the High Court had overstepped its jurisdiction by virtually setting aside earlier civil court orders that had attained finality. The original suit by Syndicate Bank for loan recovery was decreed, and subsequent attempts by the respondent to injunct execution or claim damages were dismissed and had attained finality. The Court acknowledged that while the revival of the respondent's unit is a matter for the government and other agencies, it cannot affect the legal rights accrued to the appellant Bank due to the final court orders. The appeal was allowed, setting aside the High Court's order concerning the Civil Revision, with a rider that any succor provided by the government to the respondent would not affect the appellant Bank's rights. title: RAM KISHAN v. STATE OF RAJASTHAN & ORS.
text: The Supreme Court has set aside the Order dated 23.01.2015 passed by the Rajasthan High Court, which had quashed FIR No. 217 of 2006 registered by the appellant, a Police Constable, under Sections 332 and 353 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) against respondent No. 3. The High Court's decision was deemed erroneous as it substituted its own opinion by concluding that FIR No. 217 was a 'counter blast' despite being registered earlier than FIR No. 218 and the matter still being under investigation. Furthermore, the High Court failed to consider the appellant's Injury Report dated 22.07.2006 and the submissions made on his behalf. The Supreme Court directed the police to conduct a complete and proper investigation relating to FIR No. 217 of 2006 and submit a report under Section 173 of the Criminal Procedure Code (Cr.P.C.) expeditiously, given that the matter has been pending for approximately a decade and a half. The appeal has been allowed.
