title: The Appellant v. Hanuman
text: The Supreme Court of India has ruled in favor of the company, upholding the automatic termination of an employee's service under a specific standing order. The court held that the standing order clearly states that a workman's lien on their appointment will stand terminated if they do not join duty within 8 days of the expiry of their leave. The court rejected the argument that this provision is different from losing one's appointment, as once a workman loses their lien on their appointment, they lose their appointment. title: CHHOTE LAL v. STATE OF M.P.
text: The appellant, Chhote Lal, convicted under Sections 376(2) and 302 of the Indian Penal Code for rape and murder of a 10-year-old girl, had his sentence of life imprisonment confirmed by the High Court. While this Court found no reason to interfere with the conviction based on the evidence, it modified the sentencing aspect in light of the judgment in Mulla v. State of U.P. The Court held that while it is open for the sentencing court to prescribe the length of incarceration, including life imprisonment, this is subject to the government's power to grant remissions. Accordingly, the appeal was dismissed, but the appellant is to serve the sentence of imprisonment for life, subject to any remissions the Government may grant. The State Government is also directed to decide on the appellant's continued detention or release within six months, considering he has been in custody since January 10, 1989. The fee for the Amicus was fixed at Rs. 7,000/-. Citations: Mulla v. State of U.P. title: ADDITIONAL DISTRICT MAGISTRATE(CITY) AGRA v. PRABHAKAR CHATURVEDI & ANR.
text: The Supreme Court of India allowed the appeal filed by the Additional District Magistrate (City), Agra, setting aside the order of the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad. The High Court had quashed the dismissal order of respondent No.1, Prabhakar Chaturvedi, and directed his reinstatement with full back wages, citing inadequate opportunity to defend (non-examination of witnesses and non-supply of documents). The Supreme Court held that the High Court's order was unsustainable. It was observed that the contention regarding non-supply of the Enquiry Officer's report was not raised in the writ petition. Furthermore, regarding the non-examination of witnesses and non-supply of documents, the High Court erred in overlooking respondent No.1's written admission dated 14th December 1984, acknowledging receipt of the misappropriated amount of Rs. 21,094.80 and his failure to deposit it due to carelessness. The Enquiry Officer's record clearly showed that respondent No.1 had stated he had no documentary or oral evidence, and his subsequent request to examine witnesses was rightly rejected as an afterthought. The Supreme Court concluded that the charge of misappropriation stood proved on admission, and the punishment of dismissal from service for such misconduct was neither uncalled for nor grossly disproportionate. Consequently, the High Court's order was quashed, and the writ petition filed in the High Court stands dismissed. title: Brij Lal & Ors. v. Commissioner of Income Tax, Jalandhar
text: The Supreme Court, in this Constitution Bench judgment, addressed three pivotal questions concerning the Income Tax Act, 1961 (for short "the Act"), particularly Chapter XIX-A relating to Settlement of Cases. Firstly, it was held that Sections 234A, 234B, and 234C of the Act are indeed applicable to the proceedings of the Settlement Commission under Chapter XIX-A, to the extent indicated within the judgment. The Court noted that Chapter XIX-A, while a self-contained code, incorporates mechanisms for the computation of total income, akin to assessment, thereby engrafting provisions related to regular assessment, self-assessment, and the levy/computation of interest into its special procedure under Sections 245C and 245D. Secondly, regarding the terminal point for the levy of interest under Section 234B, the Court concluded that such interest is payable up to the date of the order passed under Section 245D(1) (when the Settlement Commission allows the application to be proceeded with), and not up to the date of the final Order of Settlement under Section 245D(4). This distinction arises from the scheme of pre-assessment collection of tax and the legislative intent to not extend interest liability beyond the admission stage of the settlement application. Thirdly, the Court ruled that the Settlement Commission cannot re-open its concluded proceedings by invoking Section 154 of the Act to levy interest under Section 234B. This decision is primarily grounded in Section 245I, which declares every order of settlement passed under Section 245D(4) to be final and conclusive, with the only exceptions being fraud and misrepresentation. The nature of settlement proceedings is distinct from regular assessment proceedings, and the power of rectification under Section 154 is not conferred upon the Settlement Commission within Chapter XIX-A. title: 6975 /2019 v. 317/2008
text: माननीय उच्चतम न्यायालय ने सिविल अपील संख्या 6975/2019 (विशेष अनुमति याचिका (सी) संख्या 12783/2015 से उत्पन्न) में राजस्थान उच्च न्यायालय द्वारा दिनांक 12.01.2015 को पारित निर्णय और आदेश को रद्द कर दिया, जो एस.बी. सिविल द्वितीय अपील संख्या 317/2008 में था। उच्च न्यायालय ने गलत रूप से यह माना था कि राजस्थान सिंचाई और जल निकासी अधिनियम, 1954 के तहत जल वितरण से संबंधित विवादों का निर्णय करने का अधिकार सिविल न्यायालय के पास नहीं है, विशेषकर अधिनियम की धारा 53 की गलत व्याख्या करते हुए। उच्चतम न्यायालय ने स्पष्ट किया कि यद्यपि प्रारंभिक विवादों को संभागीय सिंचाई अधिकारी के पास संदर्भित किया जाना चाहिए, सिविल न्यायालयों के पास ऐसे विवादों का निर्णय करने और अधिकारियों द्वारा पारित आदेशों को रद्द करने का अधिकार क्षेत्र है, जिसमें एकमात्र प्रतिबंध यह है कि सिविल न्यायालय आदेश पारित करते समय बोई गई या खेती की गई फसलों के संबंध में कोई आदेश नहीं दे सकता। परिणामस्वरूप, मामले को गुण-दोष के आधार पर निर्णय के लिए उच्च न्यायालय को वापस भेज दिया गया है, साथ ही यह निर्देश भी दिया गया है कि द्वितीय अपील को वर्ष 2008 में दायर माना जाए और प्राथमिकता के आधार पर इसका निपटारा किया जाए। सिविल अपील स्वीकृत की जाती है और सभी लंबित आवेदन निस्तारित किए जाते हैं। Citations: 53; 53 (2) Legal tags: सिविल अपील; उच्चतम न्यायालय; राजस्थान उच्च न्यायालय; राजस्थान सिंचाई और जल निकासी अधिनियम, 1954; धारा 53; सिविल न्यायालय का क्षेत्राधिकार; जल विवाद; अपीलीय प्राधिकारी; उच्च न्यायालय को पुनर्प्रेषित; प्राथमिकता के आधार पर निपटारा; सांविधिक व्याख्या; कृषि जल उपयोग

title: P. Liaquat Ali Khan v. State of Andhra Pradesh
text: The Supreme Court of India, in Criminal Appeal No. 665 of 2006, dismissed the appeal filed by P. Liaquat Ali Khan, challenging the judgment of the Andhra Pradesh High Court. The High Court had upheld the conviction of the appellant by the learned IV Additional Sessions Judge, Kurnool, for an offence punishable under Section 364-A of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, and sentenced him to undergo imprisonment for life. The appellant's primary contention was that the contents of Exh.P2 and P3 (ransom letters) were not proven to have been written by him, thus arguing the inapplicability of Section 364-A IPC on the grounds that kidnapping for ransom is relatable only to cases where the intention was to cause death or hurt, not to a case of this nature. However, the Supreme Court noted that the leave to appeal was restricted to the nature of the offence only. The Court, after examining Section 364-A IPC, which deals with a separate type of offence where ransom is a distinguishing feature, concluded that the demand for ransom was clearly established. The role played by the accused had been thoroughly analyzed by both the trial Court and the High Court. Finding no infirmity in the present appeal that would warrant interference, the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, thereby affirming the conviction and sentence under Section 364-A IPC. title: Public Service Commission v. Amita Puri & Ors.
text: The Public Service Commission has issued a notification for selecting candidates for the post of Assistant Commercial Taxes Officer (ACTO). The notification stated that preference will be given to candidates who possess a degree in Commerce and Law, followed by those with a degree in Commerce only. However, the A.P. Labour Officers Subordinate Service Rules, 1985, which are applicable to the post of ACTO, state that preference shall be given to those who possess a degree in Law, subject to other things being equal. However, the High Court and the Tribunal held that the new rules were applicable and the respondents should be given preference as per those rules. title: U.P. State Road Transport Corporation v. Ramesh Chandra
text: In Civil Appeal No. 2837 of 2008, arising out of S.L.P.(C)No.13005 of 2006, the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India, after condoning the delay and granting leave, partly allowed the appeal filed by U.P. State Road Transport Corporation. The appeal challenged the High Court's order, which had directed the reinstatement of the respondent, Ramesh Chandra, a conductor, with 50% back wages. The respondent's service had been terminated following a domestic enquiry that found him guilty of charges including non-deposit of collected amounts from ticket sales, unauthorized absence, and being found in an inebriated state while on duty. The Labour Court had initially upheld the termination. The High Court, in a writ petition, had held that the punishment of dismissal from service was not commensurate with the charges levelled, thus ordering reinstatement with 50% back wages. While upholding the High Court's order insofar as the reinstatement of the respondent is concerned, the Supreme Court deemed it appropriate to set aside the impugned order regarding the award of 50% back wages. The appeal was thus partly allowed, with no costs. title: Triloki Nath & Ors. v. State of U.P.
text: The Supreme Court upheld the conviction of Jitendra for murder under Section 302/34 IPC, maintaining his sentence. The conviction of other appellants was altered from Section 302/149 IPC to Section 326/149 IPC, with a sentence of seven years' rigorous imprisonment and a fine. Triloki Nath's appeal was dismissed as abated due to his death. The court found that the appellants were the aggressors and not entitled to the right of private defence, as the incident occurred away from the disputed land and they were armed. The common object was to cause grievous hurt to the complainant party, and the shooting of Nanhe was a result of a specific exhortation by Triloki to Jitendra, establishing common intention for murder between them. title: The Appellants v. The State of Bihar
text: The Supreme Court of India upheld the conviction and sentence imposed on four appellants for their role in the murder of three brothers. The court found that the number of persons who constituted the unlawful assembly was more than five, and therefore Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) could be applied. The court also held that the common intention of all the accused had been established, and therefore Section 34 of the IPC could be applied to make each of them liable for the murder. The court rejected the appellants' argument that they could not be convicted under Section 34 because some acquitted persons might have given the fatal blows. The court found that the acquittal was good for all purposes and could not be used to argue against the conviction of the appellants. title: GURDEV SINGH v. STATE OF PUNJAB
text: The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the conviction and sentence of 15 years rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 2 Lakhs (with default sentence of one year RI) against the appellant for an offense under Section 21 of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985. The Court held that while Section 32B of the Act outlines factors for imposing a punishment higher than the minimum, courts have discretion to consider other relevant factors, including the quantity of the substance involved. In this case, the possession of 1 kg of heroin, four times the commercial quantity, was deemed a sufficient aggravating factor to justify the sentence higher than the minimum of 10 years, even considering the appellant's claims of being a poor carrier and first-time offender. The Court emphasized the deleterious impact of drug trafficking on society and that public interest weighs in favor of suitable higher punishment in such cases. Citations: CRA-DB No.311 of 2018; (2019) 6 SCC 492; (2013) 11 SCC 382; (2015) 8 SCC 39 Legal tags: Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985; Section 21; Section 32B; Conviction; Sentence; Rigorous Imprisonment; Fine; Commercial Quantity; Mitigating Circumstances; Aggravating Circumstances; Public Interest; Drug Trafficking; Societal Impact; Criminal Appeal; Supreme Court of India; Article 21

title: H.P. Pyarejan v. Dasappa(dead) by L.Rs. & Ors.
text: The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, thereby setting aside the judgment rendered by a learned Single Judge of the Karnataka High Court, which had allowed the plaintiff's second appeal for specific performance. The High Court's decision was found to suffer from serious infirmities, as it had interfered with concurrent findings of fact recorded by the Trial Court and the First Appellate Court. Both lower courts had dismissed the plaintiff's suit for specific performance on the ground that the plaintiff failed to aver and prove continuous readiness and willingness to perform his part of the contract, a mandatory requirement under Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963. The Supreme Court reiterated that Section 16(c) demands both pleading and proof of readiness and willingness, and that the High Court's action of upsetting these findings, particularly on a mixed question of law and fact, without even formulating a question of law or providing reasons for reversing the lower courts' conclusions, amounted to an impermissible exercise of jurisdiction under Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, which confines High Court's interference to substantial questions of law and does not warrant re-appreciation of evidence. Citations: AIR 1928 PC 208; AIR 1968 SC 1355; 1999 (6) SCC 337; 2000 (6) SCC 420; 1969 (2) SCC 539; 1989 (4) SCC 313; 1970 (3) SCC 140; 2005 (7) SCC 534; 1997 (4) SCC 713; 1997 (5) SCC 438 Legal tags: Specific Relief Act, 1963; Section 16(c) Specific Relief Act; Readiness and Willingness; Proof of Readiness and Willingness; Pleading Requirements; Specific Performance of Contract; Code of Civil Procedure, 1908; Section 100 CPC; Second Appeal; Jurisdiction of High Court; Interference with Findings of Fact; Mixed Question of Law and Fact; Agreement of Sale; Trial Court Findings; First Appellate Court Findings; Supreme Court of India; Karnataka High Court; Personal Bar to Relief

title: Chaturbhuja Modi & Ors. v. State of Orissa & Anr.
text: The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal against the High Court's judgment, which had enhanced compensation for acquired land to Rs. 3,00,000/- per acre. The Court found that while Exhibit 1 (a sale deed dated 04.10.1982 for a small plot) was the most reliable evidence, due allowance must be made for the fact that the acquired land was a large tract. The Court referred to the precedent in Administrator General of West Bengal v. Collector, Varanasi, emphasizing that valuation based on small plots requires appropriate deductions for internal development and amenities. The High Court's determination of Rs. 3,00,000/- per acre, after considering these factors, was deemed just and proper. Therefore, the appeal was dismissed without costs. title: Haryana Urban Development Authority v. Dr. Ashok Kumar Aggarwal
text: The appeal is allowed and the order of the National Commission is set aside. The Haryana Urban Development Authority (HUDA) shall pay to the Respondent Dr. Ashok Kumar Aggarwal within one month from the date of this Order, the amount deducted as TDS with interest thereon at 12% from the date of deduction till payment. However, the payment already made and the refund of TDS amount will be sufficient recompense. This order shall not be taken as a precedent in any other matter as it is being passed taking into account special features of this case. title: M/s. Mangalore Ganesh Beedi Works v. Commissioner of Income Tax, Mysore & Anr.
text:
The Supreme Court disposed of the appeals, setting aside the judgment and order of the High Court of Karnataka. The Court restored the view of the Income-Tax Appellate Tribunal on two key questions of law. Firstly, it was held that the sum of Rs. 12,24,700/- claimed as revenue expenditure by the Association of Persons (AOP-3) constituted by the erstwhile partners of M/s. Mangalore Ganesh Beedi Works (MGBW) is an allowable deduction under Section 37 of the Income-Tax Act, 1961, as it was laid out wholly and exclusively for the purpose of the business. The High Court was deemed unjustified in upsetting the Tribunal's finding of fact in this regard. Secondly, concerning the expenditure for acquisition of intellectual property rights, namely trademarks, copyrights, and technical know-how, the Court affirmed that the Assessee is entitled to claim depreciation by treating these intangible assets as 'plant' under Section 32 read with Section 43(3) of the Income-Tax Act, 1961. The definition of 'plant' under Section 43(3) was interpreted broadly to include such commercially necessary intellectual property rights, noting that Section 32 at the relevant time did not distinguish between tangible and intangible assets for depreciation. The Court also emphasized that Clause 16 of the partnership deed explicitly provided for the vesting of trademarks with the highest bidder, countering the Revenue's claim that only goodwill was auctioned. The question regarding deductions under Section 35A and 35AB of the Act was left open for consideration in an appropriate future case. title: COMMISSIONER OF INCOME TAX v. M/S JINDAL STEEL & POWER LIMITED
text: The Supreme Court dismissed the civil appeals filed by the revenue, affirming the decisions of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal and various High Courts. On the core issue of recomputation of deduction under Section 80 IA of the Income Tax Act, 1961, the Court held that the 'market value' of electricity supplied by an assessee's captive power plants to its industrial units should be determined by the rate at which the State Electricity Board supplied power to industrial consumers (Rs. 3.72 per unit), rather than the lower contracted rate at which the assessee sold surplus power to the State Electricity Board (Rs. 2.32 per unit). The Court reasoned that the lower rate was a 'contracted price' under a statutory monopoly and not indicative of an 'open market' value as defined by free trade and competition. Regarding the exercise of option to adopt the Written Down Value (WDV) method for depreciation, the Court affirmed that no specific mode is prescribed for exercising such an option; the assessee's claim of depreciation in the return itself, filed before the due date, is sufficient compliance with Rule 5(1A) of the Income Tax Rules, 1962. For the issue of deletion of addition made by the assessing officer on account of payment to Shri S.K. Gupta and his group of companies, the Court upheld the High Court's decision, finding that the assessing officer's reliance on retracted statements without providing an opportunity for cross-examination to the assessee was unjustified. Finally, the Court declined to address whether carbon credit is a capital or revenue receipt, as this issue was not raised or urged by the revenue before the High Court and thus, the revenue was estopped from raising it at the Supreme Court stage, leaving the question open for an appropriate proceeding. title: Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation & Anr., State of Gujarat, Ahmedabad Urban Development Authority, Vadodara Sheheri Sankulan Khedut Mandal & Ors., Bhikhubhai Vitthalbhai Patel & Ors. v. Ahmedabad Green Belt Khedut Mandal & Ors., Vadodara Urban Development Authority & Anr., The State of Gujarat & Ors.
text: The Supreme Court set aside the Gujarat High Court's judgment to the extent that it held that land, once its designation lapses under Section 20 of the Gujarat Town Planning and Urban Development Act, 1976, cannot be re-reserved in a town planning scheme. The Court also rejected the High Court's finding that such land cannot be acquired indirectly under Section 40(3)(jj) if acquisition under Section 20 for want of compensation under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 was not possible. The Court found that the High Court's interpretation was erroneous and contrary to the intention of the Act, potentially frustrating the scheme by leaving portions of land without infrastructural facilities. Consequently, Civil Appeal Nos. 1542-44 of 2001, 1545-50 of 2001, and 1551-56 of 2001 were allowed, and the impugned judgments were set aside to the extent mentioned. Civil Appeal No. 1864 of 2014 and Transferred Case (C) Nos. 12-13 of 2010 were dismissed, with a clarification that observations in the transferred cases would not adversely affect either party. The Court ruled that the percentages prescribed under Section 40(3)(jj)(a) are not excessive, the State Legislature has the competence to specify these percentages, and a mere increase in percentages does not constitute excessive legislation. The Court also rejected claims based on Article 300-A of the Constitution, stating that while it creates a human right, it is not a fundamental right, and reasonable restrictions are valid exceptions. The contention that compensation under Section 82 was inadequate was also rejected. The Court clarified that the town planning scheme involves pooling and re-shuffling of land, and any loss to a landowner is to be compensated as per statutory provisions, and that the vesting of land in the local authority occurs only upon the commencement of the scheme, not upon notification of intention. title: M/s Subhash Projects & Marketing Ltd. v. West Bengal Power Development Corporation Ltd. & Ors.
text: The Supreme Court upheld the Division Bench's decision that the contract award to Subhash Projects was illegal, influenced by undue pressure from the Minister of State for Power. However, it dismissed L&T's appeal seeking to set aside the contract award and order a fresh tender, considering the project's completion. Instead, the court confirmed the Division Bench's direction for Subhash Projects to pay Rs. 1 crore as compensation to L&T, with interest at 5% per annum from August 8, 2003, until deposit. The court ordered Subhash Projects to deposit this amount within four weeks, failing which the interest would escalate to 10% per annum from the High Court's judgment date. The appeal by the Union of India, challenging the High Court's remarks about the Minister's interference, was also dismissed. Consequently, Subhash Projects' appeal was dismissed with costs, the Union of India's appeal was dismissed without costs, and L&T's appeal was dismissed, subject to the compensation payment terms. title: MERAMBHAI PUNJABHAI KHACHAR & ORS. v. STATE OF GUJARAT
text: The Supreme Court set aside the conviction of all appellants under Section 302/149 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) and Section 3 of the Terrorist and Disruptive Activities (Prevention) Act (TADA), finding Section 149 IPC inapplicable and Section 3 TADA unwarranted by the facts. Appellant No.1 (Merambhai) was solely convicted under Section 302 IPC for the murder of Rajabhai, sentenced to life imprisonment and a fine of Rs.10,000/-, with default simple imprisonment for 2 years, the fine directed to the deceased's heirs. For the offence under Section 307 IPC, only Appellant No.3 (Bhupatibhai) was convicted for causing injury to Jagdishbhai, receiving 5 years' rigorous imprisonment, while other appellants were acquitted of this charge. Appellant No.13 (Nathubhai) was acquitted of all charges. Appellant No.9 (Shivrajbhai) was convicted under Section 324 IPC for injuries to Sanjubhen, sentenced to 1 year's rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs.1,000/-, with default simple imprisonment for one month. The convictions of Appellants 2, 6, and 7 under Section 326 IPC were confirmed, maintaining 5 years' rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs.2,000/-, with default simple imprisonment for 3 months. Appellant No.8 (Babubhai) had his convictions under Sections 325 and 323 IPC confirmed, receiving 3 years' rigorous imprisonment and a fine for Section 325, and 6 months' rigorous imprisonment and a fine for Section 323, with sentences to run concurrently. Lastly, the convictions of Appellant Nos. 1, 3, 5, 10, and 12 under Sections 25 and 27 of the Arms Act were confirmed, leading to 1 year's rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs.1,000/-, with default simple imprisonment for 3 months, and confirming the order for taking fire arms into custody; these sentences for Appellant Nos. 1 and 3 are to run concurrently with other sentences. Appellant Nos. 4, 11, 14, and 15 were acquitted of offences under Sections 25 and 27 of the Arms Act. The appeals were allowed accordingly in part. title: STATE OF WEST BENGAL v. PRANAB RANJAN ROY
text: The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the impugned judgment of the High Court and the order of discharge passed by the Special Judge. The Court held that the phrase "made his appearance" in Section 167(5) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, as amended by the West Bengal Act No.24/1988, necessitates the physical appearance of the accused and their surrender to the court's custodial domain. This interpretation is consistent with the understanding of "appearance" in bail provisions under Sections 436 and 437 of the CrPC. The Court reasoned that filing a vakalatnama through an advocate for seeking the return of documents, without the physical presence or surrender of the accused, does not constitute "making appearance" for the purpose of initiating the two-year period for investigation specified in Section 167(5)(iii). A contrary interpretation would lead to inept consequences, allowing an accused to evade interrogation and subsequently claim discharge. As the respondent had not made a physical appearance before the Special Judge prior to the charge-sheet being laid, the bar contemplated in Section 167(5) was not invokable. The Special Judge was directed to proceed with the case and dispose of it in accordance with law. title: Vimlesh Kumari Kulshrestha v. Sambhajirao and Anr
text: The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, affirming the High Court's judgment to reverse the decree of specific performance. While the Supreme Court held that the High Court erred in applying Order XXIII Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, as the second suit was filed during the pendency of the first suit and implied permission for a fresh suit could be inferred, it upheld the High Court's finding that the agreement of sale dated 01.04.1986 was vague and uncertain. The Court observed that the agreement, read in its entirety and considering the circumstances, including the appellant's partial tenancy and the absence of a crucial attached plan, did not sufficiently describe the subject matter of sale, making it incapable of specific performance. Consequently, no infirmity was found in the High Court's ultimate decision to dismiss the suit for specific performance. title: HEM SINGH (DEAD) BY L.RS. AND ORS. v. GIANOO AND ORS.
text: The Supreme Court of India, in Civil Appeal No. 2699 of 2002, set aside the judgment and order of the High Court of Himachal Pradesh dated April 17, 2000. The High Court had previously overturned the judgment and decree of the Additional District Judge, Mandi. The Supreme Court found the High Court's conclusion that the parties had arrived at a compromise recognizing the defendants' customary rights to take earth from Khasra No. 611 to be erroneous and contrary to the record. The Court noted that the compromise decree did not mention such rights, nor did the statement of Nandlal, who was the sole signatory to the compromise, failing to establish any customary rights for the respondents. The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court decided the case on non-existent facts, specifically regarding the estoppel principle based on alleged admissions. Consequently, the Supreme Court restored the judgment and order dated April 29, 1989, of the First Appellate Court (Additional District Judge, Mandi), allowing the appeal and directing the parties to bear their own costs. title: INDIAN OIL CORPORATION LTD. & ORS. v. SUBRATA BORAH CHOWLEK , ETC.
text: The Supreme Court, in Civil Appeal Nos. 9726-9727 of 2010, allowed the appeals filed by Indian Oil Corporation Ltd. & Ors., setting aside the impugned judgment and order dated 29th January, 2010, of the Gauhati High Court. The High Court had rejected the appellants' application for condonation of a 59-day delay in preferring their appeal and dismissed the writ appeal in limine as barred by limitation. The Supreme Court held that a 'sufficient cause' had been made out for condonation of delay in filing the appeal, noting that the High Court erred in declining to condone the same. Citing precedents like Shakuntala Devi Jain, N. Balakrishnan, and Ramlal, Motilal & Chhotelal, the Court emphasized a liberal approach to 'sufficient cause' under Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963, particularly where no negligence, inaction, or mala fides can be imputed. The Court also acknowledged the need for a pragmatic approach, especially concerning governmental functioning, where delays due to procedural red tape are common, and public interest suffers if appeals are lost on such defaults. Finding no inaction, negligence, or mala fides in the appellants' conduct and deeming the explanation for the marginal delay of 59 days as 'sufficient cause,' the Supreme Court remanded the matter back to the Division Bench of the High Court for consideration on merits, with no order as to costs. title: AKMAL AHMAD v. STATE OF DELHI
text: The Supreme Court of India partly allowed the appeal, setting aside the conviction and sentence passed by the Designated Court on the appellant under Section 12 of the Passports Act, 1967. The Court held that merely holding a foreign passport, in the absence of an attempt to depart from India, does not constitute an offence under Section 12 read with Section 3 of the Passports Act. However, the conviction and sentence passed on the appellant for the offence under Section 5 of the Terrorist and Disruptive Activities (Prevention) Act (TADAA) were confirmed. This confirmation was based on the credible evidence of the seizure of a revolver loaded with live cartridges from the appellant in New Delhi, which is a notified area, and such articles fall within Category III of Schedule I to the Arms Rules, 1962, with the appellant lacking any licence. The Court reiterated that Section 5 of TADAA is a more aggravated offence than Section 25 of the Arms Act and emphasized that the statutory presumption, as elucidated in Sanjay Dutt vs. State, arising from the unauthorized possession of such arms in a notified area, suggesting they were meant for a terrorist or disruptive act, was not rebutted by the appellant. title: THE ORISSA FINANCIAL CORPORATION & ANR v. SMT. SUKANTI MOHAPATRA & ORS
text: The Supreme Court held that the impugned judgment by the Division Bench of the High Court was unsustainable on facts and law. The Orissa State Financial Corporation had granted a loan to the respondents, secured by mortgaged immovable property. Despite demand notices and opportunities for settlement through various One Time Settlement (OTS) proposals, the respondents defaulted. The Corporation proceeded with the seizure and sale of the mortgaged property under Section 29 of the State Financial Corporations Act, 1951. The Court found that the High Court erroneously interfered with the Corporation's decision regarding the OTS, stating that commercial decisions by the Corporation are not subject to judicial review unless extraordinary facts or procedural irregularities are present. The Court overruled the reliance on Mahesh Chandra v. Regional Manager, U.P. Financial Corporation, which placed undue restrictions on the Corporation's powers under Section 29. While acknowledging that the Corporation may have erred in executing the sale deed during the pendency of interim orders, the court decided to balance equities. The respondents were given an option to pay the entire sale consideration of Rs. 13,20,000/- along with registration and stamp duty, plus 18% annual interest compounded, to the third respondent by July 31, 2024. If this payment is not made, the Corporation is entitled to police aid to put the third respondent in possession of the property. The appeals were disposed of accordingly. title: Ajoy Debbarma & Ors. v. State of Tripura & Ors.
text: The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals, affirming the High Court's decision to set aside the selection and appointment of 10,323 teachers by the Government of Tripura. The Court found the selection process to be arbitrary, illegal, irrational, illogical, and marred by nepotism and favoritism, violating the National Council for Teacher Education Act, 1993, and constitutional principles of fairness and equality under Articles 14 and 16. While the appointments were quashed, the High Court allowed the selected teachers to continue until December 31, 2014, and directed the State to frame a new employment policy and complete a fresh selection process by the same date. The Supreme Court, in subsequent orders, modified these directions, extending the continuation of services for already appointed teachers until the end of the academic session 2019-2020 and directing the State to provide age relaxation for candidates participating in the fresh selection process until March 31, 2023. The Court held that the past service of illegally selected teachers could not be recognized, and any alternate employment offered by the State was a matter of solace and not a right, and did not constitute degradation. The Court also dismissed subsequent petitions seeking to reopen issues already decided, finding them to be an abuse of process. title: Aspi Jal & Anr. v. Khushroo Rustom Dadyburjor
text: The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the impugned order of the trial court, as affirmed by the High Court. The Court held that Section 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (CPC) was not attracted in this case. The Court reasoned that although the parties and the court were the same, and the grounds for eviction in the three suits (R.A.E. Suit No.1103/1976 of 2004, R.A.E. Suit No.1104/1977 of 2004, and R.A.E. Suit No.173/256 of 2010) were similar (non-user), the specific periods of non-user alleged in each suit were different, leading to different causes of action. The Court emphasized that for Section 10 to apply, the matter in issue must be directly and substantially the same in both suits, meaning the entire subject-matter must be identical, not just some common issues. The Court clarified that the plaintiffs might succeed in the third suit based on the specific period of non-user alleged therein, even if they failed in the earlier suits. The Court did not issue directions to hear all suits together but granted liberty to the parties to make such a prayer before the trial court. title: MADHAVI v. CHAGAN & ORS.
text: The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order allowing the review of a dismissed writ petition, thereby dismissing the writ petition and allowing the appeals. The Court held that the High Court failed to appreciate the distinction between Clause 1 and Clause 2 of Schedule 'F' of the Maharashtra Employees of Private Schools (Conditions of Service) Rules, 1981. Clause 1, dealing with seniority in primary schools, was interpreted in Viman Vaman Awale, while Clause 2, pertaining to secondary schools, was interpreted in Bhawna. Since the school in question is a secondary school, Clause 2 of Schedule 'F' determines seniority. Chagan was not a trained teacher at the time of his appointment and was rightly placed in Category 'E', later upgrading to Categories 'D' and 'C' upon acquiring graduate and B.Ed. degrees. Madhavi, conversely, was qualified as a graduate with a B.Ed. degree at the time of her appointment. The Court found the High Court's reliance on Viman Vaman Awale to be misplaced as it pertained to primary schools, whereas Bhawna was directly applicable to the case of secondary school seniority. Consequently, Chagan could not claim seniority from his initial appointment date as he lacked the requisite qualifications. The contempt petition was also dismissed. Citations: (2014) 13 SCC 219; (2019) 4 SCC 300; 2019 SCC OnLine Bom 597; 2006 (6) Mh.L.J. 682 Legal tags: Seniority Dispute; Secondary School Appointment; Qualifications for Teachers; Viman Vaman Awale; Bhawna; Vaijanath; Schedule F; Category C; Category D; Category E; Trained Graduate Teacher; Untrained Teacher; Date of Appointment; Acquisition of Qualification; Maharashtra Employees of Private Schools (Conditions of Service) Rules, 1981; Head Master Promotion; School Tribunal; Writ Petition; Review Petition; Supreme Court; High Court; Contempt Petition

title: Kishori Lal v. State of M.P.
text: The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the conviction of the appellant under Section 306 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, which was upheld by the Madhya Pradesh High Court. The Court found that the prosecution failed to establish direct or indirect acts of incitement to the commission of suicide, which is a prerequisite for abetment of suicide under Section 107 IPC. Merely treating the deceased-wife with cruelty was deemed insufficient for conviction under Section 306 IPC. The Court noted that alleged incidents of torture occurred 4-5 years prior to the occurrence and that the deceased was distressed due to her inability to bear a child, rather than the accused's actions. The presumption under Section 113A of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, was not applicable as the marriage was more than a decade old. Consequently, the bail bonds of the accused were ordered to be discharged. title: KRISHI UTPADAN MANDI SAMITI,HALDWANI ETC.ETC. v. M/S.INDIAN WOOD PRODUCTS LTD.AND ANOTHER
text: The Supreme Court, in this batch of appeals, addressed the question of liability to pay market fee in transactions of sale of specified agricultural produce between two traders, specifically when the selling trader does not collect the fee from the purchasing trader. Interpreting Section 17(iii)(b) of the Uttar Pradesh Krishi Utpadan Mandi Adhiniyam, the Court held that the primary and ultimate liability to pay the market fee is always upon the purchaser. While sub-clause (3) of Section 17(iii)(b) states that the 'trader selling the produce may realise it from the purchaser and shall be liable to pay the market fee to the Committee', the Court clarified that this 'shall' implies an obligation to remit the fee if collected. However, if the selling trader does not realise the fee from the purchaser, the liability to pay the market fee continues to rest with the purchasing trader. The Court emphasized that this interpretation aligns with the overall scheme of clause (b) of Section 17(iii) and the general policy that producers are not liable. The decision of the High Court was set aside, and the appeals were allowed, with the observation that any individual factual questions raised by respondents should be pursued through the prescribed legal remedies and not in a writ petition. title: BHASKAR @ PRABASKAR AND ORS. v. INSPECTOR OF POLICE,VELLORE TALUK POLICE STATION, VELLORE
text: The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, concurring with the High Court's decision that a de novo trial was not necessary. The Court held that Section 326 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which allows a successor judge to act on evidence recorded by a predecessor, is applicable even when a Designated Court under TADA ceases to exist and the case is transferred to a regular Sessions Court. The Court reasoned that the judge of a Designated Court is effectively a Sessions Judge, and thus, the Sessions Court judge who takes over the trial is a successor judge. The Court emphasized that this interpretation prevents undue repetition of trials, saving costs, time, and inconvenience to witnesses, and that the accused can still seek further examination of witnesses if necessary under the proviso to Section 326(1) of the Code, thus preventing prejudice. title: MOHAMMED AJMAL MOHAMMAD AMIR KASAB @ ABU MUJAHID v. STATE OF MAHARASHTRA
text: The Supreme Court upheld the convictions and sentences of Mohammed Ajmal Mohammad Amir Kasab, dismissing his appeal against the State of Maharashtra. The Court affirmed his guilt for numerous heinous crimes, including waging war against the Government of India (Section 121 IPC), conspiracy to wage war (Section 121A IPC), collecting arms with intent to wage war (Section 122 IPC), multiple counts of murder (Section 302 IPC, both personally and with common intention), attempt to murder, abduction for murder, robbery, and offences under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967, Explosives Act, 1884, Explosive Substances Act, 1908, and Arms Act, 1959. He was sentenced to five death penalties and an equal number of life terms. The Court confirmed that Kasab's actions were an integral part of a deep, vicious, and unprecedented conspiracy, hatched in Pakistan, aimed at destabilizing India, inflicting terror, undermining its economic strength, inciting communal strife, and attempting to dictate its foreign policy. The Court dismissed the defense's arguments concerning the denial of due process, affirming the adequacy of Indian legal safeguards (CrPC Sections 161-164, Evidence Act Sections 25-27) for self-incrimination, and noting Kasab's initial refusal of legal aid. His confessional statement was deemed voluntary and truthful, barring minor discrepancies regarding co-accused. The conviction for 'waging war' was upheld, interpreting 'Government of India' as the Indian State and its people, with the acts demonstrating hostile intent akin to a foreign enemy. Citing Kasab's complete lack of remorse and continued identification as a 'patriotic Pakistani' at war with India, the Court deemed the case 'rarest of rare' and confirmed the death penalty, concluding that no possibility of his reform or rehabilitation existed. Conversely, the Court dismissed the State of Maharashtra's appeal against the acquittal of Fahim Harshad Mohammad Yusuf Ansari and Sabauddin Ahamed (Accused Nos. 2 and 3), concurring with the trial court and High Court that the evidence presented against them was 'completely unacceptable' and lacked the requisite confidence. The related Transfer Petition (Criminal) No. 30 of 2012 was also dismissed. In an obiter dictum, the Court critically remarked on the live media coverage of the terrorist attacks, highlighting its detrimental impact on national security by inadvertently aiding terrorists and their handlers. title: N. MASTHAN SAHIB v. CHIEF COMMISSIONER, PONDICHERRY
text: The Supreme Court held that Pondicherry is not comprised within the territory of India as specified in Article 1(3) of the Constitution. The Court was bound by the Union Government's answer on this issue. While complete administrative control had been transferred to India, this did not equate to a transfer of territory as the treaty of cession had not been ratified. Consequently, the Court could not entertain appeals under Article 136 of the Constitution against decisions of authorities in Pondicherry. Regarding writ petitions under Article 32, a majority of the court held that no writ could be issued to authorities in Pondicherry as it was outside the territory of India, citing Article 142 which limits the enforceability of Supreme Court orders to the territory of India. A dissenting opinion argued that writs could still be issued under Article 32 to quasi-judicial authorities in Pondicherry, even if they were under the control of the Government of India, as the right to a writ is a fundamental right and the court should not refuse it due to enforceability issues. The appeals and writ petitions were dismissed. Citations: 1962 AIR 797; 1962 SCR Supl. title: Coromandel Indag Products (P) Ltd. v. Garuda Chit & Trading Co. P. Ltd. & Anr.
text: The Supreme Court upheld the decision of the Division Bench of the Madras High Court, dismissing the appeal filed by Coromandel Indag Products (P) Ltd. The Court found that the appellant-Company had not made out a case for a decree of specific performance. The Court concluded that time was of the essence in the contract for sale dated 28.08.1981, and the appellant-Company's conduct, including the repeated requests for documents not explicitly mentioned in the agreement, indicated a lack of readiness and willingness to perform their obligations. The appellant-Company's failure to pay the balance consideration and get the sale deed registered was considered a breach of the agreement. Therefore, the appeal was dismissed, with parties directed to bear their own costs. Citations: O.S.A. title: Ashoka Kumar Thakur v. Union of India and Ors
text: The Supreme Court, addressing challenges to the Central Educational Institutions (Reservation in Admission) Act 2006 and the 93rd Constitutional Amendment, laid down several directives regarding reservations for Other Backward Classes (OBCs) in higher educational institutions. It was held that for the implementation of the impugned Statute, the 'creamy layer' must be excluded from the identifiable OBCs. A periodic review, every five years, is mandated to assess the desirability of continuing the operation of the Statute. The Central Government is directed to examine the feasibility of fixing cut-off marks for OBC candidates, suggesting a grace of five marks below the minimum eligibility for general categories to ensure quality and merit, with any remaining vacant seats to be filled by general category candidates. For the proper determination of backward classes, the Union of India must issue a notification after obtaining necessary data from States and Union Territories regarding the exclusion of the creamy layer, with norms fixed considering regional peculiarities. The Commission constituted under Indra Sawhney No.1 is to work more effectively for identifying backward classes, using graduation (not technical graduation) or professional qualification as the standard yardstick for measuring educational backwardness. To achieve constitutional balance, it is deemed necessary and desirable to ear-mark a suitable percentage of seats within the 27% permissible limit for 'socially and economically backward classes'. The Court clarified that for purposes of Articles 15 and 16, 'caste' is not synonymous with 'class', but an identifiable class emerges once the 'creamy layer' is excluded from a caste. Emphasis was placed on strengthening primary and secondary education as a foundation for higher education. Constitutional provisions, specifically Articles 16(1) and 16(4), are to be construed harmoniously, with one not being an exception to the other. Similarly, Articles 15(4) and 15(5) operate in different fields, and Article 15(5) does not render Article 15(4) inactive. The Court noted that foreign decisions, particularly regarding the 'strict scrutiny' test, do not hold great determinative value in the Indian context, advocating for an in-depth scrutiny to assess constitutionality. Finally, the Central Government is obligated to consider applications for including institutions in the Schedule of the Act if material demonstrates their status as institutions of excellence, research, or national/strategic importance. The challenge concerning private unaided educational institutions was not deliberated upon due to the absence of direct challenges from affected parties. title: M/s Metal Seam Co. of India (P) Ltd. v. M/s Avadh Delicacies & Others
text: The Supreme Court, in Civil Appeal No. 361 of 2016, modified the High Court's judgment dated 28.03.2014. The Court sustained the cancellation of allotment of Shed No. B-5 made in favour of M/s Surya Chemicals vide letter dated 09.06.1998, finding that M/s Surya Chemicals had not commenced work and had attempted an unauthorized transfer. The claim of Respondent No.1 (M/s Avadh Delicacies) for the shed was rejected, as the Court found that they had ceased operations in 1997 and failed to substantiate any manufacturing activity despite being afforded adequate opportunity. Consequently, Respondent No.1 was directed to immediately surrender possession of the concerned shed. Simultaneously, the order of allotment dated 15.06.1998, which granted the shed to the Appellant (M/s Metal Seam Co. of India (P) Ltd.), was set aside. This decision was based on the Appellant already possessing three other sheds (B-6, C-1, and C-2) in the same Industrial Estate, thereby negating any special equity in their favour, and acknowledging that the previous allotment was made without public auction or inviting tenders, which the Court deemed unsustainable. The authorities are now directed to forthwith recover possession of Shed No. B-5 and proceed to conduct a fresh public auction or invite tenders for its allotment at the present market value, allowing all interested parties, including the Appellant and Respondent No.1, to participate. title: ENFORCEMENT DIRECTORATE AND ANR. v. M. SAMBA SIVA RAO & ORS.
text: The Supreme Court, hearing appeals against a common judgment of the Delhi High Court, addressed the question of whether refusal to comply with summons issued under Section 40 of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1973 (FERA) would attract the provisions of Section 56 of the Act. The High Court had concluded that Section 56 would not apply to such violations, leading to the quashing of complaints. The Supreme Court rejected this interpretation, finding that the High Court, along with the Kerala High Court and Madras High Court, erred in restricting the applicability of Section 56(1)(ii) (pertaining to 'any other case') to contraventions involving money value. The Court emphasized that Section 40(3) makes it binding for summoned persons to attend and Section 40(4) deems such investigations or proceedings as judicial proceedings under Sections 193 and 228 of the Indian Penal Code. Furthermore, relying on its own authoritative pronouncement in *Central Bureau of Investigation vs. State of Rajasthan and Ors.*, the Court reiterated that FERA is a self-contained code for investigation, inquiry, and trial, rendering Section 5 of the Code of Criminal Procedure inapplicable. Consequently, the Court held that prosecuting the accused for offences under Section 174 or other relevant provisions of the IPC for contempt of lawful authority is unsustainable. The Supreme Court concluded that a violation or contravention of directions given under summons under Section 40 of FERA squarely falls within the purview of Section 56, making it punishable thereunder. Accordingly, the impugned judgments of the Delhi High Court and the similar views of the Kerala High Court were set aside, the appeals were allowed, and directions were issued for the complaint proceedings to be continued in accordance with law. title: S. PRATAP SINGH v. THE STATE OF PUNJAB
text: The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the Punjab Government's orders dated June 3, 1961, which revoked the appellant's leave and placed him under suspension, and the order dated June 29, 1961, directing a departmental inquiry into charges against him. The Court held that while the Government possessed the power to revoke leave, suspend a civil servant, and retain him in service past superannuation under the Punjab Civil Services (Punishment and Appeal) Rules, 1952 (including Rule 3.26(d)), and that such actions were not inherently contrary to service rules or a contravention of Articles 19 and 23 of the Constitution, the *exercise of this power* in the present case was vitiated by mala fides. The dominant motive that induced the Government to take action against the appellant was not to initiate bona fide disciplinary proceedings for misconduct, but to wreak vengeance upon him for incurring the Chief Minister's wrath and for the discredit brought upon the Chief Minister through allegations published in the 'Blitz' newspaper in January 1961 and subsequently affirmed by the appellant's wife. The Court reiterated that an authority exercising power must not take into account extraneous factors, and if the dominant purpose is unlawful or an abuse/misuse of power, the action is bad and subject to judicial interference. Tape-recorded conversations were deemed legal evidence for corroboration, with their weight depending on other established factors. As the appellant failed to make out the point about the orders being contrary to the Service Rules, there was no order as to costs. title: M/S. UNIWORTH TEXTILES LTD. v. COMMISSIONER OF CENTRAL EXCISE, RAIPUR
text: The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the orders of the authorities below. The Court held that the extended period of limitation under the proviso to Section 28 of the Customs Act, 1962, could not be invoked against the appellant. This was due to the fact that the burden of proof for proving mala fide conduct lay with the Revenue, and the show cause notice lacked specific averments required for invoking the proviso. Furthermore, the evidence did not demonstrate a willful default on the part of the appellant. The Court emphasized that mere non-payment of duties does not equate to collusion or willful misstatement or suppression of facts, and that for the proviso to apply, there must be a deliberate intention to evade duty, which was not established in this case. The appellant's conduct in seeking clarification from the Development Commissioner was considered bona fide. The Court also highlighted that the extended period of five years under the proviso is applicable only in cases of fraud, collusion, willful misstatement, or suppression of facts, and not for ordinary defaults. title: Chandrabhai K. Bhoir & Ors. v. Krishna Arjun Bhoir & Ors.
text: The Supreme Court of India, in Civil Appeal No. 6575 of 2008, set aside the impugned judgment of the High Court. The Court held that Section 302 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, which allows the High Court to give directions to an executor or administrator regarding the estate, was not applicable in this case. The Court reasoned that the agreement entered into between the parties, which included a development agreement and terms for settlement concerning the property, was a collateral document and not part of the Will itself. The Court emphasized that a probate court must give effect to the Will and not to an agreement that contradicts the testator's wishes. The Court clarified that while the executor's actions as an executor are subject to the directions of the testamentary court, his actions as a developer are not. The Court stated that the testamentary court cannot enforce a contract as a contract, even if the executor is a party to it, especially when the agreement conflicts with the terms of the Will. The Court found that the High Court erred in exercising its testamentary jurisdiction to enforce the development agreement. Therefore, the appeal was allowed, and the impugned judgment was set aside. No costs were awarded. title: State of M.P. v. Abdul Kadir & Anr.
text: The Supreme Court, while allowing the appeal, set aside the impugned order of the Division Bench of the Madhya Pradesh High Court. The Court directed the Division Bench to rehear the Letters Patent Appeal on the issue of condonation of delay, emphasizing the need to consider the parameters laid down in the Arvind Yadav v. Ramesh Kumar case. The judgement highlighted that neither the Single Judge nor the Division Bench adequately considered the Probation Board's reasons for rejecting the release on probation, particularly the gruesome nature of the murder. The Court reiterated that convicts do not have an indefeasible right to release; they only have a right to be considered. Factors such as the manner of commission of the offence, the convict's antecedents, the effect of release on victims, and the propensity to commit further crimes must be considered individually. Mere recommendations from individuals or the absence of objections from victims' families are not solely decisive. The State Government and the Board must consider all relevant factors, and their decision should not be interfered with merely because another view is possible. title: Amarjit Singh & Ors. v. State of Punjab & Ors.
text: The Supreme Court, in disposing of these Civil Appeals, upheld the decisions of the High Court, dismissing challenges to land acquisition proceedings for the expansion of SAS Nagar (Mohali). The Court addressed three core questions. Firstly, it held that the notification dated 10th February, 2004, issued under Section 178(2) of the Punjab Regional and Town Planning and Development Act, 1995, exempting areas in sectors 81, 88, and 89 from provisions of Section 14 and Chapters VIII, X, and XII of the said Act, suffered from no legal infirmity. The Court noted the appellants' failure to challenge this exemption notification in their writ petitions and, on merits, found the State Government's exercise of power to grant exemption for "expediency" and to avoid "undue hardship" due to Mohali's rapid growth and the urgent need for planned development to be justified and valid, aligning with previous judicial interpretations of "expedient" and the upholding of an analogous exemption for sectors 76 to 80 in Jasmer Singh v. State of Punjab. Secondly, with the exemption notification upheld, the contention that the land acquisition proceedings were rendered invalid for non-compliance with the 1995 Act was deemed not to survive. The Court explicitly distinguished this case from Sanjeet Singh's case, clarifying that the present acquisition was for the expansion of an existing local planning area (SAS Nagar/Mohali), validly declared under Section 56(5) of the 1995 Act, and not for a new town where the site selection process was flawed. Procedural adherence to the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, was not found to be lacking. Thirdly, the Court reiterated that rehabilitation measures for expropriated owners are not a condition precedent for compulsory acquisition under Article 300-A of the Constitution or the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, as adequate compensation is provided. While acknowledging the State's 'Land Pooling Scheme', the Court ruled against its retrospective application to the already finalized acquisitions, citing its prospective nature and the potential for confusion and further litigation. However, demonstrating fairness, the Court directed that if the appellants submit applications under Section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act for a reference to the Civil Court for determination of higher compensation within six weeks from the date of this judgment, the Collector shall make such a reference, ensuring expeditious disposal by the competent Civil Court. The appeals were consequently dismissed, subject to this specific directive on compensation. Citations: SLP (C) No.9924 of 2007; SLP (C) No.9926 of 2007; C.W.Ps. title: SANDHYA v. STATE OF MAHARASHTRA & ORS.
text: The Supreme Court of India allowed the appeal, setting aside the judgment and order dated 15th March, 2013, passed by the Division Bench of the High Court of Judicature of Bombay. The High Court had erroneously held that the appellant was not entitled to regularization of her service as per Government Resolution dated 10th March, 2005, on the ground that she was not in service on the date of the GR. The Supreme Court clarified that since the appellant's termination order dated 20th April, 1998, had been set aside by the Maharashtra Administrative Tribunal on 24th November, 2011, she shall be deemed to have continued in service, including on 10th March, 2005. Consequently, the appellant is entitled to regularization. The respondents are directed to comply with the order and directions passed by the Tribunal on 24th November, 2011, in Original Application No. 293/1998, and regularize the services of the appellant with retrospective effect within two months from the date of receipt of a copy of this judgment. No costs were awarded. title: MAHMADHUSEN ABDULRAHIM KALOTA SHA IKH v. UNION OF INDIA & ORS.
text: The Supreme Court held that Section 2(3) and 2(5) of the Prevention of Terrorism (Repeal) Act, 2004 are constitutional. The Court ruled that once the Review Committee opines that there is no prima facie case for proceeding against an accused under POTA, cases in which cognizance has been taken by the Court shall be deemed to have been withdrawn. The Court further clarified that Section 321 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is not applicable in such cases, as the Repealing Act's provision for deemed withdrawal is clear and unambiguous. The Court also held that the opinion of the Review Committee is subject to judicial review under Article 226 of the Constitution, providing a remedy for aggrieved parties. The judgments of the High Courts were upheld in declaring the provisions constitutional but set aside to the extent they mandated following the Section 321 Cr.P.C. procedure. title: JAGRAJ SINGH v. BIRPAL KAUR
text:
The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal filed by the appellant-husband, upholding the interim order of the High Court of Punjab & Haryana dated May 04, 2006, which issued a non-bailable warrant against him for failing to appear in person. The Apex Court affirmed that a Matrimonial Court is statutorily mandated by Section 23(2) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, to make every endeavour for reconciliation and, for this purpose, possesses the power to direct the personal presence of parties, a power also supported by Order III Rule 1 proviso and Order IX Rule 12 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. The Court observed that the District Judge had erroneously decided the divorce petition on merits after ruling on a lack of territorial jurisdiction and without making reconciliation efforts. Finding no legal infirmity in the High Court's direction for personal appearance and subsequent issuance of a non-bailable warrant, especially given the husband's repeated non-compliance despite undertakings, the appeal was dismissed with costs. title: U.P. State Road Trasnport Corporation v. U.P. Rajya Sadak Parivahan Karamchari Union
text: The Supreme Court allowed the appeals, setting aside the impugned judgment of the High Court and the order of the Labour Court dated 19.9.2001. The Court held that the Labour Court's power under Section 11-C of the U.P. Industrial Disputes Act or Section 13-A of the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946, is limited to interpreting and applying standing orders and does not extend to granting reliefs that could only be awarded through a regular reference under Section 10 of the Industrial Disputes Act or Section 4-K of the U.P. The concerned workmen were given the liberty to raise their grievances before the appropriate authority under Section 4-K of the U.P. title: RAKESH BABAN BORHADE v. STATE OF MAHARASHTRA & ANR.

title: HYDRO-ELECTRIC EMPLOYEES UNION, U.P. & ORS. v. SUDHIR KUMAR SHARMA & ORS.
text: The Supreme Court, in this batch of cases, dealt with two sets of judgments from the Allahabad High Court concerning the amalgamation of posts like Meter Readers, Sub Station Operators, and Switch Board Attendants under the U.P. State Electricity Board. The Court set aside the Division Bench judgment which had allowed writ petitions filed by Meter Readers, reinstating the Single Judge's decision that dismissed these petitions. The Supreme Court held that the Board's decision from 1963 to create a combined cadre for these three categories of employees, making their services interchangeable, was valid. Subsequent decisions by the Board in 1977 and 1994, which included additional posts like Junior Meter Tester and reiterated the interchangeability, were also upheld. The Court found that the formation of a unified cadre for Meter Readers, Switch Board Attendants, and Sub Station Operators did not violate Article 14 of the Constitution, as the duties, qualifications, and pay scales were found to be similar. The Court also affirmed the validity of the U.P. State Electricity Board Operational Employees Category Service Regulation, 1995, holding that it was intra vires and that no notice under Section 4(i) of the U.P. Industrial Disputes Act was required for its framing. Consequently, all writ petitions filed by the Meter Readers challenging the amalgamation and the regulations were dismissed. title: Saheb Reddy v. Sharanappa and Ors
text: The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the High Court's judgment and restoring the judgment of the first appellate court. The court held that the adoption of defendant no.1 by Smt. Sharnappa did not divest the shares of property that had already vested in Smt. Sharnappa and her daughters (including the plaintiff's mother, Smt. Nagamma) prior to the adoption, as per Section 12(c) of the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956. Consequently, the plaintiff was entitled to 1/16th share from his mother's share and an additional 1/64th share from his grandmother's (Smt. Sharnappa's) property, totaling a 5/64th share, while defendant no.1 was entitled to a 1/16th share. title: GOVERNOR GENERAL IN COUNCIL v. MUSADDI LAL.
text: The Supreme Court of India allowed the appeal, thereby dismissing the respondent's suit for compensation for non-delivery of goods against the railway administration. Overruling the Full Bench decision of the Allahabad High Court, the Supreme Court held that a claim for compensation for non-delivery of goods is not distinct from a claim for compensation for loss, destruction, or deterioration of goods under the Indian Railways Act, 1890. Consequently, the requirement of serving a written notice of claim under Section 77 of the Indian Railways Act within six months from the date of delivery of goods for carriage is a condition precedent for the maintainability of such a suit. The Court clarified that failure to deliver goods is a consequence of loss or destruction, and the provisions of Articles 30 and 31 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908, which prescribe different points of time for limitation for suits against carriers, cannot be projected upon Sections 72 and 77 of the Indian Railways Act to infer a distinct cause of action for non-delivery that exempts the claim from the notice requirement of Section 77. The railway administration's responsibility is that of a bailee, not an insurer. The suit was found to be barred due to non-compliance with the statutory condition precedent under Section 77. No order was made as to costs throughout the proceedings. title: PRADEEP MEHRA v. HARIJIVAN J. JETHWA
text: The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the High Court's order dated 08.01.2021 and the appellate court's order dated 22.12.2017, while upholding the executing court's order dated 28.09.2017. The Court directed the executing court to complete the execution proceedings expeditiously, within six months from the date a copy of the order is placed before it. The Court noted that the judgment debtors had delayed execution proceedings under Order XXI of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (CPC), and abused the process by challenging an earlier order dated 12.02.2013, which had allowed the execution of a consent decree dated 11.06.2005 and had attained finality. The executing court correctly held that the judgment debtors' application under Section 47 CPC was not maintainable as it sought to re-open a decided matter. The Supreme Court found that the appellate court and the High Court erred in setting aside the executing court's order, despite the principles of res judicata. The Supreme Court emphasized that the executing court cannot go behind the decree and that objections under Section 47 CPC are limited to the execution, discharge, or satisfaction of the decree, and cannot be used to reopen issues already decided. title: L. Krishna Reddy v. State by Station House Officer & Ors.
text: The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's order discharging the parents of the deceased husband (Accused Nos. 2 and 3) from the case. The court noted that while the husband committed suicide after murdering his wife, the charge sheet and witness statements did not sufficiently implicate the parents in the murder under Section 302 IPC or the dowry demand under Section 498-A IPC. The court emphasized that a prima facie case must be established to proceed against an accused, and in the absence of direct evidence or reasonable inference of conspiracy or abetment linking the parents to the crime, continuing prosecution would be an exercise in futility. The court cited previous judgments to clarify that mere bald statements without supporting evidence are insufficient to proceed, especially when the deceased couple lived separately and the primary allegations of dowry demand were directed at the deceased son-in-law. The appeal filed by the father of the victim was dismissed. title: COMMISSIONER OF AGRICULTURALINCOME-TAX, BENGAL v. SRI KESHAB CHANDRA MANDAL
text: The Supreme Court, by a majority decision (Fazl Ali, Patanjali Sastri, Mukherjea, and Das JJ., with Mahajan J. dissenting), reversed the judgment of the Calcutta High Court. The Court held that the Bengal Agricultural Income-tax Act, 1944, and its rules, particularly Rule 11 and Form 5, intended to exclude the common law rule of 'qui facit per alium facit per se' (he who acts through another acts himself) concerning the signing of income tax returns by individuals. The Court found that the return in question, signed by the assessee's son on behalf of the illiterate assessee, was not properly signed and therefore not a valid return, as there was no physical contact between the assessee and the signature. The appeal was allowed, and the assessment made based on the invalid return was set aside. Mahajan J., in his dissent, opined that the question referred to the High Court assumed physical contact and that the High Court was correct in its affirmative answer, as there was no evidence to establish the absence of such contact. He also emphasized dealing with illiterate individuals more sympathetically. title: RAM RATAN alias RATAN AHIR AND OTHERS v. THE STATE OF BIHAR AND ANOTHER
text: The Supreme Court held that when a person seizes cattle on the grounds that they are trespassing and causing damage to crops, and intends to take them to the pound, they commit no offense of theft, regardless of any mistaken belief about their right to the land or crops. The remedy for the owner of such seized cattle lies in taking action under Section 20 of the Cattle Trespass Act, 1871, and they have no right to use force to rescue the cattle. Consequently, individuals who, while attempting to rescue seized cattle, used force and caused injuries and death to the party seizing the cattle, did not commit any offense, as the seizing party had the right of private defense against the use of unlawful force for the rescue of the cattle. The appeal was allowed, and the convictions were set aside, leading to the release of the appellants. title: KARANPURA DEVELOPMENT CO., LTD. v. RAJA KAMAKSHYA NARAIN SINGH
text: The Supreme Court allowed the appeals, setting aside the High Court's decrees and restoring the trial court's judgments. The Court held that the deeds dated March 26, 1915, and November 23, 1917, were valid and binding. However, the deed dated June 1, 1937, was deemed invalid. Consequently, the leases granted to the appellant were upheld, but a specific clause postponing the payment of minimum royalty in the lease deeds dated August 2, 1937, was declared inoperative. The Court found that the Court of Wards had acted within its powers under Section 18 of the Court of Wards Act, 1879, in executing the deeds of 1915 and 1917, and that these actions were taken after due application of mind and consideration of the ward's benefit. The argument that the deeds were not for the benefit of the ward or lacked proper sanction was rejected. The Court emphasized that the Court of Wards, as a statutory body, has powers defined by the Act, and its decisions, when made bona fide and after applying its mind, are not subject to challenge on the merits. title: The Managing Director The North East Karnataka Road Transport Corporation v. K. Murti
text: The Supreme Court of India, while hearing an appeal against a High Court order, set aside the order passed by the High Court of Karnataka in Writ Appeal No.1565 of 2004. Consequently, the orders passed by the learned Single Judge of the High Court and the Labour Court were also set aside. The Court found the High Court's decision to reinstate the delinquent employee, a badli conductor, to be erroneous, given the established misconduct. The misconduct included failing to issue tickets to passengers after collecting fares and manipulating ticket denominations, which were found to be acts of dishonesty or gross negligence. The Court referred to previous judgments emphasizing that such misconduct, especially by a conductor entrusted with faith and trust, warrants dismissal and that Labour Courts and High Courts should not lightly interfere with disciplinary actions unless the punishment is shockingly disproportionate. The appeal filed by the Management was allowed, and no costs were imposed. title: ABHINASH CHAND & ORS. v. STATE OF HIMACHAL PRADESH & ORS.
text: The Supreme Court of India, while allowing the appeals, fixed the land value at Rs. 10,000/- per marla. title: S.K. Dheri v. Mukesh Prakash
text: The Supreme Court of India allowed the appeal and set aside the impugned order passed by the Central Administrative Tribunal, Principal Bench, New Delhi. The appellant was convicted under Section 17 of the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985, read with Section 12 of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971, and sentenced to simple imprisonment for one month. However, as the directions in the order dated 6th October, 1999, passed in O.A. title: Management Committee of Montfort Senior Secondary School v. Shri Vijay Kumar and Ors.
text: The Supreme Court dismissed both Civil Appeal No. 6593 of 2003 and Civil Appeal No. 5143 of 2005, holding that the Delhi School Tribunal was not required to refer the appeal of a dismissed employee to an arbitrator when an application was filed by the school management under Section 8(1) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. The Court affirmed the Delhi High Court's decision, stating that while Chapter V of the Delhi School Education Act, 1973, pertains to un-aided minority schools and provides for contractual rights including arbitration, the interpretation in cases like Frank Anthony Public School Employees' Association v. Union of India and The Ahmedabad St. Xavier's College Society v. State of Gujarat has extended the statutory rights and privileges of Chapter IV to employees of such schools. Consequently, the employees' conditions of service are governed by the statutory regime, and the Tribunal, being a judicial authority with powers akin to a civil appellate court, is the appropriate forum for adjudicating disputes related to dismissal, removal, or reduction in rank. The Court rejected the argument that the employer could insist on arbitration, emphasizing that once a remedy under one provision is exhausted, the other cannot be availed. The appeals were dismissed without any order as to costs. title: State of Rajasthan v. Kheraj Ram
text: The Supreme Court allowed the appeal of the State of Rajasthan, setting aside the High Court's acquittal and restoring the trial court's conviction of the respondent-accused, Kheraj Ram, for the murder of his wife, two children, and brother-in-law. The Court found that the circumstances, including the accused's motive (suspected infidelity of his wife), his false explanation of the incident, his conduct after the crime, and the recovery of incriminating items, unerringly pointed to his guilt. The Court upheld the death sentence awarded by the trial court, deeming the crime to be of an extremely brutal, grotesque, diabolical, revolting, and dastardly nature, committed in a planned and meticulous manner without remorse, thus fitting the criteria for the "rarest of rare cases" warranting capital punishment. title: M/S O.R.G. SYSTEMS, BARODA v. COLLECTOR OF CENTRAL EXCISE, VADODARA
text: The Supreme Court, in this case, allowed the appeals filed by M/s O.R.G. SYSTEMS, BARODA, setting aside the impugned demand and penalty. The Court relied on its previous judgment in PSI Data Systems Ltd. Vs. Collector of Central Excise. The core issue revolved around the inclusion of the value of peripheral devices and service charges in the assessable value of computers for excise duty purposes. The Court held that computers manufactured by entities like Orbit Electronics and DSI, even when supplied with specifications and designs by the appellant, were not to be treated as manufactured by the appellant for excise duty. Furthermore, the value of peripheral devices and service charges could not be included in the assessable value of the computers, as these were considered distinct and separate from the computer itself, analogous to a cassette being separate from a cassette recorder. The Court clarified that even if a computer requires software to function, the software's value, if sold separately or as an add-on, is not includible in the computer's assessable value. The Tribunal's finding that a distinct product came into existence by the supply of peripherals was overturned, as was the inclusion of service charges based on an unsupported warranty assumption. Consequently, the entire demand and the reduced penalty of Rs. 10 lacs were set aside. Citations: 1997 (89) E.L.T. 3 (S.C.) title: State v. Individuals
text: The appeal of the government against the decision of the High Court upholding the rights of two individuals to seek asylum in India, having committed crimes in British possessions, has been dismissed. The Supreme Court has ruled that India is no longer a British possession and therefore the Fugitive Offenders Act, 1881, which governed extradition between British possessions, does not apply. The court has also stated that without radical legislative changes, it is not possible to adapt the Act to the changed conditions of a sovereign democratic republic.
