title: E.   D. SASSOON AND COMPANY LTD. v. THE COMMISSIONER OF INCOME-TAX,BOMBAY CITY.
text: The Supreme Court, by a majority (S.R. DAS and BHAGWATI JJ.), allowed the appeals, holding that the Managing Agency commission was not liable to be apportioned between E.D. Sassoon and Company Ltd. (assignors) and their transferees (assignees). The Court construed the Managing Agency agreements as constituting an entire and indivisible contract of service, where remuneration or commission became due yearly on the completion of a definite period of service (the full accounting year, typically 31st March or 31st December, depending on the agreement) and at stated intervals, not for broken periods. It was a condition precedent for the Sassoons to fully perform the service for the entire year to earn any remuneration. Consequently, no income was deemed to have 'accrued' to the Sassoons for the broken periods they served prior to the assignments, nor did any debt become due to them by the managed companies at the dates of transfer. What was transferred was an expectancy of earning commission, not actual earned or accrued income. The true test for income-tax liability under Section 4(1)(a) of the Indian Income-tax Act is whether income accrued to the assessee within the chargeable accounting period, not merely the work done. The Court clarified the meanings of 'income', 'accrues', 'arises', and 'earned', stating that income accrues when a right to receive it is acquired, i.e., a debt (debitum in presenti, solvendum in futuro) is created. Sections 36 of the Transfer of Property Act and 26(2) of the Indian Income-tax Act were held inapplicable, the former due to a 'contract to the contrary' implied by the assignment of future rights, and the latter because no actual share of income, profits, or gains had accrued to the Sassoons for the broken periods. JAGANNADHADAS J., dissenting, argued that the income for the year accrued on completion of the year, jointly to both the assignor and assignee, and was apportionable between them. He viewed the assignment as a transfer of a future right to a share of income, and maintained that the assignor remained liable for tax on their accrued share despite the assignment, emphasizing that the 'continuous functioning' as Managing Agent, rather than mere ownership of the Agency, was the effective source of income under Section 10(1) of the Indian Income-tax Act. title: Chairman-cum-M.D. ITI Limited v. K. Muniswamy & Ors.
text: The Supreme Court held that clause 17(7)(iii) of the Certified Standing Orders does not create any right for an employee to seek continuation in service after attaining the age of 58 years. The word 'may' in the clause indicates a discretionary power vested in the appellant company to continue an employee in service until the age of 60 years, subject to medical fitness. Consequently, the court modified paragraph 28 of the impugned judgment, clarifying that while the rollback of retirement age from 60 to 58 years cannot be interfered with, it cannot affect the existing rights recognized in employees and the company as per clause 17(7)(iii). The appeal was allowed on these terms. title: Rakesh and Another v. State of Haryana
text: The Supreme Court of India dismissed the Criminal Appeal No. 1779 of 2009, thereby confirming the final judgment and order dated 15.05.2006 passed by the High Court of Punjab and Haryana, which had upheld the judgment of conviction and sentence dated 27.09.2001 and 28.09.2001 respectively, by the Additional Sessions Judge, Sonepat. The appellants, Rakesh and Smt. Ram Piari, were held guilty for offences punishable under Sections 498-A (cruelty) and 302 (murder) read with Section 34 (common intention) of the Indian Penal Code, 1860. They were sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for one year and a fine of Rs.500/- each for Section 498-A, and rigorous imprisonment for life and a fine of Rs.2000/- each for Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC, with sentences to run concurrently. The Court found the dying declaration of the deceased – Kailash, recorded by a Judicial Magistrate after due medical certification of her fitness, to be fully acceptable and reliable. This declaration specifically implicated the husband and mother-in-law in dowry harassment, assault, and setting her ablaze. The defence argument regarding the husband's alleged burn injuries as indicative of a rescue attempt was rejected due to the delay in seeking medical treatment. The Court also declined to alter the conviction from Section 302 to Section 304 Part I, concluding that the prosecution had established its case beyond reasonable doubt. title: Union of India & Ors. v. Diler Singh
text: The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the High Court's judgment and restoring the first appellate court's decision, thereby dismissing the respondent's suit. The court held that under Section 11(1) of the Central Reserve Police Force Act, 1949, the punishment of dismissal can be imposed. The High Court's reliance on the Calcutta High Court's decision in Akhilesh Kumar, which was not in consonance with this Court's ruling in Ghulam Mohd. Bhat, was found to be erroneous. The court also addressed the proportionality of the punishment, stating that unless the punishment shocks the conscience, there is no scope for interference. Given the misconduct of the respondent, a member of a disciplined force, in leaving the campus without permission, consuming liquor, and quarreling with civilians, the dismissal was deemed appropriate and not disproportionate. title: THE LIQUIDATORS OF PURSA LIMITED v. COMMISSIONER OF INCOME-TAX, BIHAR.
text: The Supreme Court held that for the second proviso to Section 10(2)(vii) of the Income-tax Act to apply, the machinery or plant must have been used for the purpose of the business carried on by the assessee during the accounting year. Since the machinery and plant of the sugar factory were not used at all for the purpose of business during the relevant accounting year, the proviso was not applicable. The Court found that the Tribunal had misdirected itself in law regarding the interpretation of Section 10 of the Act. The sale of the machinery and plant was considered a realization of assets in the process of winding up the business, not an operation in furtherance of the business. Therefore, the surplus arising from the sale of the machinery and plant was not chargeable to tax under Section 10(2)(vii). The appeal was allowed, and the respondent was ordered to pay the costs. title: KARAN SINGH & OTHERS v. UNION OF INDIA
text: The Supreme Court dismissed the Civil Appeals and Special Leave Petitions, affirming the judgment of the Delhi High Court concerning the quantum of compensation for land acquisition in village Gharoli, Delhi. The Court held that the High Court correctly rejected post-notification lease deeds (Ext. A-8, A-9, A-10, A-12, A-13) as evidence for market value, as the appellants failed to establish that there was no appreciation in land value between the date of the Section 4 notification (17.11.1980) and the dates of these transactions, a condition precedent for relying on such evidence as per Administrator General of West Bengal vs. Collector, Varanasi, AIR 1988 SC 943. Furthermore, the Court upheld the rejection of Ext. A-11, an award for land in Jhilmil Tahirpur, on the ground that it was not a 'previous' judgment, as its Section 4 notification date (27.7.81) was subsequent to the present case's notification, following the principle established in Pal Singh and others vs. Union Territory of Chandigarh, JT 1992 (5) SC 371, which mandates that for a judgment or award to be relied upon for market value assessment, it must be a previous judgment. title: RAJIV DAWAR v. HIGH COURT OF DELHI
text: The Supreme Court of India allowed the criminal appeal, setting aside the conviction and sentence imposed on the appellant by the High Court of Delhi under Section 2(c) read with Sections 10 & 15 of the Contempt of Courts Act and Article 215 of the Constitution of India. The original conviction entailed a fine of Rs.2,000/- and suspension from practice for two months. The Supreme Court found that the appellant was not afforded an adequate opportunity to adduce evidence or cross-examine the de facto complainant, either before the Additional Sessions Judge or the High Court, which constitutes a failure to comply with procedural formalities and safeguards in contempt proceedings. Furthermore, it was noted that the Bar Council of Delhi, which had looked into the complaint regarding exorbitant fees and withdrawal from the case, had absolved the appellant of misconduct, though ordering a refund of Rs.4 lakhs for deficiency of professional services, a direction with which the appellant had complied. Given the non-observance of procedural safeguards and the findings of the Disciplinary Authority, the conviction and sentence were deemed unsustainable and consequently set aside. title: DELHI DEVELOPMENT AUTHORITY v. HELLO HOME EDUCATION SOCIETY
text: The Supreme Court allowed the appeals, setting aside the orders of the Division Bench and Single Judge. The Court held that the respondent society had an inordinate delay of 11 years in filing the writ petition, which ought to have been dismissed on this ground alone. Furthermore, the Court found that the society lacked the mandatory Essentiality Certificate and Sponsorship Letter for the Vasant Kunj area, making it ineligible for land allotment. The Court also noted that the change in policy from allotment to auction/tender, implemented from December 15, 2003, was not challenged by the society, and no vested right accrued from internal office notings or in-principle approvals, as these do not constitute final orders until communicated. The principle of negative parity was also rejected, as allotments to other societies, if made contrary to policy, would not create a basis for the respondent's claim. Consequently, the appeals were allowed, the impugned orders were set aside, and the writ petition filed by the society was dismissed. title: M. J. Jacob v. A. Narayanan & Ors.
text: The Supreme Court of India allowed the appeals filed under Section 116A of the Representation of People Act, 1951, thereby setting aside the final judgment and order of the High Court of Kerala. The High Court's judgment had declared the election of the appellant (M.J. Jacob) from no.79 Piravom Legislative Assembly Constituency to be a member of the Kerala Legislative Assembly as void, based on a finding of corrupt practice under Section 123(4) of the Act, concerning the preparation, publication, and distribution of a pamphlet (Ex.P1). The Supreme Court held that the statement in paragraph 2 of the pamphlet, which alleged that a member of the rival candidate's (Shri T.M. Jacob) personal staff had attempted murder and was absconding, did not relate to the personal character or conduct of Shri T.M. Jacob himself. The Court emphasized that for an allegation of corrupt practice, the standard of proof is akin to a criminal charge, requiring proof beyond reasonable doubt, and not a mere preponderance of probabilities. It further clarified that if two views are possible, the benefit of doubt must go to the elected candidate. The Court found no clear pleading of innuendo in the Election Petition to suggest that the pamphlet conveyed an accusation of Shri T.M. Jacob harbouring the absconder. Given that Shri T.M. Jacob himself had not complained about the pamphlet, the Court inferred he did not consider it an aspersion against his personal character. Therefore, the Supreme Court concluded that all five ingredients required to establish a corrupt practice under Section 123(4) of the Act, particularly the requirement that the false statement relates to the personal character or conduct of any candidate, were not met. The appeals were allowed, the High Court's judgment was set aside, and the Election Petition was dismissed with no order as to costs. Citations: Manmohan Kalia vs. Yash & Ors. title: Mahindra and Mahindra Financial Services Ltd. v. Nizamuddin
text: The Supreme Court of India, while adjudicating Civil Appeal No. 8043 of 2022 concerning a dispute between Mahindra and Mahindra Financial Services Ltd. and Nizamuddin, modified the order passed by the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission. The National Commission had upheld the District Forum's order directing the return/refund of Rs. 3,45,000/- (insurance amount) after deducting 10% depreciation, and also awarded Rs. 300/- per day as compensation for the period the hypothecated vehicle was not in use from December 19, 2004, until the date of payment. The Supreme Court found that the District Forum had not provided cogent reasons for awarding Rs. 300/- per day as compensation, especially in the absence of evidence for the loss suffered. However, acknowledging that the seizure and sale of the hypothecated vehicle were illegal, and that the complainant was the owner-cum-driver who paid installments, the Court decided to award reasonable compensation. Instead of remanding the matter, the Court modified the compensation to Rs. 5,000/- per month from December 19, 2004, to December 31, 2007, with interest at 7.5% per annum from December 2004 until actual payment, to be paid within six weeks. The appeal was allowed in part to this extent. title: T.L.THATHACHARIAR v. THE COMMISSIONER, H.R.C.E.  & ORS.
text: The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals, upholding the Madras High Court's decision. The Court held that the Deputy Commissioner had the jurisdiction under Section 64(5) of the Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1959 (Act of 1959) to modify a scheme that was originally framed under Section 92 of the Civil Procedure Code, 1908. The Court reasoned that subsequent legislation, including the Act of 1927, the Act of 1951, and ultimately the Act of 1959, contained provisions (Section 75 of the Act of 1927, Section 103(d) of the Act of 1951, and Section 118(2)(a) of the Act of 1959) that deemed schemes settled under previous acts or under Section 92 of the CPC to be schemes settled under the respective new acts. Consequently, the scheme in question was deemed to be settled under the Act of 1959, making it subject to modification by the Deputy Commissioner under Section 64(5) of the Act of 1959. The contention that the Deputy Commissioner lacked jurisdiction was thus rejected. Citations: 1970 2 M.L.J. 475 Legal tags: Hindu Religious Endowments; Trusteeship; Scheme Administration; Devarajaswamy Temple; Kancheepuram; Civil Procedure Code; Section 92 CPC; Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act; Act of 1927; Act of 1951; Act of 1959; Section 64(5); Jurisdiction; Modification of Scheme; Writ Petition; High Court; Deputy Commissioner; Commissioner; Appeals; Supreme Court

title: SHAM KARTIK SINGH v. MATHURA
text: The Supreme Court held that there was sufficient compliance with the provisions of the amended Section 19 of the U.P. Tenancy Act, 1939, and the rules framed thereunder. The Board of Revenue was not justified in remanding the cases for retrial. The Court found that Section 19 did not bring about any substantial change in the substantive law affecting the determination of whether land was 'sir' or not. The key difference was procedural, requiring the sir-holder to furnish particulars before the recording of evidence. The Court concluded that the particulars had been furnished, even prior to the amendment, and the Additional Commissioner had correctly decided the appeals. The Board of Revenue erred in its assessment due to not considering all relevant documents. Consequently, the appeals were allowed, the order of the Board of Revenue was set aside, and the cases were remanded to the Board for decision in accordance with law, including the contention regarding adivasi rights. Citations: 1967 AIR 732; 1963 SCR (3) 904 Legal tags: Tenancy Law; Sir Lands; Ejectment of Tenants; Decree; Appeal; Filing Particulars; Dismissal of Suit; Substantial Compliance; U.P. title: MST. KHARBUJA KUER v. JANGBAHADUR RAI
text: The Supreme Court held that the High Court was not justified in interfering with the findings of fact of the lower courts in a second appeal. The High Court had wrongly placed the burden of proof on the appellant. The burden of proof is always on the person seeking to sustain a transaction entered into with a pardanashin lady to establish that the document was executed by her after clearly understanding the nature of the transaction. It must be established not only that it was her physical act but also her mental act. This burden can be discharged not only by proving that the document was explained to her and that she understood it, but also by other evidence, direct and circumstantial. The Court allowed the appeal, set aside the decree of the High Court, and decreed the suit with costs. Citations: 1963 AIR 1203; 1963 SCR Supl. title: PU Myllai Hlychho & Ors. v. State of Mizoram & Ors.
text: The Hon'ble Supreme Court, comprising a Constitution Bench, dismissed the appeals, thereby upholding the decision of the Division Bench of the Gauhati High Court. The Court held that the termination of four nominated members from the Mara Autonomous District Council (MADC) vide Notification dated 5.12.2001 was constitutionally valid. This was based on the interpretation of Paragraph 2(6A) of the Sixth Schedule, which stipulates that nominated members hold office 'at the pleasure of the Governor,' and the finding that this power is not a discretionary one under Paragraph 20BB. Consequently, the Governor was bound to act on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers, as per Article 163(1) of the Constitution. The Court also determined that the principles of natural justice regarding notice or hearing are not applicable in such cases of termination under the 'pleasure doctrine.' Furthermore, the Court affirmed the legality of the nomination of four new members to the MADC vide Notification dated 6.12.2001. This power of nomination, under Paragraph 2(1) of the Sixth Schedule, is expressly included in Paragraph 20BB as one to be exercised 'in his discretion' by the Governor, after consulting the Council of Ministers. The Court rejected the contention that the Governor failed to exercise independent discretion, noting that consultation is mandated and that Article 163(2) prohibits challenging the validity of such discretionary acts. The argument that the Sixth Schedule functions as a 'Constitution within the Constitution,' making the Governor independent of the Council of Ministers, was also rejected, emphasizing its integration within the broader constitutional framework. Therefore, the termination and subsequent nomination were upheld as being in accordance with the Constitutional provisions and the Sixth Schedule. Citations: AIR 1955 SC 549; (1970) 3 SCR 505; (1971) 2 SCC 63; (1971) 3 SCR 461; (1974) 2 SCC 831; (1994) 5 SCC 267; (1969) 2 SCC 262 Legal tags: Sixth Schedule to the Constitution; Governor's Powers; Mara Autonomous District Council (MADC); Nomination of Members; Termination of Members; Discretionary Powers of Governor; Aid and Advice of Council of Ministers; Article 163 of the Constitution; Paragraph 2(1) of Sixth Schedule; Paragraph 2(6A) of Sixth Schedule; Paragraph 20BB of Sixth Schedule; Principles of Natural Justice; Pleasure Doctrine; Constitutional Interpretation; Tribal Areas Administration; Mizoram Autonomous District Councils (Constitution and Conduct of Business of the District Councils) Rules, 1974; Gauhati High Court; Supreme Court of India; Constitution (Amendment) Act, 1988; Parliamentary System of Government; Cabinet System of Government; Executive Powers of State

title: EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE OF U.P. STATE WAREHOUSINGCORPORATION, LI v. CHANDRA KIRAN TYAGI
text: The Supreme Court held that the termination of the respondent's service was in violation of Regulation 16(3) of the Uttar Pradesh State Warehousing Corporation Regulations, 1961, as the prescribed procedure was not followed. However, the Court ruled that a declaration for reinstatement would not be granted. The Court reasoned that while the breach of the regulation made the dismissal wrongful and liable for damages, it did not render the dismissal order a nullity that entitled the respondent to be treated as still in service. The Court distinguished this case from those where statutory bodies acted in breach of mandatory statutory obligations, which would render the dismissal void. In this instance, the regulations were made under Section 54 of the Agricultural Produce (Development and Warehousing) Corporation Act, 1956, and a breach of these regulations did not amount to a breach of a statutory obligation. Therefore, the respondent's remedy was limited to a claim for damages, not reinstatement. The High Court's judgment granting reinstatement was set aside. Citations: 1970 AIR 1244; 1970 SCR  (2) 250; 1970 SCC  (2) 838 Legal tags: Wrongful Dismissal; Breach of Regulations; Reinstatement Claim; Damages for Wrongful Termination; Statutory Obligation; Contract of Personal Service; Termination of Employment; Disciplinary Proceedings; Principles of Natural Justice; Agricultural Produce (Development and Warehousing) Corporation Act, 1956; Uttar Pradesh State Warehousing Corporation Regulations, 1961; Regulation 16(3); Master and Servant Relationship; Void Order; Nullity of Order; Statutory Status; Specific Relief Act, 1877; Article 311; Industrial Law; Public Servants; Statutory Body; Mandatory Obligation

title: THAKUR RAGHUBIR SINGH v. COURT OF WARDS, AJMER, AND ANOTHER.
text: The Supreme Court held that Section 112 of the Ajmer Tenancy and Land Records Act, 1950, when read with Sections 6 and 7 of the Ajmer Government Wards Regulation, 1888, infringed the fundamental rights of the petitioner under Article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution. The Court found that the said provisions allowed the Court of Wards to assume superintendence of a landlord's property based on its subjective determination of habitual infringement of tenant rights, and this discretion could not be questioned in a civil court. The Court ruled that these provisions were not reasonable restrictions in the interest of the general public under Article 19(5), nor were they validated by Article 31-A of the Constitution, as the "modification" in Article 31-A refers to extinguishment or substantial alteration of proprietary rights, not mere suspension of management rights. Consequently, the Court directed the Court of Wards to restore possession of the petitioner's estate and properties to him and allowed the costs of the petition. Citations: 1953 AIR 373; 1953 SCR 1049 Legal tags: Constitution of India, 1950, arts. 19(1)(f), 19(5), 31-A; Ajmer Tenancy and Land Records Act, 1950, s. 112; Ajmer Government Wards Regulation, 1888, ss. 6, 7; Landlord and Tenant Rights; Fundamental Rights; Article 19(1)(f); Article 19(5); Article 31-A; Reasonable Restrictions; Subjective Determination; Discretion of Executive; Vagueness of Law; Property Management; Restoration of Property; Writ Petition; Article 32; Petitioner's Rights; Court of Wards; Penal Provisions; Validity of Law; Fundamental Rights Infringement; Property Rights; Suspension of Rights

title: DIPALI BISWAS & ORS. v. NIRMALENDU MUKHERJEE & ORS.
text: The Supreme Court dismissed the Civil Appeal, upholding the High Court's order that confirmed the executing court's dismissal of the appellants' application under Section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. The appellants, legal representatives of the judgment-debtor, had challenged the auction sale on the ground of non-compliance with Order XXI, Rule 64 CPC, arguing that only a portion of the property sufficient to satisfy the decree should have been sold, and that selling the entire property constituted a jurisdictional error. The Court rejected this contention, citing several reasons: (i) the objection relating to Order XXI, Rule 64 was raised for the first time in the fifth round of a decades-long litigation, despite prior opportunities; (ii) the second petition under Section 47 was barred by the principle of res judicata, as clarified by Explanation VII to Section 11 CPC, which applies to execution proceedings; (iii) the appellants failed to provide details on the property's divisibility, given its small extent (17 decimals or 7450 Sq.ft.); (iv) an earlier High Court order dated 20.12.1990, which had attained finality, explicitly stated that the purchased property was the absolute property of the auction purchasers, leaving no further claim to the judgment-debtor; and (v) the sale had progressed through all stages, including the sale becoming absolute (Order XXI, Rule 92) and the issuance of a sale certificate (Order XXI, Rule 94), making the belated objection at the stage of delivery of possession untenable. Consequently, the appeal was found to be devoid of merits. Citations: (1977) 3 SCC 337; (1989) Supp. 2 SCC 693 Legal tags: Civil Appeal; Supreme Court of India; Execution Proceedings; Code of Civil Procedure 1908; Section 47 CPC; Order XXI Rule 64 CPC; Order XXI Rule 90 CPC; Order XXI Rule 66 CPC; Res Judicata; Jurisdictional Error; Money Decree; Auction Sale; Sale Proclamation; Sale Certificate; Delivery of Possession; Litigation History; Judgment Debtor; Auction Purchasers; Finality of Orders; Dismissal of Appeal

title: SIVAYOGESWARA COTTON PRESS,DEVANGERE AND OTHERS v. M. PANCHAKSHARAPPA AND ANOTHER
text: The Supreme Court held that the lease, when read as a whole and properly construed, created a permanent tenancy and not a tenancy at will or one for an indefinite period valid only during the life of the lessee. The Court found that the stipulation granting the lessee the right to surrender the lease at any time after the first twenty years did not, in the absence of a corresponding provision for the lessor, give the lessor the right to call upon the lessee to quit at any time, nor was it inconsistent with a permanent tenancy. The presumption attaching to a lease for building purposes for no fixed period was therefore not weakened. The Court further held that it is always open to a lessee to surrender their leasehold interest to the lessor by mutual consent, and it is not necessary for such consent to be present at the time of surrender. Since the surrender after twenty years had been agreed upon by the parties and was for the benefit of the lessee, it could not be construed as derogating from the right to a permanent tenancy. Consequently, the appeal was allowed, the judgments and decrees of the lower courts were set aside, and the suit was dismissed with costs. Citations: 1962 AIR 413; 1962 SCR Supl. (3) 876 Legal tags: Lease; Permanent Tenancy; Tenancy at Will; Construction of Lease Deed; Right to Surrender; Heritable and Assignable Lease; Building Lease; Landlord-Tenant Law; Property Law; Indian Contract Act; Civil Procedure Code; Ejectment Suit; Lessor's Rights; Lessee's Rights; Registered Lease; Subletting; Rent Enhancement

title: AASTHA DIAGNOSTIC CLINICAL LAB. & ORS. v. STATE OF J&K & ORS.
text: Leave granted. The appeals are disposed of in terms of the signed order. The appellants, running hospitals/clinics and diagnostic centres in the State of Jammu and Kashmir, were directed by the High Court to comply with basic infrastructure facilities. While acknowledging the appellants' contentions regarding difficulty in acquiring space and potential increase in healthcare costs, the Court upheld the necessity of the guidelines issued by the Government for registration and licensing of private hospitals, nursing homes, and clinical establishments. However, considering that the appellants had been operating under previous licenses, the Court granted them six months to update facilities and one year for structural alterations to comply with the new norms. Applications for exemption or modification of guidelines are to be filed with the Director of Health Services for consideration. title: SENIOR MANAGER (P&D),RIICO LTD. v. THE STATE OF RAJASTHAN & ANR
text: The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the judgment of the Rajasthan High Court which had affirmed the dismissal of the appellant's Criminal Revision and Protest Petition. The Court clarified that the bar under Section 195(1)(b)(ii) Cr.P.C. is not attracted when an offence like forgery of a document is committed prior to its production or being given in evidence in a court proceeding, aligning with the Constitution Bench judgment in Iqbal Singh Marwah. However, the Chief Judicial Magistrate, after remand, and subsequently the Revisional Court and the High Court, had dismissed the appellant's plea not on the grounds of Section 195(1)(b)(ii) Cr.P.C., but on merits, finding no prima facie case of forgery or fraud made out against Respondent No. 2 based on the materials and evidence on record, including the FSL report which, while confirming forgery of the appellant's signature, did not establish that Respondent No. 2 committed it. Consequently, the Supreme Court found no infirmity in the High Court's view. title: Maharashtra Ekta Hawkers Union and another v. Municipal Corporation, Greater Mumbai and others
text:
The Supreme Court, in response to the persistent issues faced by street vendors and the inadequacy of previous measures, has directed the implementation of the National Policy on Urban Street Vendors, 2009 throughout the country until appropriate legislation is enacted. The Court emphasized the importance of Town Vending Committees (TVCs) at the city/town level, which will be responsible for demarcating vending zones, registering vendors, and ensuring a participatory approach involving vendors, resident welfare associations, and other civil society organizations. The policy prioritizes the registration of vendors, with a focus on transparency and non-discretionary allocation of spaces, including time-sharing models and the development of specific vending markets. The Court has lifted the embargo on High Courts entertaining matters related to street vending, allowing aggrieved parties to seek redressal. Additionally, physically challenged individuals previously permitted to operate stalls will be allowed to continue, and if there's any conflict between the 2009 Policy and municipal laws, the policy will prevail. The Chief Justices of High Courts are requested to nominate benches to monitor the implementation of the 2009 Policy and any future legislation. title: DR. (SMT.) SHIPRA v. SHRI SHANTI LAL KHOIWAL
text: The Court, concurring with the High Court's decision, held that the 'true copy' of the election petition furnished by the appellant (election petitioner) to the respondent (successful candidate) was fatally defective. This defect arose because the 'true copy' did not indicate that the appellant's affidavit, supporting allegations of corrupt practice, had been duly sworn or affirmed as required by law. An affidavit alleging corrupt practice must be in the prescribed format and properly sworn or affirmed. The omission in the 'true copy' misled in a material particular by giving the impression that the affidavit was not properly executed, rendering the supply of such a copy fatal to the election petition. Citations: 1996 AIR 1691; 1996 SCC  (5) 181; JT 1996 (5)   681; 1996 SCALE  (3)369 Legal tags: Election Petition; Corrupt Practice; Affidavit; True Copy; Material Particular; Sworn Affidavit; Affirmed Affidavit; Legal Procedure; Fatal Defect; High Court Decision; Supreme Court Agreement

title: State Civil Service Officers v. Government of India
text: The Supreme Court upheld the decision of the Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT) to strike down two notifications issued by the Government of India, which had increased the cadre strength in relation to State Civil Service officers and promoted them to the Indian Administrative Service (IAS). The court ruled that the notifications were invalid and inoperative. Citations: [Supreme Court Judgment] Legal tags: Central Administrative Tribunal; Government of India; Indian Administrative Service

title: THE STATE OF RAJASTHAN & ORS. v. PHOOL SINGH
text: The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the Rajasthan High Court's orders that reinstated the respondent with 50% back wages. The Court held that a departmental proceeding and a criminal proceeding are distinct. Acquittal in a criminal trial, especially when granted on the 'benefit of doubt,' does not automatically mandate reinstatement in service if the employee was found guilty of misconduct in departmental proceedings. The Court distinguished the present case from Capt. M. Paul Anthony v. Bharat Gold Mines Ltd., emphasizing that the latter's specific facts, including denial of subsistence allowance and denial to stay departmental proceedings pending criminal trial, were crucial. The Court reiterated that the standard of proof in departmental proceedings (preponderance of probabilities) differs from criminal trials (beyond reasonable doubt). The respondent was dismissed for gross indiscipline, negligence, and misconduct, which tarnished the police force's image, and the departmental inquiry found him guilty, which should not be overturned merely due to his acquittal in the criminal case on benefit of doubt. Citations: (1999) 3 SCC 679; (2019) 20 SCC 588; (2005) 7 SCC 764; (2020) SCC OnLine SC 886 Legal tags: Departmental Proceedings; Criminal Proceedings; Acquittal; Reinstatement; Benefit of Doubt; Misconduct; Gross Indiscipline; Negligence; Standard of Proof; Preponderance of Probabilities; Beyond Reasonable Doubt; Service Law; Disciplinary Authority; Natural Justice; Judicial Review; Capt. M. Paul Anthony; Sitaram Mishra; Ajit Kumar Nag; Rajasthan Police Service; Indian Penal Code; Arms Act

title: Contractor v. State
text: The court finds that the subordinate judge had allowed the contractor's application under Section 80(2) C.P.C., which permits dispensation of notice requirement in case of urgent and immediate orders. The court also holds that the State waived its objection to the maintainability of the suit by not raising it at the earliest point of time. However, the court notes that the order allowing the application is cryptic and does not specify the reasons for granting leave under Section 80(2) C.P.C. Citations: L.J. Leach & Co. Ltd. v M/s Jardine Skinner & Co.; Smt Ganga Bai v Vijay Kumar; B K Narayana Pillai v Parmeswaran Pillai; Ma Shwe Mya v Maung Mo Hnaung Legal tags: Judgment; Contractor; State; Section 80(2) C.P.C.; Notice requirement; Urgent and immediate orders; Waiver of objection

title: STATE OF PUNJAB v. DEEPAK MATTU
text: The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the orders of the High Court which had suspended the conviction of a public servant, Deepak Mattu, under Sections 7 and 13(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act. The High Court had initially allowed the suspension of conviction under Section 389 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, citing potential delay in the appeal and arguable points, and subsequently dismissed an application for vacation of stay, maintaining that it was an 'exceptional case'. The Supreme Court held that an order of suspension of conviction is not to be readily granted and should be limited to very exceptional cases, especially for public servants convicted of corruption, in line with its prior judgments in K.C. Sareen Vs. C.B.I., Chandigarh and State of Maharashtra Vs. Gajanan. Mere delay in the disposal of an appeal or the existence of arguable points are not sufficient 'special reasons' to suspend a conviction. The Court emphasized that allowing a public servant convicted of corruption to continue holding public office impairs public morale and the integrity of institutions. It further clarified that the High Court was empowered to modify its own interlocutory order when an apparent error existed and the matter was yet to be finally disposed of. Citations: K.C. Sareen Vs. C.B.I., Chandigarh [(2001) 6 SCC 584]; State of Maharashtra Vs. Gajanan and Another [(2003) 12 SCC 432]; Union of India Vs. Atar Singh [(2003) 12 SCC 434] Legal tags: Criminal Appeal; Suspension of Conviction; Section 389 Cr.P.C.; Prevention of Corruption Act; Public Servant; Corruption Charges; Appellate Court Powers; Exceptional Cases; Interlocutory Order; High Court Review; Supreme Court of India; Judicial Precedent; K.C. Sareen Case; State of Maharashtra Vs. Gajanan Case; Rigorous Imprisonment; Sections 7 and 13(2) of Prevention of Corruption Act

title: NIVRUTTI & ORS v. STATE OF MAHARASTRA
text: The Supreme Court, in this appeal, partly allowed the appeal and set aside the conviction of the appellants under Section 302/34 IPC. The conviction was altered to one under Section 326/34 IPC, and the sentence was reduced to 5 years of rigorous imprisonment. The conviction and sentence under Section 323/34 IPC were upheld. The court noted that while one appellant was armed with an iron rod, the evidence did not conclusively prove the intention to murder, as most injuries were simple and on non-vital parts. The court relied on precedents like Ram Lal vs. Delhi Admn. and Bhima @ Bhimrao Sida Kamble vs. State of Maharashtra, which dealt with cases where grievous hurt was intended, leading to death, falling under Section 325 or 326 IPC rather than Section 302 IPC. The court also disbelieved the prosecution's claim of obstruction in the removal of the deceased to the hospital, as it was an improvement not mentioned in police statements. title: Tapan Kumar Dutta v. Commissioner of Income Tax, West Bengal
text: The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the High Court's decision. The core issue was the validity of the second notice issued under Section 158BD of the Income Tax Act, 1961. The Court found that the Assessing Officer (AO) had correctly issued a fresh notice under Section 158BD on November 20, 2000, after determining that the initial notice under Section 158BC dated September 9, 1999, was not in conformity with the requirements of Section 158BD. The Court clarified that Section 158BD applies when undisclosed income belongs to a person other than the one searched, and the AO must be satisfied of this. The Court noted that the AO, being the same for both the firm and the appellant, had the jurisdiction to proceed against the appellant if prima facie satisfaction was reached. However, the AO's initial notice to the appellant on September 9, 1999, was issued concurrently with the notice to the firm, before any perusal or verification of seized documents, thus not satisfying the conditions of Section 158BD. Consequently, the AO rightly issued a second notice under Section 158BD after proper satisfaction. The court also found the order passed by the Additional Commissioner of Income Tax under Section 144A to be contravention of law. Therefore, the appeal was dismissed. title: KRISHNA PRASAD AND OTHERS v. GAURI KUMARI DEVI
text: The Supreme Court confirmed the order passed by the Patna High Court, thereby dismissing the appeal with costs. The High Court had held that Section 4(d) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, constituted a bar against the execution of a personal decree by proceeding to sell the other, non-mortgaged properties of the respondent, given that the mortgaged estate had vested in the State. The Supreme Court reasoned that the Act's scheme, particularly Chapters IV, V, and VI, provides an integrated and self-sufficient code for determining and paying claims of secured creditors. Section 24(5) of the Act makes the compensation payable on the acquisition of the mortgaged estate a kind of substituted security, against which the mortgage claim must be enforced under the Act's provisions. Furthermore, the original decree explicitly provided for personal liability only if the mortgaged properties were insufficient to satisfy the decretal amount. Since the appellants had already filed a claim under Section 14 of the Act, and an amount had been determined by the Claims Officer, they must first seek to recover that amount from the compensation money as provided by Section 24(5) of the Act before they can proceed to execute the personal decree against the respondent's other properties. Thus, Section 4(d) of the Act, on proper construction and in light of the Act's objectives, precluded the executing Court from enforcing the direction for a personal decree for realizing the mortgage debt at the present stage, especially since the entire mortgaged property was an estate for which a claim was pending. Citations: 1962 AIR 1464; 1962 SCR Supl. title: John K. Abraham v. Simon C. Abraham & Another
text: The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the impugned order, conviction, and sentence imposed on the appellant. The Court found that the High Court committed a serious illegality in reversing the trial court's judgment, which had acquitted the appellant. The trial court had noted several vital defects in the complainant's case, including inconsistencies regarding the date of payment, the source of funds, and contradictions about who wrote the cheque and the amount in words. The Supreme Court held that the complainant failed to establish a case under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act due to these lacunae in evidence, which were improperly disregarded by the High Court. Consequently, the presumption under Sections 118 and 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act could not be drawn, and the appellant's acquittal by the trial court was upheld. title: Sushil Thomas Abraham v. M/s Skyline Build. Thr. Its Partner & Ors.
text: The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the impugned order of the High Court, and remanded the case back to the High Court for a fresh decision. The Court held that the dismissal of the appellant's application to file a suit as an indigent person under Order 33 Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure by the Trial Court, and the subsequent upholding of this rejection by the High Court, did not preclude the appellant from filing an application under Order 44 Rule 1 of the Code to appeal as an indigent person. The Court clarified that the grant or refusal of such a status by the Trial Court is confined to the disposal of the suit, and Order 44 Rule 3(1) and 3(2) contemplate holding an inquiry at the appellate stage to determine if the applicant has become an indigent person since the date of the decree appealed from. The High Court's reasoning that the prior rejection barred a fresh application was found to be contrary to the relevant orders and thus unsustainable. The High Court is directed to hold an inquiry as contemplated under Order 44 Rule 3(2) or direct the Trial Court to do so, and pass appropriate orders based on the outcome of the inquiry, preferably within six months. The Court also noted that if the appellant had not paid the ad valorem court fees in the trial court, it should be recovered from him. Citations: SLP (C) No. 19516 of 2014; RFA No. .../2011; CMC No.78/2011; CMA No.248 of 1998; OS No.227/2000; OS No.921/95 Legal tags: Civil Procedure Code; Order 33; Order 44; Indigent Person; Court Fees; Appeal; Remand; Inquiry; Financial Capacity; Ad Valorem Court Fees; Trial Court; High Court; Supreme Court

title: Citibank N.A. v. Geekay Agropack (P) Ltd. & Anr
text: The Supreme Court upheld the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission's decision, finding both Citibank N.A. and State Bank of Mysore jointly and severally liable for deficiency in service in failing to collect sale proceeds from a purchaser. The National Commission's award of Rs. 5 lakhs compensation to Geekay Agropack (P) Ltd. and Rs. 50,000/- costs to Citibank N.A. was deemed adequate for the deficiency in service. The Court clarified that Geekay's appeal for further compensation for total loss was misconceived, and advised Geekay to pursue recovery of the total amount of loss through a civil suit, which had reportedly already been filed. Consequently, all appeals were dismissed. title: The State of Kerala v. Sister Amala & Anr.
text: The Supreme Court of India, in its order dated 05.08.2022, dismissed the Special Leave Petition filed by the State of Kerala against the High Court of Kerala's order quashing proceedings against the respondents (nuns) in Crime No. 1019/2018. The respondents were accused of disclosing the identity of a rape victim under Section 228A of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) by publishing her photograph via WhatsApp. While acknowledging that the High Court's finding was not appreciated, the Supreme Court decided not to pursue the matter further, citing the passage of four years since the occurrence in 2018. The Court emphasized the legislative intent behind Section 228A of the IPC, which aims to prevent social victimisation of sexual offence victims, referencing the Nipun Saxena case. Considering the peculiar circumstances, including the respondents being nuns who have entered a religious order, the Court concluded that further proceedings might defeat the object of the provision, thus dismissing the Special Leave Petition. title: DARYAO SINGH v. STATE OF MADHYA PRADESH
text: The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the conviction of the appellant under Section 302/34, Indian Penal Code, for the murder of Negji. The High Court had reversed the Trial Court's order of acquittal, finding the evidence of prosecution witnesses (PWs 1, 3, and 4), though related to the deceased, to be credible and corroborated by PW 10 and medical evidence. The Supreme Court affirmed that interested testimony cannot be discarded solely on that ground but requires cautious evaluation. The Court rejected the appellant's contention that the medical evidence (blisters on the body) indicated death occurred 14-20 days prior, clarifying that blisters appear within eighteen to forty-eight hours of decomposition, especially given the body's prolonged exposure to heat and humidity. The chain of events established that death occurred on 25th September 1970. The argument regarding the appellant's physical disability preventing him from inflicting the fatal injury was also rejected in favour of the direct evidence of three witnesses. Consequently, the appeal was dismissed, bail cancelled, and the appellant was directed to surrender. title: Madhya Pradesh Administration v. Tribhuban
text: The Supreme Court modified the High Court's order of reinstatement with full back wages. While acknowledging that the termination of the respondent's services violated Section 25F of the Industrial Disputes Act, the Court, considering the nature of appointment as a daily wager and the principles laid down in cases like Secretary, State of Karnataka v. Umadevi (3), decided that full reinstatement with back wages was not appropriate. Instead, the Court directed the appellant (Madhya Pradesh Administration) to pay a sum of Rs. 75,000/- as compensation to the respondent, considering the peculiar facts and circumstances of the case, and that the Industrial Court's award of retrenchment compensation was not questioned. The appeal was allowed to this extent with no order as to costs. title: SH MEDICAL CENTRE HOSPITAL v. STATE OF KERALA & ORS.
text: The Supreme Court of India, in Civil Appeal No. 665 of 2014, upheld the judgment and order dated 13th March, 2009, passed by the High Court of Kerala at Ernakulam in W.A. No. 362 of 2007, thereby dismissing the appeal filed by SH Medical Centre Hospital. The primary issue before the Court was whether the appellant-hospital was entitled to building tax exemption under the Kerala Building Tax Act, 1975. The High Court had previously dismissed the appellant's writ appeal, affirming that the hospital was not entitled to full building tax exemption, relying on its previous judgments in Medical Trust Hospital v. State of Kerala and Thirurangadi Muslim Orphanage Committee v. The Government of Kerala. The High Court interpreted the 'Explanation' clause of Section 3(1) of the Act, which defines "charitable purpose" to include "relief of the poor and free medical aid," concluding that buildings are only eligible for exemption if principally used for providing free medical relief. As the appellant hospital charged nominal fees from patients who could afford them, in addition to providing free services to others, the High Court determined that the entire building was not used "principally" for charitable purposes. The Supreme Court considered two pivotal questions: (i) whether the application of income derived from a building for charitable purpose is sufficient to hold that a building is used 'principally' for 'charitable purpose' as per Section 3(1)(b) of the Act for exemption from building tax, and (ii) whether the Kerala High Court correctly interpreted the 'Explanation' clause to Section 3(1) to mean solely 'relief of the poor and free medical relief'. The Supreme Court concurred with the High Court's interpretation, affirming that the mere application of income for charitable purposes is not sufficient to deem the entire building "principally used" for charitable purposes without more specific evidence regarding the proportion of free versus paid services and the actual utilization of the building area for charitable activities. The Court reiterated that for building tax exemption under the Act, the focus is on the direct use of the building. Consequently, only the specific portions of the building directly utilized for providing free medical aid are eligible for exemption. The appeal was dismissed, and the interim stay order was vacated, without costs. title: AJIT KUMAR PALIT v. STATE OF WEST BENGAL
text: The Supreme Court held that a Special Court, constituted under the West Bengal Criminal Law Amendment (Special Courts) Act, 1949 (W.B. XXI of 1949), takes cognizance of an offence as soon as it receives the State Government's order of allotment under Section 4(2) of the Act and the records of the case. Upon such receipt, the Special Court becomes vested with jurisdiction to apply its mind to the facts and issue process to the accused, thereby commencing the trial. The Court clarified that the provisions of Section 190(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, are inapplicable to a Special Court, as such a court is not among the Magistrates designated by that section. Furthermore, Section 5(1) of the 1949 Act specifically exempts the Special Court from requiring an order of commitment for trial, thus rendering Section 193(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, inapplicable despite the Special Court being 'deemed' a Court of Session under Section 5(2). The term 'cognizance' in criminal law merely signifies taking judicial notice, and where the statute does not prescribe specific material beyond the allotment order, no additional material is required. Regarding the West Bengal Criminal Law Amendment (Special Courts) (Amending) Act, 1960, the Court ruled that this amendment, which altered Section 5(1) to allow cognizance in the manner laid down in Section 190(1)(a) and (b) without commitment, was not declaratory but effected a change. Therefore, it did not retrospectively invalidate proceedings validly taken before its enactment under the proper construction of the unamended Act. The appeal was dismissed. Citations: 1963 AIR 765; 1963 SCR Supl. title: RAJASTHAN FINANCIAL CORPN. & ANR. v. THE OFFICIAL LIQUIDATOR & ANR.
text: The Supreme Court held that when a company is in liquidation, the distribution of sale proceeds of assets, whether realized by a financial institution under the Recovery of Debts Act or by a financial corporation under the SFC Act, must be in accordance with Section 529A read with Section 529 of the Companies Act. The Official Liquidator must be associated with the sale process to ensure proper price realization and distribution under the supervision of the company court. While the right to sell may not be taken away, it is restricted by the need for the Official Liquidator's association and the company court's oversight to ensure distribution according to Section 529A. The Court affirmed the company court's directions but modified them to include a fresh valuation of the properties due to the lapse of time. The appeal was disposed of with these directions, making no order as to costs. Citations: AIR 1993 Bombay 392; AIR 1993 Bombay 392; (1991) 70 Comp. Cas. 38; (1991) 71 Comp. title: M/s. Craft Interiors Pvt. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Central Excise,Bangalore & Anr.
text: The Supreme Court held that items like storage cabinets, kitchen counters, running counters, large reception/conference tables etc., which are ordinarily immovable or cannot be removed without cannibalizing (reducing them to broken pieces), are not furniture and hence not excisable under Sub-heading 9403 of the Central Excise Tariff Act, 1944. However, items like tables, desks, chairs, etc., even if affixed to the ground, are considered furniture and are excisable. The Court emphasized that the popular meaning of the word 'furniture' should prevail over its dictionary or etymological meaning. The appeals were allowed, and the matter was remitted to the Tribunal for a fresh order in light of these observations. title: BHAU RAM v. B. BAIJNATH SINGH
text: The Supreme Court, in a split decision (3-2), ruled that Section 10 of the Rewa State Pre-emption Act, 1946, which allowed pre-emption based on vicinage, imposed unreasonable restrictions on the right to property under Article 19(1)(f) and was thus void. The majority held that this provision restricted a vendor's right to sell to a buyer of their choice and exposed buyers to litigation. Conversely, the dissenting judges (Sarkar and Das Gupta, JJ.) opined that vicinage pre-emption was a reasonable restriction, promoting community living and preventing disputes, and that pre-constitution customary laws were not necessarily rendered unreasonable by the Constitution. Regarding the Punjab Pre-emption Act, 1913, the Court held that grounds for pre-emption based on co-sharership (Section 16, first ground), common staircases (third ground), and common entrances (fourth ground) were valid as they imposed reasonable restrictions in the interest of the general public. However, the sixth ground, also based on vicinage, was deemed invalid for similar reasons as Section 10 of the Rewa Act. The Court also found no contravention of Article 14 due to exemptions in Section 5 of the Punjab Act, as the exempted properties (shops, katras, etc.) formed distinct classes from private residential property. Finally, Chapter XIV of the Berar Land Revenue Code, 1928, concerning pre-emption among occupants of a survey number, was upheld as valid. The Court reasoned that this provision, akin to co-sharership, promoted consolidation of agricultural holdings, which was in the public interest. Consequently, the appeal concerning the Rewa Act was allowed, while appeals concerning the Punjab Act and the Berar Code were dismissed. Citations: 1962 AIR 1476; 1962 SCR Supl. title: The petitioner v. The respondent
text: A writ petition was filed to appoint a sole arbitrator in an international arbitration dispute. The court considered the provisions of the Arbitration and Conciliation (Amendment) Act, 2015, specifically Section 11(9), which deals with the appointment of arbitrators. The court analyzed various institutional arbitration rules from different countries that provide for consideration of nationality as a factor in appointing an arbitrator. The court concluded that the word 'may' in Section 11(9) is not intended to be read as 'must' or 'shall', and therefore, it is not mandatory to appoint an arbitrator not belonging to the nationality of either party. Based on this interpretation, the court appointed a retired judge from India as the sole arbitrator in the case. Citations: 1. Swiss Essays on International Arbitration (1984); 4. title: Union of India & Anr. v. Manik Lal Banerjee
text: The Supreme Court allowed the appeal filed by the Union of India, setting aside the impugned judgment of the High Court and the Central Administrative Tribunal. The Court held that the Respondent, a railway servant, being an employee of the Central Government and governed by the Railway Services (Pension) Rules, 1993, is excluded from the applicability of the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, by virtue of Section 2(e) of the 1972 Act. The decision in Pritam Singh, relied upon by the lower forums, was deemed per incuriam and not a binding precedent, as it failed to consider the exclusionary clause in Section 2(e) of the 1972 Act. Furthermore, the Court clarified that Rule 15(4)(ii) of the 1993 Rules is irrelevant to gratuity computation and the Fifth Pay Commission recommendations regarding dearness pay linkage were prospective from 1.4.1995, thus not applicable to the Respondent who retired on 31.1.1995. title: Nagaraj v. Union of India
text: The Supreme Court, in Criminal Appeal No. 324 of 2019, affirmed the concurrent findings of guilt by the three lower courts (JMFC, Additional District and Sessions Judge, and High Court) and upheld the appellant's conviction under Section 160(2) of the Railways Act, 1989, for causing damage to a railway crossing gate. The Court found no perversity or illegality in the appreciation of evidence. However, the appeal was allowed in part concerning the sentence. While the initial sentence was six months simple imprisonment, the Supreme Court reduced this to the period already undergone by the appellant (approximately one month). This reduction was based on the considerations that the appellant had already served a portion of his sentence, the offence did not involve injury to any human being or moral turpitude but only damage to railway property, and the incident was 13 years old. The plea for release under the Probation of Offenders Act, 1958, was rejected as it was not raised before the lower courts. Consequently, the appellant is not required to undergo any further jail sentence, and his bail bond stands discharged. Citations: CRIMINAL APPEAL No.324 OF 2019; S.L.P.(Crl.) title: STATE OF KERALA & ANR. ETC. ETC. v. M/S RDS PROJECT LIMITED & ORS. ETC. ETC.
text: The Supreme Court of India allowed the appeals filed by the State of Kerala, setting aside the judgment and review judgment of the Kerala High Court. The High Court had erroneously directed the State Government to conduct a load test on the Palarivattom Flyover, despite the State Government having accepted the recommendations of a High Level Expert Committee. This Committee, after considering divergent opinions from IIT Madras and Dr. E. Sreedharan, concluded that demolishing and reconstructing the flyover, as proposed by Dr. E. Sreedharan, was preferable due to the assured 100-year service life, notwithstanding the higher cost, given the extensive strengthening required for 97 out of 102 girders. The Supreme Court held that the High Court, instead of applying the well-established parameters of judicial review to ascertain if the State Government's decision violated Article 14, had improperly delved into the technical merits of the matter itself. The apex court affirmed that accepting an expert committee's reasoned report by the Government does not constitute arbitrary behaviour. Consequently, the pending Writ Petitions in the High Court are to be disposed of within six months. title: Radha Lakshmy S.A. v. Assainar.A.
text: The Supreme Court of India, having considered the appeals challenging various orders of the High Court of Kerala concerning the reconstruction and redevelopment plan and the functioning of the Empowered Agency, has issued the following directions: (i) The State Government is directed to proceed with the Empowered Agency for the reconstruction/redevelopment plan, ensuring that all concerned stakeholders are duly assisted through this agency. (ii) The entire proceedings in Writ Petition (Civil) No. 26030/2019, pertaining to the reconstruction, shall be proceeded with. (iii) Any third party in the ongoing process shall be afforded a full and fair opportunity. (iv) The State Government is directed to file a writ petition in the High Court related to the Empowered Agency and the reconstruction plan to seek further legal action or clarification for its implementation. The judgment acknowledges the previous orders of the High Court of Kerala, the constitution and recommendations of an Empowered Committee, and the proposals for a Master Plan and Detailed Project Report, emphasizing the continuity of reconstruction efforts in adherence to legal procedures. title: Commissioner of Income Tax, Nagpur v. Baba Saheb Kedar Ginning and Pressing Cooperative Society Ltd.
text: The Supreme Court disposed of the appeals filed by the Department with no order as to costs. The Court held that the Department failed to consider factors such as the provisions of the Cotton Ginning and Pressing Factories Act, 1925, and the expenses incurred towards labour charges. The Department should have also examined the proportion of income from storage facilities versus ginning and pressing activities, rather than applying an ad-hoc 50% rule. The Court noted that remitting the matter to the Assessing Officer after fifteen years would not be in the interest of justice. For future assessment years, the Department must examine the total income of the assessee and determine the allocation of rental income within the composite charge using the principle of proportionality. title: Commnr. Of Central Excise, Calcutta v. M/s. Panihati Rubber Ltd
text: The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the Tribunal's and High Court's findings that the respondent was entitled to a refund of excise duty paid under protest. The Court found that the price of the goods supplied to the Indian Railways did not include an element for excise duty, especially considering the correspondence and certificates from the Railway Administration indicating 'E.D.-Nil' for certain contracts and specifying rates inclusive of duty for others, with no separate payment arranged for Central Excise Duty. The doctrine of unjust enrichment was held not to be attracted as the excise duty burden was not passed on to the buyer. The appeal by the Commissioner of Central Excise, Calcutta against M/s. Panihati Rubber Ltd. was dismissed, with the appellant directed to comply with the Tribunal's order within four weeks and pay costs of Rs. 10,000/-. title: JAGMAIL SINGH & ANR. v. KARAMJIT SINGH & ORS.
text: The Supreme Court allowed the Civil Appeal, setting aside the judgment dated 09.01.2017 passed by the High Court of Punjab and Haryana at Chandigarh in Civil Revision No. 7271 of 2015. The High Court had confirmed the order of the Civil Judge (Junior Division), Moga, which dismissed the appellants' application filed under Sections 65 and 66 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, seeking permission to prove a copy of the Will dated 24.01.1989 by way of secondary evidence. The High Court had erroneously observed that the pre-requisite condition of the Will's existence was not proved. The Supreme Court found that the High Court committed a grave error of law by not properly evaluating the evidence and holding that the pre-requisite condition, i.e., existence of the Will, remained unestablished on record, thereby denying an opportunity to the appellants to produce secondary evidence, despite the appellants having laid the factual foundation for such evidence. The Supreme Court held that the impugned judgment suffered from material irregularity and patent errors of law. Consequently, the appellants are now entitled to lead secondary evidence in respect of the Will in question. However, it was clarified that the admission of such secondary evidence does not automatically attest to its authenticity, truthfulness, or genuineness, which must be established during the course of the trial in accordance with law. title: Union of India and Ors. v. Sri Janardhan Debanath and Anr.
text: The Supreme Court of India allowed the appeals, setting aside the judgment of the Division Bench of the Guwahati High Court which had quashed the transfer orders of the respondents. The High Court's decision was deemed indefensible, having erroneously interpreted Rule 37 of the Posts and Telegraphs Manual, Volume IV, and Fundamental Rule 15 (FR 15). The Supreme Court clarified that FR 15 does not prohibit transfers on account of inefficiency or misbehaviour, even to a post carrying less pay, and that the High Court misconstrued this rule. It was emphasized that a government servant has no legal right to be posted at a particular place, and transfer is an incident and condition of service, essential for public interest and administrative efficiency. Courts and Tribunals should not interfere with transfer orders unless they are a result of mala fide exercise or in violation of statutory provisions, and should not act as appellate authorities substituting their own decisions for the employer's. Furthermore, the Court held that for the purpose of effecting a transfer based on allegations of misbehaviour, a prima facie satisfaction of the authority is sufficient, and an elaborate enquiry is not a prerequisite, as it would frustrate the purpose of maintaining discipline and decorum in public service. The contention that the term 'undesirable' warranted an enquiry was also rejected in the context of transfer, distinguishing it from cases of discharge from service. The writ petitions filed before the High Court were directed to be dismissed. Citations: 2001 (8) SCC 574; AIR 1964 SC 449 Legal tags: Supreme Court of India; Appeal (Civil); Service Law; Transfer Order; Guwahati High Court; Central Administrative Tribunal; Union of India; Postal Services Department; Rule 37 Posts and Telegraphs Manual Vol IV; Fundamental Rule 15 (FR 15); FR 14-B; Administrative Exigencies; Public Interest; Misbehaviour; Inefficiency; Disciplinary Action; Judicial Review; Articles 226 and 227 of Constitution; Seniority; Promotional Prospects; Malafide Exercise; Inter-Divisional Transfer; Enquiry before Transfer; Stigma; Undesirable Employees

title: THE JIYAJEERAO COTTON MILLS LTD. v. STATE OF MADHYA PRADESH
text: The Supreme Court upheld the validity of the Central Provinces and Berar Electricity Duty Act, 1949 as amended by the Madhya Pradesh Taxation Laws Amendment Act, 1956. The court held that a producer who generates electrical energy over 100 volts for his own consumption is liable to pay duty on the units of electrical energy consumed by himself. The levy of duty upon consumption of electrical energy cannot be regarded as duty of excise falling within Entry 84 of List I. The taxable event with respect to a duty of excise is 'manufacture' or 'production', and not 'consumption'. Citations: 1963 AIR 414; 1962 SCR Supl. title: DR. SRIDIP CHATTERJEE v. DR. GOPA CHAKRABORTY & ORS.
text: The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the judgment of the High Court. The appellant, Dr. Sridip Chatterjee, was appointed as an Assistant Professor in Physical Education (Yoga Therapy) at Jadavpur University. The respondent challenged the appellant's eligibility, stating that his 'Diploma in Yoga Education' was not equivalent to the advertised 'Post Graduate Diploma in Yoga/Yoga Therapy'. Both the Selection Committee and a subsequently constituted Equivalence Committee found the appellant's qualification equivalent. The Supreme Court held that the High Court erred in interfering with the decision of the expert committees solely based on the nomenclature of the diploma. The Court emphasized that once experts deemed the qualification equivalent, judicial review should not substitute the experts' opinion. The appellant is to be reinstated with consequential benefits, seniority, and pay fixation, but without back wages for the period out of service. title: STATE OF WEST BENGAL v. ANIL NASKAR
text: The Supreme Court, exercising its powers under Order 47, Rule 1 of the Supreme Court Rules, allowed Mr. Bijan Ghosh to represent the West Bengal Housing Board, resolving a minor controversy regarding the filing of a fresh vakalatnama. title: Laxmi Kant Bajpai v. Hazi Yaqoob & Ors.
text: The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal against the Allahabad High Court's order. The High Court had rejected the election petition filed by the appellant, a defeated candidate, challenging the election of the respondent. The appellant contended that the election result was materially affected by the improper reception of votes from 23,431 voters residing in 21 localities that were allegedly outside the territorial boundaries of the 381 Meerut Assembly Constituency as delimited by the 1973 Delimitation Order. The appellant argued that the inclusion of these localities and voters in the electoral roll, despite communication from the Election Commission stating that geographical boundaries delimited during previous delimitation could not change without a new delimitation order, rendered the election void under Section 100 (1)(d)(iii) and (iv) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. The Supreme Court, however, upheld the High Court's finding that the election petition did not disclose a cause of action. The Court reasoned that once an electoral roll is finally published, it becomes the final electoral roll for the constituency, and no court can interfere with it. The Court further clarified that the power to delimit constituencies rests solely with the Delimitation Commission, and the Election Commission cannot alter electoral rolls due to changes in geographical boundaries unless a fresh delimitation order is issued. The Court emphasized that the inclusion of names in the electoral roll, even if alleged to be illegal, cannot be a ground for setting aside an election, as the electoral roll, once published, is final and cannot be questioned in an election petition except for specific grounds like disqualification under Section 16 of the 1950 Act. The Court found that the appellant's pleadings did not disclose material facts and a definite cause of action, as the core issue was the inclusion of certain areas into the constituency rather than a defect in the electoral roll itself. The Court noted that the territorial boundaries of the Meerut constituency were as per the Delimitation Commission's notification and that the State Government has the power to alter or amend delimitation orders under the U.P. Municipalities Act, which did not invalidate the electoral roll used for the election. Therefore, the appeal was dismissed. title: Commissioner of central excise, hyderabad v. Sunder Steels Ltd.
text: The Supreme Court upholds the decision of the Customs, Excise and Gold (Control) Appellate Tribunal in allowing Sunder Steels Ltd. to benefit from Notification No. 30/97-C.E. dated 1st August, 1997. The court holds that the notification does not require 100% of the production of ingots or billets or other rolled products to be manufactured from the stage of iron ore within the factory itself. Merely because the majority of sponge iron is purchased from outside, the benefit of the Notification is not lost. title: Bhagawati Oxygen Ltd. v. Hindustan Copper Ltd.
text: The Supreme Court allowed the appeals filed by BOL and dismissed the appeals filed by HCL. The Court set aside the orders passed by the learned single Judge and confirmed by the Division Bench, thereby restoring the award passed by the Arbitrator in its entirety. The Court held that the Arbitrator was correct in allowing BOL's claim and was also justified in awarding interest at the rate of eighteen per cent per annum, considering that HCL had provided an advance to BOL at the same rate. The Court further held that the learned single Judge and the Division Bench were not justified in interfering with the Arbitrator's dismissal of HCL's counter-claim, as this would amount to re-appreciation of evidence, which is beyond the scope of judicial review under Section 30 of the Arbitration Act, 1940. The Court emphasized that an Arbitrator's award can only be set aside on specific grounds like misconduct or illegality apparent on the face of the award, and not merely on the ground of being erroneous. Therefore, the dismissal of HCL's counter-claim by the Arbitrator was upheld, and the orders of the High Courts reducing the interest rate and remitting the counter-claim for fresh consideration were set aside. title: Tara Singh v. State thr. Home Secretary, Uttarakhand
text: The Honourable Supreme Court dismissed the appeals filed by the appellants, upholding the impugned judgment and order dated 16.5.2006 passed by the High Court of Uttranchal. The High Court had confirmed the conviction and sentence of the appellants to undergo life imprisonment under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) and four years rigorous imprisonment under Section 201 IPC for the murder and concealment of the dead body of a 5-year-old boy, Bharat Singh. The Court found a complete chain of circumstances, including enmity, prior threats, the deceased being last seen with the appellants, the discovery of the dead body in a cave, and post-mortem findings of strangulation, proving the charges against the appellants. The Court also addressed the argument regarding the validity of investigation conducted by a Patwari, citing a notification from 1916 that empowers Patwaris to conduct investigations in the absence of police officers in certain districts, thereby dismissing the appeals as devoid of merit. title: PRABHU v. RAMDEV & ORS.
text: The Supreme Court held that while a mortgagee cannot create an interest in the mortgaged property that extends beyond the termination of their mortgage, the rights of tenants inducted by the mortgagee can be improved by statutory provisions that come into operation during the mortgage period. In this case, Section 15 of the Rajasthan Tenancy Act, 1955, which came into force during the usufructuary mortgage, conferred 'Khatedar' status on the respondents (tenants). Consequently, under Section 161 of the same Act, they could only be ejected in accordance with its provisions, and since none of the grounds for ejectment were proven by the appellant, their possession was protected. The Court dismissed the appellant's appeal, upholding the High Court's decision to dismiss the writ petition challenging the Board of Revenue's order, which had ruled in favor of the tenants. The Court distinguished this case from previous rulings by emphasizing the impact of subsequent statutory provisions on tenant rights. title: M/s. Bhuwalka Steel Industries Ltd. & Another v. Union of India & Others
text: The Supreme Court, in these Civil Appeals concerning the Central Excise & Salt Act, 1944, and the Hot Re-Rolling Steel Mills Annual Capacity Determination Rules, 1997, clarified that Section 3A(2) of the Act and Rule 5 of the 1997 Rules embody a rule of evidence (presumption) regarding the Annual Capacity of Production (ACP), not a legal fiction, and thus Rule 5 is not ultra vires the parent Act or Article 14 of the Constitution. The Court recognized Rule 5 as a mechanism to correct potential errors in formula-based ACP determination. However, the Court found that the vires and interpretation of Rule 96ZP(3) of the Central Excise Rules, 1944, which restricts assessees opting for a concessional monthly payment scheme from availing the benefit of Section 3A(4) (right to claim lower actual production), raise significant questions of law. It noted that prior judgments in *Commissioner of Central Excise & Customs v. Venus Castings (P) Ltd.* and *Union of India & Others v. Supreme Steels and General Mills & Others* concerning Rule 96ZO(3) are not determinative for Rule 96ZP(3) due to differences in their schemes and did not deal with the vires of Rule 96ZP(3). Considering the recurring nature of the opportunity under Section 3A(4) and the potential for illogical or unconstitutional consequences if the option under Rule 96ZP(3) is held to be perpetual, the Court deemed the questions of law unsettled and requiring an authoritative decision. Therefore, the Court referred the matter to the Hon'ble Chief Justice of India for constitution of a larger bench. Citations: (1997) 5 SCC 516; (1980) 3 SCC 358; (2000) 4 SCC 206; (2001) 9 SCC 645; AIR 1972 SC 2427 : (1972) 2 SCC 601; AIR 1966 SC 828 Legal tags: Civil Appeals; Supreme Court of India; Central Excise & Salt Act, 1944; Section 3A; Hot Re-Rolling Steel Mills Annual Capacity Determination Rules, 1997; Rule 5; Central Excise Rules, 1944; Rule 96ZP(3); Annual Capacity of Production (ACP); Legal Fiction; Presumption; Rule of Evidence; Subordinate Legislation; Ultra Vires; Article 14 of Constitution of India; Excise Duty Levy; Tax Liability; Concessional Rate of Duty; Reference to Larger Bench; Non-alloy Steel Hot Re-rolled Products; Interpretation of Statutes; Constitutional Law

title: The Bharat Coking Coal Ltd. & Ors. v. AMR Dev Prabha & Ors.
text: The Supreme Court allowed the appeals filed by Bharat Coking Coal Ltd. and others, setting aside the High Court's judgment that had quashed the auction process and award of tender. Consequently, the writ petition filed by AMR Dev Prabha was dismissed. The Court held that while judicial review in tender matters is permissible for illegality, irrationality, or procedural impropriety, the writ petition in this case was not maintainable as it primarily concerned contractual disputes and lacked substantial public interest. The Court found that the initial connectivity issues were genuine and that the resumption of the auction process was in accordance with the terms of the NIT and in public interest, leading to better price discovery. The Court also noted that AMR Dev Prabha's conduct, including offering a lower bid during the appeal and delaying the filing of the writ petition, indicated a private rather than public interest. Therefore, the appeals were allowed, the High Court's judgment was set aside, and the writ petition was dismissed. Citations: RD Shetty v. International Airport Authority of India; Tata Cellular v. title: M/s Electrotherm (India) Ltd. v. Patel Vipulkumar Ramjibhai & Ors.
text: The Supreme Court of India, in Civil Appeal No. 7222 of 2016, modified the judgment and order dated 11.05.2012 of the High Court of Gujarat. The High Court had set aside the Environmental Clearance (EC) dated 27.01.2010 granted to M/s Electrotherm (India) Ltd. for its plant expansion, directing the cessation of operations, on the ground that public consultation/public hearing, a mandatory requirement under the Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) Notification, 2006, was improperly exempted. The Supreme Court affirmed that the decision to exempt public consultation/public hearing was invalid and improper, especially considering the substantial increase in production capacity, pollution load, and water requirement, which ought to have necessitated a fresh public hearing. However, recognizing that the expansion had already been undertaken and the Appellant had largely complied with pollution control recommendations from the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB), the Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order for plant closure. Instead, the Supreme Court directed the concerned authorities to organize a post-decisional public consultation/public hearing within three months. It was stipulated that if this post-decisional consultation results in a negative mandate against the expansion, the authorities shall direct scaling down of activities to the level permitted by the earlier EC dated 20.02.2008. Conversely, if the public consultation reflects in favour of the expansion, the EC dated 27.01.2010 would hold good and be fully operative.
