title: Post Master General, Kolkata & Ors v. Tutu Das (Dutta)
text: The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, thereby setting aside the impugned judgment of the Division Bench of the Calcutta High Court. The High Court had erroneously directed the regularisation of the respondent's services, proceeding on the premise of a long period of service and a 1987 circular, despite a disputed factual finding regarding the completion of 240 days of service prior to 7.5.1985. The Supreme Court held that the legal landscape concerning regularisation had undergone a significant change, particularly in light of the Constitution Bench decision in *Secretary, State of Karnataka and Others v Umadevi (3) and Others [(2006) 4 SCC 1]*. It was reiterated that appointments made in infraction of statutory rules, recruitment procedures, or in violation of constitutional provisions are illegal and cannot be regularised; regularisation is intended only to cure procedural irregularities that do not go to the root of the appointment process. The Court clarified that the 'one-time measure' exception in paragraph 53 of *Umadevi (3)* applied only to irregularly (not illegally) appointed persons who had worked for ten years or more in duly sanctioned vacant posts without the intervention of court orders. In the present case, the respondent's appointment was deemed illegal due to non-compliance with recruitment rules and procedures. The argument of discrimination vis-à-vis Niva Ghosh was also rejected, affirming that equality is a positive concept and cannot be invoked to perpetuate an illegality. Furthermore, the concept of completing 240 days of continuous service in a year was held to be relevant only for cases of retrenchment under the Industrial Disputes Act, not for the regularisation of service. title: U.P. State Road Transport Corporation v. Man Singh
text: The Supreme Court condoned the delay and granted leave to appeal. The respondent was appointed on a temporary basis by the appellant Corporation and his services were terminated. An industrial dispute was raised after approximately 12 years. The Labour Court found that the termination violated Section 25F of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, and directed reinstatement but granted back-wages only from 1986. The High Court refused to interfere. The Supreme Court, considering that the respondent was temporarily appointed, likely found other employment, and that it would be unjust to direct reinstatement after over 30 years, modified the Labour Court's order. Instead of reinstatement and back-wages, the appellant was directed to pay a sum of Rs. 50,000/- to the respondent within eight weeks, with interest at 6% per annum if not paid. The appeal was allowed to this extent, with parties bearing their own costs. title: WORKMEN OF JOINT STEAMER COMPANIES v. JOINT STEAMER COMPANIES
text: The Supreme Court, in the instant Civil Appeals, upheld the decision of the Labour Appellate Tribunal, thereby rejecting the workmen's claim for bonus for the years 1949, 1950, 1951, and 1952. The Court determined that the operations of the Joint Steamer Companies in India and Pakistan constituted one integrated industrial activity. It was held that, based on the materials on record, it was not feasible to apply the Full Bench Formula to a part only of the total operations (i.e., solely the Indian operations), primarily due to the inherent difficulties in segregating and apportioning income, expenditure, paid-up capital, working capital, and rehabilitation costs for distinct Indian activities. The Court further noted that while Industrial Tribunals are ordinarily justified in directing employers to grant workmen reasonable access to relevant account books, subject to the protection of Section 21 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, such access in the present case would not have enabled the proper application of the Full Bench Formula to segregated Indian operations due to the fundamental lack of apportionable data. The appeals were accordingly dismissed. title: RANI PURNIMA DEVI AND ANOTHER v. KUMAR KHAGENDRA NARAYAN DEV AND ANOTHER
text: The Supreme Court held that the due execution and attestation of the will were not proven. Despite the High Court's affirmation based on the registration of the will dispelling suspicious circumstances, the Supreme Court found the evidence inadequate. Suspicious circumstances included the will being unnatural (leaving out close relations like the daughter and inadequately providing for the widow and sister), the propounder benefiting significantly and taking part in the execution, the testator's signature appearing unusual, the possibility of the will being created on pre-signed blank papers, and the testator's signature possibly being in different ink. The court noted that the attesting witnesses produced were interested, and independent witnesses were not called. Furthermore, the registration process was found to be perfunctory, with the sub-registrar's clerk handling it instead of the sub-registrar himself. The evidence did not establish that the testator understood the document he was admitting execution of was his will. Therefore, the appeals were allowed, the judgments of the High Court and the trial court were set aside, and the suit arising from the application for probate by the respondent was dismissed. The appellants were awarded costs. Citations: 1962 AIR 567; 1962 SCR Supl. title: Munna @ Surendra Kumar v. State of M.P.
text: The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal filed by the 4th accused, upholding the High Court's judgment which reversed the trial court's acquittal. The High Court had convicted the appellant for offences under Sections 302, 307, and 324 IPC, sentencing him to life imprisonment for murder and other sentences for lesser offences. The Supreme Court agreed with the High Court that the trial court had given undue importance to minor discrepancies and misread the evidence, rendering its finding perverse and arbitrary. The Court found that the High Court correctly appreciated the evidence, concluding that the appellant fired indiscriminately after moving from the initial location onto the road, causing the death of the victim and injuries to others. The arguments regarding the blackening of wounds and the trajectory of the pellet injuries were found to be unsubstantiated by the High Court's re-appreciation of the evidence, which established proximity between the appellant and the victims. The Court also noted that the prosecution did not rely on the recovery of a gun, rendering arguments about its improper recovery irrelevant to the case's weakness. Consequently, the appeal was dismissed. title: CHATTAR SINGH & ORS. v. MADHO SINGH (D) & ORS.
text: The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the High Court's decision. The land in question was recorded as 'Charnoi' (common land for grazing cattle), which vested in the State upon the abolition of Zamindari. Section 4 of the Madhya Bharat Zamindari Abolition Act, 1951, stipulates that such lands vest in the State, and Section 5(f) concerning 'groves' does not apply to common grazing land. The Court clarified that 'Charnoi' land does not qualify as a 'grove' as defined and interpreted in prior judgments, emphasizing that the primary use of the land was for common grazing and not exclusively for trees that would preclude other uses. Therefore, the erstwhile proprietor or their legal heirs could not claim ownership or settlement rights over this common land. The Court found the Board of Revenue's order favoring the ex-zamindar to be perverse and illegal, while affirming the Trial Court's decree in favor of the villagers. Citations: Shrimant Sardar Chandrojirao Angre v. title: STATE OF TAMIL NADU v. A. JAGANATHAN
text: The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order suspending the conviction of the respondents, holding that the decision relied upon by the High Court in Rama Narang's case was not applicable. The Court noted that in the present case, any damage caused by the suspension of conviction could be rectified if the revisions were allowed, unlike the irreversible damage in Rama Narang's case. Furthermore, the High Court failed to consider the moral conduct of the respondents, who were convicted for serious offenses including those under the Prevention of Corruption Act and Indian Penal Code sections related to extortion, fabricating evidence, and forgery. The Court emphasized that discretionary powers under Section 389(1) or Section 482 Cr.P.C. should not have been exercised in such circumstances. However, the Court maintained the High Court's order with regard to the suspension of sentences. title: State of U.P. v. Abdul Karim and Ors
text: The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal filed by the State of U.P. against the acquittal of the respondents by the Allahabad High Court. The High Court had found that the prosecution failed to establish its accusations. The Supreme Court agreed with the High Court's assessment that the evidence of the prosecution witnesses (PWs 1, 2, and 3) was unreliable due to inconsistencies and the inability to clearly identify the assailants from a considerable distance, especially with intervening crops. The court also noted the discrepancy between the prosecution's claim of sharp weapons being used and the nature of the injuries, which were mostly lacerated wounds and contusions. Consequently, the Supreme Court upheld the High Court's judgment of acquittal, finding no reason to interfere. title: SETH JAMNADAS DAGA AND OTHERS v. COMMISSIONER OF INCOME-TAX, SOUTH BOMBAY
text: The Supreme Court held that the High Court was correct in its view that under Sections 14(2) and 16(1)(a) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, the profit from an unregistered firm and the loss from registered firms had to be set off against each other to determine the total income for the purpose of rate applicable to other income. Although the share of a partner in the profits of an unregistered firm is exempt from tax, it is included in the total income for rate purposes. However, the Supreme Court disagreed with the High Court's conclusion that the losses suffered by the registered firms could not be carried forward to the following year because they were deemed to have been absorbed by the profits of the unregistered firm. The Court clarified that the carrying forward of losses under Section 24 is a separate matter from the computation of total income for determining the applicable tax rate, and setting off losses against profits for rate calculation does not mean the losses are absorbed in a manner that prevents them from being carried forward. title: THE CENTRAL BANK OF INDIA LTD. v. P.S. RAJAGOPALAN ETC.
text: The Supreme Court allowed the appeals, setting aside the orders of the Labour Court, and remanded the matters back for fresh disposal. The Court held that Section 33C(2) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, takes within its purview cases where workmen claim monetary computation of benefits, even if the employer disputes the right to such benefits. The Labour Court, for making the necessary determination under Section 33C(2), is empowered to interpret the award or settlement on which the workman's right rests, distinguishing this from the general interpretation function of Section 36A. The scope of Section 33C(2) is wider than Section 33C(1), and no period of limitation is prescribed for applications under Section 33C(2). However, on merits, the Court found the Labour Court's acceptance of the respondents' claim for special allowance as 'Comptists' solely based on their operation of adding machines, and the Imperial Bank of India's nomenclature equating adding machine operators with Comptists, to be erroneous. The Court clarified that the nomenclature is not decisive; the entitlement to special allowance depends on the nature of duties and responsibilities, which requires specific skill for a 'Comptist' as per the Sastry Award. Given this, the case was remanded to the Labour Court, allowing parties to amend pleadings and lead evidence to establish if the work performed by the respondents genuinely corresponds to that of 'Comptists' in the banking industry. Citations: 1964 AIR  743; 1964 SCR  (3) 140; 1962 (1) L.L.J.234; [1959] S.C.R. 1; [1961] 3 S.C.R. 220; (1962) 65 Bom.L.R. 91 Legal tags: Industrial Disputes Act, 1947; Section 33C(2); Labour Court Jurisdiction; Interpretation of Awards; Sastry Award; Special Allowance; Comptists; Adding Machine Operators; Disputed Rights; Computation of Benefits; Execution Proceedings; Workmen's Rights; Section 36A; Section 33C(1); Remand; Limitation Period; Industrial Relations; Banking Industry

title: United India Insurance Co. Ltd. v. M/s Kiran Combers & Spinners
text: The Supreme Court upheld the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission's decision, dismissing the appeal filed by the United India Insurance Co. Ltd. The Court ruled that the insurance company was liable to compensate M/s Kiran Combers & Spinners for damages caused by flooding. The Court found that the policy covered flood perils, and the exclusion clause cited by the appellant regarding 'subsidence' was not applicable as it was not explicitly mentioned in the policy's exclusion list. Furthermore, the Court noted that the insurance company had certified the building as 'first class construction' prior to the incident. It was held that any pre-existing structural defects were aggravated by the flood, and thus the company could not escape liability. The claim of Rs. 10,13,571.90, as assessed by the second surveyor, was thus rightly decreed by the National Commission. text: यह अपील स्वीकार की जाती है, और तदनुसार, अपीलार्थी सुधीर कुमार जैन को राजस्थान उच्च न्यायालय द्वारा आईपीसी की धारा 302 के तहत आजीवन कारावास और शस्त्र अधिनियम की धारा 3 सहपठित धारा 25 के तहत दो साल के कारावास तथा ₹1,000 के जुर्माने की सजा से दोषसिद्ध करने वाले निर्णय और आदेश को अपास्त किया जाता है। सभी चश्मदीद गवाहों के मुकर जाने, मृत्युकालीन घोषणा पत्र में आरोपियों का नाम न होने, पी.डब्ल्यू.-18 कांस्टेबल सुरेश कुमार की गवाही में घटना के 18 दिन बाद दर्ज किए गए बयान में गंभीर संदेह उत्पन्न होने, तथा बरामद 12 बोर देसी पिस्तौल के बैलिस्टिक विशेषज्ञ द्वारा वर्तमान स्थिति में काम करने योग्य न पाए जाने के कारण, अभियोजन पक्ष अपीलार्थी के विरुद्ध अपराध को उचित संदेह से परे साबित करने में विफल रहा। अतः अपीलार्थी को आईपीसी की धारा 302 और शस्त्र अधिनियम की धारा 3/25 के तहत सभी आरोपों से बरी किया जाता है। Citations: 1392/ 2008; 1717/2003 Legal tags: आपराधिक अपील; हत्या (आईपीसी 302); शस्त्र अधिनियम (धारा 3/25); बरी करना; राजस्थान उच्च न्यायालय; भारत का सर्वोच्च न्यायालय; मुकर गए गवाह; मृत्युकालीन घोषणा; हथियार की बरामदगी; बैलिस्टिक विशेषज्ञ की रिपोर्ट; उचित संदेह; दोषसिद्धि रद्द; साक्ष्य मूल्यांकन; गवाह की विश्वसनीयता; बयान में देरी

title: S. RAJAN v. CHENNAI METROPOLITAN TRANSPORT CORPORATION LTD
text: The Supreme Court partly allowed the appeals, enhancing the compensation awarded to the appellant. The Court added an additional Rs. 1,00,000 under the head of 'loss of earning power', thereby increasing the compensation under this head from the Tribunal's awarded Rs. 1,00,000 to Rs. 2,00,000. The other sums awarded by the Tribunal and affirmed by the High Court, including Rs. 75,000 for loss of marital alliance, Rs. 25,000 for inability to participate in family and social functions, and Rs. 75,000 for pain and suffering, were not disturbed. The total compensation, as enhanced, and the interest rate of 9% per annum as reduced by the High Court, remain applicable for the other heads, acknowledging the appellant's 100% permanent physical disability due to grievous injuries sustained in a motor vehicle accident, including amputation of the right leg and multiple compound fractures. title: Abdul Khader (D) b y L.Rs. v. Tarabai and others
text: The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal filed by the legal representatives of Abdul Khader, upholding the concurrent findings of the Land Tribunal and the Karnataka High Court. The Court affirmed the grant of occupancy rights to the respondents, Smt. Tarabai W/o Basavannappa and Shivapalsingh S/o Jeshwanthsingh, over the disputed lands (Survey Nos. 5, 6, and 7 of Badepur village), which were deemed Service Inam Land. The Court rejected the appellants' arguments, inter alia, on the grounds that the Hyderabad Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1950, upon which reliance was placed, stood repealed by Section 142(1) of the Karnataka Land Reforms Act, 1961. Furthermore, the Court found that the appellants failed to adduce any evidence to establish that Basavannappa was a money lender whose income exceeded the limit prescribed under Section 79-A of the 1961 Act, and this plea was not agitated at the appropriate stages. The contention regarding Service Inam Lands being governed by the Hyderabad Act, 1955, and thus precluding occupancy rights, was also rejected as a new plea not raised before the Tribunal or the High Court. The Court relied on the concurrent finding that Basavannappa was in possession of the land as a lessee/tenant since 1957, a fact supported by the arbitration award, and noted that Abdul Khader himself had initially applied for occupancy rights and later for re-grant under Section 5(3) of the Karnataka Certain Inams Abolition Act, 1977, acknowledging the abolition of Inam land rights. Citations: Writ Appeal No. 963 of 2000; Suit No.35/1 /1959-60; Writ Petition No.8584 of 1977; Writ Petition No.8583 of 1977; Writ Petition No. 19622/1991; Writ Appeal No.963 of 2000; Writ Appeal No. 972 of 2000 Legal tags: Civil Appeal; Occupancy Rights; Land Tribunal; Karnataka High Court; Supreme Court of India; Karnataka Certain Inams Abolition Act, 1977; Section 5(1); Section 5(3); Karnataka Land Reforms Act, 1961; Section 48-A; Section 79-A; Hyderabad Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1950; Repeal and Savings; Section 142(1); Service Inam Land; Lessee/Tenant; Arbitration Award; Evidence; Jurisdiction; Pleadings; First Time Plea; Finality of Proceedings

title: M/s. Pleasantime Products and Anr. v. Commissioner of Central Excise, Mumbai-I
text: The Supreme Court dismissed the civil appeals, affirming that the branded word game "Scrabble" (and "Junior Scrabble") is classifiable under sub-heading 9504.90 of the First Schedule to the Central Excise and Tariff Act, 1985, as an article for table or parlour games. It was determined that "Scrabble" is not a puzzle or an educational toy, which would fall under sub-heading 9503.00, based on distinguishing features such as outcome (not pre-determined in Scrabble), absence of clues, and the presence of elements of chance and skill inherent in a game. The Court applied the 'companion test' for interpreting Chapter 95 entries and the 'common parlance' or 'trade meaning' test. Furthermore, the Court upheld the invocation of the longer period of limitation under the proviso to Section 11A(1) of the Central Excise Act, 1944, finding that the assessee had deliberately suppressed facts by not specifically mentioning "Scrabble" in their declarations and failing to prove the submission of a comprehensive list of manufactured items. Citations: AIR 1980 SC page 611 Legal tags: Central Excise and Tariff Act, 1985 (CETA); Classification of Goods; Sub-heading 9503.00; Sub-heading 9504.90; Scrabble; Junior Scrabble; Board Game; Puzzle; Educational Toy; Central Excise Act, 1944; Limitation Period; Section 11A(1); Deliberate Suppression; Suppression of Facts; Statutory Interpretation; Companion Test; Common Parlance; Trade Meaning; Excise Duty

title: EXECUTIVE OFFICER, ARULMIGU CHOKKANATHA SWAMY KOIL TRUST VIRUDHUNAGAR v. CHANDRAN & ORS
text: The Supreme Court set aside the judgment of the High Court, restoring the decrees of the trial court and the First Appellate Court. The High Court had erred in reversing the concurrent findings of fact by the lower courts, which had held that the plaintiff failed to prove title and possession, that Survey No. 188/1 and 188/3 belonged to the Temple, and that the suit was not maintainable due to non-joinder of a necessary party (Janaki Ammal) and for seeking only declaratory relief without possession. The Supreme Court found the High Court's reasoning contradictory and unsustainable, particularly in decreeing the suit while affirming the Temple's ownership of parts of the property. title: GOLD QUEST INTERNATIONAL PRIVATE LIMITED v. THE STATE OF TAMIL NADU & ORS.
text: The Supreme Court, allowing the appeal, set aside the order of the Division Bench of the High Court and restored the order passed by the learned Single Judge. The Court held that the Single Judge had not committed any error of law in quashing the First Information Report (FIR) in a case involving allegations under Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code read with Sections 4, 5 & 6 of the Prize Chits and Money Circulation (Banning) Act, 1978. This decision was based on the fact that the complainant and other alleged sufferers had settled their money disputes and claims with the appellant-company. The Supreme Court reiterated the principle that High Courts, in exercise of their inherent powers under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure read with Article 226 of the Constitution, can quash criminal proceedings or FIRs in disputes that are substantially matrimonial in nature or civil property disputes with criminal facets, where parties have entered into a settlement and the chances of conviction are remote. This power is distinct from the power of compounding offenses under Section 320 CrPC and should be exercised to secure the ends of justice and prevent abuse of the process of any court, but not in cases of very serious offenses like rape, murder, robbery, dacoity, or offenses under special statutes like the Prevention of Corruption Act or Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act. The Court affirmed that continuing such criminal proceedings after a full and complete settlement would be a futile exercise and cause extreme injustice. Citations: AIR 1992 SC 604 : 1992 Supp.(1) SCC 335; (2003) 4 SCC 675; (2008) 9 SCC 677; (2012) 10 SCC 303; (1977) 4 SCC 551; (1999) 5 SCC 238; (2008) 16 SCC 1; (2011) 10 SCC 705 Legal tags: Civil Appeal; Quashing of FIR; Compromise and Settlement; Section 482 CrPC; Article 226 of the Constitution; Indian Penal Code (IPC); Section 420 IPC; Prize Chits and Money Circulation (Banning) Act, 1978; Inherent Powers of High Court; Non-compoundable Offence; Matrimonial Disputes; Civil Disputes with Criminal Facets; B.S. title: THE STATE OF RAJASTHAN v. RAM SARAN
text: The Supreme Court held that the Standing Orders issued by the Inspector-General of Police were administrative instructions and not conditions of service, thus their violation did not constitute a breach of service conditions. The Court also ruled that there is no legal right for an officer to hold an officiating post and that reversion to a substantive post does not alter service conditions as contemplated by the States Reorganisation Act, 1956. The Court found no alteration of service conditions under Section 115(7) of the Act and no curtailment of the State Government's powers by Central Government directions under Section 117. Section 116(2) of the Act preserved the State Government's powers to pass orders affecting an officer's continuance in an officiating post. The Court cited the case of Parshotam Lal Dhingra v. Union of India to support the view that an officer has no right to continue in an officiating post. Regarding the contention of violation of Article 14 due to region-wise seniority, the Court found the pleadings to be vague and insufficient for a decision, suggesting the respondent file a fresh petition for a proper investigation. Consequently, the appeal was allowed, the High Court's order was set aside, and the respondent's writ petition was dismissed, without prejudice to his right to file a fresh petition on the grounds of Article 14 violation. Citations: 1964 AIR 1361; 1964 SCR (2) 982 Legal tags: Public Servant; Officiating Sub-Inspector of Police; Ajmer; Rajasthan; Reversion; Legality; Police Act, 1861; States Reorganisation Act, 1956; Standing Orders; Conditions of Service; Alteration of Service Conditions; Central Government Sanction; Article 14; Article 311; Seniority; Administrative Instructions; Substantive Post; Officiating Post; Reversion for Administrative Reasons; Article 226; Article 133(1)(c)

title: Indu sind Med ia & Commun. Ltd. & Anr v. Mam latdar & Ors.
text: The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals filed by the appellants, upholding the Gujarat High Court's decision. The Court ruled that Multi-System Operators (MSOs), like the appellants who transmit signals to cable operators who then transmit to subscribers, are considered 'Proprietors' under the Gujarat Entertainment Tax Act, 1977, and are thus liable to pay Entertainment Tax. The Court also found no violation of natural justice in the imposition of penalty, stating that the appellants had provided incorrect information and made efforts to evade tax despite notices and opportunities to be heard. Therefore, the imposition of penalty was justified. Citations: STATE OF WEST BENGAL v. PURVI COMMUNI CATIONS (P) LTD., 2005 (3) SCC 711 Legal tags: Entertainment Tax; Gujarat Entertainment Tax Act, 1977; Multi-System Operators (MSOs); Proprietor; Liability to pay tax; Penalty; Principles of Natural Justice; Wilfull misstatement; Suppression of facts; Civil Appeal; Supreme Court; Gujarat High Court

title: Suhelkhan Khudyarkhan & Anr. v. State of Maharashtra & Ors.
text: The Supreme Court of India dismissed the Criminal Appeal, thereby upholding the judgment of a learned Single Judge of the Bombay High Court, Aurangabad Bench. The High Court had dismissed the writ petition filed by the appellants, which challenged an order issued by the Sub Divisional Magistrate under Section 133 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (CrPC) for the removal of the appellants' shop, "R.K. Kitab Ghar", on grounds of public nuisance. The Supreme Court, after analyzing the scope and application of Section 133 CrPC, reiterated that it is a summary provision intended to prevent public nuisance involving a sense of urgency and applies when nuisance is in existence, not merely for future likelihood. It clarified that proceedings under Section 133 CrPC are more civil than criminal and the person against whom action is taken is not an accused. Concluding that the order passed by the High Court suffered from no infirmity, the Supreme Court disposed of the appeal. Citations: 1995 Supp (4) SCC 54; 2003 (7) SCC 389; 2005 (9) SCC 36 Legal tags: Supreme Court of India; Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction; Bombay High Court; Writ Petition; Sub Divisional Magistrate; Section 133 Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973; Public Nuisance; Removal of encroachment; Shop removal; Maintenance of Public Order and Tranquility; Summary Proceedings; Imminent danger; Trade or occupation injurious to health or physical comfort; Chapter X CrPC; Section 144 CrPC; Indian Penal Code, 1860 (Section 268); Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (Section 91); Vasant Manga Nikumba v. title: AR. PATHAN v. SAMAVALAO CHUKADA
text: The Supreme Court has allowed the appeal filed by the State of Gujarat and others, thereby quashing and setting aside the impugned judgment and order dated 18.02.2021 passed by the Division Bench of the Gujarat High Court in Letters Patent Appeal No. 2082/2011. The High Court's Division Bench had directed the State/Department to sympathetically consider the case of the respondents (original writ petitioners) for regularization of their services, by creating supernumerary posts if necessary, noting their continuous service for over 17 years. The Supreme Court held that the High Court's Division Bench erred in issuing such directions, as the original appointments of the respondents were for a period of 11 months on a fixed pay under a specific, temporary project known as the 'Earthquake Rehabilitation Project', and not against any sanctioned permanent posts in any government institution. The Court reiterated that employees appointed on a temporary basis for a specific project have no right to claim absorption or regularization in permanent government service. The Supreme Court further noted that the High Court did not properly appreciate the fact that the respondents' services were continued due to an interim order passed by the High Court in 2011. Distinguishing the precedents cited by the respondents (State of Karnataka v. Umadevi (3) and Narendra Kumar Tiwari v. State of Jharkhand), the Court found that the facts and circumstances of the present case did not warrant the application of those rulings, especially concerning project-based temporary appointments. Consequently, the Supreme Court restored the judgment and order of the Single Judge dated 25.11.2011, which had dismissed the original writ petition seeking regularization. No order as to costs. Citations: 2082/2011; 17328/2011 Legal tags: Civil Appeal; Supreme Court of India; Gujarat High Court; Letters Patent Appeal; Writ Petition; Regularization of Service; Temporary Appointment; Project-based Employment; Fixed Pay; Earthquake Rehabilitation Project; Supernumerary Posts; Interim Order; Government Employment; Contractual Employment; Jurisdictional Error; State of Karnataka v. title: Vijayalashmi Rice Mill and Ors. v. Commerical Tax Officers, Palakol and Ors.
text: The Supreme Court dismissed the Civil Appeals, upholding the Judgment and Order dated 25.09.1998 of the High Court of Andhra Pradesh, which had affirmed the Constitutional validity of the Andhra Pradesh Rural Development Act, 1996. The Court determined that the levy of cess under the Act is in substance a 'fee' and not a 'tax'. It clarified that while a tax is a compulsory exaction for general public purposes without specific services, a fee is for a special service or advantage, and the traditional concept of direct quid pro quo for individual payers has undergone a significant transformation. The Court, citing various precedents, held that a broad and general correlation between the totality of the fee collected and the totality of the expenses for the services rendered (rural development, construction of roads and bridges, augmentation of storage facilities, and strengthening of the Public Distribution System as per Section 9 of the Act) is sufficient to sustain the levy as a fee, falling under Entry 66 of List-II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. The petitioners' argument that no specific benefit was rendered to individual dealers was deemed insufficient to invalidate the cess under the evolved concept of a fee. While upholding the Act's validity, the Court granted liberty to the petitioners to file a fresh petition making a specific averment, backed by facts and figures, that there is no broad correlation between the total amount of cess realized annually and the total value of services actually rendered under Section 9, in which case the State would be required to demonstrate such correlation. Citations: AIR (1967) SC 1512; [1990] 1 SCC 12; AIR (1980) SC 1008; AIR (1983) SC 1246; AIR (1985) SC 756; AIR (1985) SC 218; AIR (2004) SC 4393; AIR (2005) SC 635; [2004] 10 SCC 201; AIR (1989) Punjab 87; [1993] Suppl. 4 SCC 461; JT (2006) 4 SC 611 Legal tags: Constitutional Law; Taxation Law; Fee vs. Tax; Andhra Pradesh Rural Development Act, 1996; Cess; Rural Development; Seventh Schedule; List II Entry 66; List II Entry 54; Writ Petition; Civil Appeal; Supreme Court of India; High Court of Andhra Pradesh; Quid Pro Quo; Public Distribution System; Infrastructure Development; Paddy and Rice Milling Business; State Legislature Powers; Judicial Precedent; Constitutional Validity; Legislative Competence; Tax on Purchase or Sale of Goods

title: Indian Contract Act, 1872 - Section 10: What agreements are contracts
text: Official statute section from Indian Contract Act, 1872. Source: India Code. URL: https://www.indiacode.nic.in/bitstream/123456789/2187/2/A187209.pdf. Section 10: 10. What agreements are contracts .—All agreements are contracts if they are made by the free consent of parties competent to contract, for a lawful consideration and with a lawful object, and are not hereby expressly declared to be void. Nothing herein contained sha ll affect any law in force in 1[India] and not hereby expressly repealed by which any contract is required to be made in writing 2 or in the presence of witnesses, or any law relating to the registration of documents.

title: Indian Contract Act, 1872 - Section 14: “Free consent” defined
text: Official statute section from Indian Contract Act, 1872. Source: India Code. URL: https://www.indiacode.nic.in/bitstream/123456789/2187/2/A187209.pdf. Section 14: 14. “Free consent” defined.—Consent is said to be free when it is not caused by— (1) coercion, as defined in section 15, or (2) undue influence, as defined in section 16, or (3) fraud, as defined in section 17, or (4) misrepresentation, as defined in section 18, or (5) mistake, subject to the provisions of sections 20, 21 and 22. Consent is said to be so caused when it would not have been given but for the exist ence of such coercion, undue influence, fraud, misrepresentation or mistake.

title: Indian Contract Act, 1872 - Section 23: What considerations and objects are lawful, and what not
text: Official statute section from Indian Contract Act, 1872. Source: India Code. URL: https://www.indiacode.nic.in/bitstream/123456789/2187/2/A187209.pdf. Section 23: 23. What considerations and objects are lawful, and what not.—The consideration or object of an agreement is lawful, unless— it is forbidden by law4; or is of such a nature that if permitted, it would defeat the provisions of any law; or is fraudulent ; or involves or implies injury to the person or property of another; or the Court regards it as immoral, or opposed to public policy.

title: Indian Contract Act, 1872 - Section 74: Compensation for breach of contract where penalty stipulated for
text: Official statute section from Indian Contract Act, 1872. Source: India Code. URL: https://www.indiacode.nic.in/bitstream/123456789/2187/2/A187209.pdf. Section 74: 74. Compensation for breach of contrac t where penalty stipulated for .—1[When a contract has been broken, if a sum is named in the contract as the amount to be paid in case of such breach, or if the contract contains any other stipulation by way of penalty, the party complaining of the breach is entitled, whether or not actual damage or loss is proved to have been caused thereby, to receive from the party who has broken the contract reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount so named or, as the case may be, the penalty stipulated for. Explanation.—A stipulation for increased interest from the date of default may be a stipulation by way of penalty.] Exception.—When any person ente rs into any bail -bond, recogni zance or other instrument of the same nature, or, under the provisions of any la w, or under the orders of the 2[Central Government] or of any 3[State Government ], gives any bond for the performance of any public duty or act in which the public are interested, he shall be liable, upon breach of the condition of any such instrument, to pay t he whole sum mentioned therein. Explanation.—A person who enters into a contract with Government does not necessarily thereby undertake any public duty, or promise to do an act in which the public are interested. Illustrations (a)A contracts with B to pay B Rs. 1,000, if he fails to pay B Rs. 500 on a given day. A fails to pay B Rs. 500 on that day. B is entitled to recover from A such compensation, not exceeding Rs. 1,000, as the Court considers reasonable. (b)A contracts with B that, if Apractises as a surgeon within Calcutta, he will pay B Rs. 5,000. A practises as a surgeon in Calcutta. B is entitled to such compensation; not exceeding Rs. 5,000, as the Court considers reasonable. (c)A gives a recognizance binding him in a pe nalty of Rs. 500 to appear in Court on a certain day. He forfeits his recognizance. He is liable to pay the whole penalty.

THE CONSUMER PROTECTION ACT, 2019 
ACT NO. 35 OF 2019 
 
[9th August, 2019.] 
An Act to provide for protection of the interests of consumers and for the said purpose, to establish 
authorities for timely and effective administration and settlement of consumers' disputes and for 
matters connected therewith or incidental thereto. 
BE it enacted by Parliament in the Seventieth Year of the Republic of India as follows:— 
CHAPTER I 
PRELIMINARY 
1. Short title, extent, commencement and application. —(1) This Act may be called the Consumer 
Protection Act, 2019. 
(2) It extends to the whole of India except the State of Jammu and Kashmir*. 
(3) It shall come into force on such date1 as the Central Government may, by notification, appoint and 
different dates may be appointed for different States and for different provisions of  this Act and any 
reference in any such provision to the commencement of this Act shall be construed as a reference to the 
coming into force of that provision. 
(4) Save as otherwise expressly provided by the Central Government, by notification, this Act shall 
apply to all goods and services. 
2. Definitions.—In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires,— 
(1) “advertisement” means any audio or visual publicity, representation, endorsement or 
pronouncement made by means of light, sound, smoke, gas, print, electronic medi a, internet or 
website and includes any notice, circular, label, wrapper, invoice or such other documents; 
(2) “appropriate laboratory” means a laboratory or an organisation— 
(i) recognised by the Central Government; or 
(ii) recognised by a State Government, subject to such guidelines as may be issued by the 
Central Government in this behalf; or 
(iii) established by or under any law for the time being in force, which is maintained, 
financed or aided by the Central Government or a State Government for carrying out analysis or 
test of any goods with a view to determining whether such goods suffer from any defect; 
(3) “branch office” means— 
(i) any office or place of work described as a branch by the establishment; or 
(ii) any establishment carrying on either the same or substantially the same activity carried on 
by the head office of the establishment;

Extracted official text: Model Tenancy Act to promote rental housing, by protecting the rights and interests of both the tenants and landlords Print X Close Press Information Bureau Government of India Ministry of Housing & Urban Affairs 09 DEC 2021 2:35PM by PIB Delhi Model Tenancy Act to promote rental housing, by protecting the rights and interests of both the tenants and landlords Union Cabinet approved Model Tenancy Act (MTA) on 2 nd June, 2021 and the same was circulated to all States / Union Territories (UTs) on 7 th June, 2021 for adoption for future tenancies by way of either enacting a fresh legislation or amending existing rental laws suitably. Model Tenancy Act aims to promote rental housing by balancing and protecting the rights and interests of both the tenants and landlords by regulating renting of premises in an efficient and transparent manner. It will also help in overhauling the legal framework with respect to rental markets across the country by providing speedier dispute resolution mechanism framework and is expected to give a fillip to private participation in rental housing. All States and UTs were consulted while finalising Model Tenancy Act. Views / comments / suggestions of States and UTs on draft Act were duly analysed and suitably incorporated in the final draft. MTA is applicable in both urban and rural areas of the States and UTs. Land and Colonization are State subjects. Tenancies in States/ Union Territories are governed by their respective rental laws. States and UTs have been advised to adopt MTA by way of eitherenacting a fresh legislation or amending their existing rental laws suitably on lines of MTA in their respective jurisdictions. This information was given by the Minister of State in the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs, Shri Kaushal Kishore, in a written reply in the Lok Sabha today. ***** YB/SS

ACT NO. 14 OF 19571 
 [4th June, 1957.] 
An Act to amend and consolidate the law relating to copyright. 
BE it enacted by Parliament in the Eighth Year of the Republic of India as follows:— 
CHAPTER I 
PRELIMINARY 
1. Short title, extent and commencement.—(1) This Act may be called the Copyright Act, 1957. 
(2) It extends to the whole of India. 
(3) It shall come into force on such date 2 as the Central Government may, by notification in the 
Official Gazette, appoint. 
2. Interpretation.—In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires,— 
(a) “adaptation” means,— 
(i) in relation to a dramatic work, the conversion of the work into a non-dramatic work; 
(ii) in relation to a literary work or an artistic work, the conversion of the work into a 
dramatic work by way of performance in public or otherwise; 
(iii) in relation to a literary or dramatic work, any abridgement of the work or any version of 
the work in which the story or action is conveyed wholly or mainly by means of pictures in a 
form suitable for reproduction in a book, or in a newspaper, magazine or similar periodical; 3***  
(iv) in relation to a musical work, any arrangement or transcription of the work; 4[and] 
 4[(v) in relation to any work, any use of such work involving its re -arrangement or 
alteration;] 
5[(aa) “Appellate Board” means the Appellate Board referred to in section 11;] 
(b) 6[work of architecture] means any building or structure having an artistic character or design, 
or any model for such building or structure; 
(c) “artistic work” means,—  
(i) a painting, a sculpture, a drawing (including a diagram, map, chart or plan), an engraving 
or a photograph, whether or not any such work possesses artistic quality; 
(ii) an 5[work of architectural]; and 
(iii) any other work of artistic craftsmanship; 
(d) “author” means,— 
(i) in relation to literary or dramatic work, the author of the work; 
(ii) in relation to a musical work, the composer; 
(iii) in relation to an artistic work other than a photograph, the artist; 
(iv) in relation to a photograph, the person taking the photograph;

title: Copyright Act, 1957 - Section 13: Works in which copyright subsists
text: Official statute section from Copyright Act, 1957. Source: India Code. URL: https://www.indiacode.nic.in/bitstream/123456789/1367/5/a1957-14.pdf. Section 13: 13. Works in which copyright subsists .—(1) Subject to the provisions of this section and the other provisions of this Act, copyright shall subsist throughout India in the following classes of works, that is to say,— (a) original literary, dramatic, musical and artistic works; (b) cinematograph films; and (c) 6[sound recording]. (2) Copyright shall not subsist in any work specified in sub -section ( 1), other than a work to which the provisions of section 40 or section 41 apply, unless— (i) in the case of a published work, the work is first published in India, or where the work is first published outside India, the auth or is at the date of such publication, or in a case where the author was dead at that date, was at the time of his death, a citizen of India; (ii) in the case of an unpublished work other than a 7[work of architecture], the author is at the date of making of the work a citizen of India or domiciled in India; and (iii) in the case of a 7[work of architecture], the work is located in India. Explanation.—In th e case of a work of joint authorship, the conditions conferring copyright specified in this sub-section shall be satisfied by all the authors of the work.

title: Copyright Act, 1957 - Section 51: When copyright infringed
text: Official statute section from Copyright Act, 1957. Source: India Code. URL: https://www.indiacode.nic.in/bitstream/123456789/1367/5/a1957-14.pdf. Section 51: 51. When copyright infringed.—Copyright in a work shall be deemed to be infringed— (a) when any person, without a licence granted by the owner of the copyright or the Registrar of Copyrights under this Act or in contraven tion of the conditions of a licence so granted or of any condition imposed by a competent authority under this Act— (i) does anything, the exclusive right to do which is by this Act conferred upon the owner of the copyright, or 3[(ii) permits for profit any place to be used for the communication of the work to the public where such communication constitutes an infringement of the copyright in the work, unless he was not aware and had no reasonable ground for believing that such communi cation to the public would be an infringement of copyright; or] (b) when any person— (i) makes for sale or hire, or sells or lets for hire, or by way of trade displays or offers for sale or hire, or (ii) distributes either for the purpose of trade or to such an extent as to affect prejudicially the owner of the copyright, or (iii) by way of trade exhibits in public, or (iv) imports 4*** into India, any infringing copies of the work: 5[Provided that nothing in sub -clause (iv) shall apply to the import of one copy of any work for the private and domestic use of the importer.] Explanation.—For the purpose s of this section, the reproduction of a literary, dramatic, musical or artistic work in the form of a cinematograph film shall be deemed to be an “infringing copy”.

ACT NO. 47 OF 1963 
[13th December, 1963.] 
An Act to define and amend the law relating to certain kinds of specific relief. 
BE it enacted by Parliament in the Fourteenth Year of the Republic of India as follow:— 
 
PART I 
PRELIMINARY 
1. Short title, extent and commencement.—(1) This Act may be called the Specific Relief Act, 1963. 
(2) It extends to the whole of India 1[***]. 
(3) It shall come into force on such date 2 as the Central Government may, b y notification in the 
Official Gazette, appoint. 
2. Definitions.—In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires,— 
(a) “obligation” includes every duty enforceable by law; 
(b) “settlement” means an instrument (other than a will or codicil as defined by the Indian 
Succession Act, 1925 (39 of 1925), whereby  the destination or devolution of successive interests  in  
movable or immovable property is disposed of or is agreed  to be disposed of; 
(c) “trust” has the same meaning as in section 3 of the Indian Trusts Act, 1882  (2 of 1882), and 
includes an obligation in the nature  of a trust within the meaning of Chapter IX of that Act; 
(d) “trustee” includes every person holding property in trust; 
(e) all other words and expressions used herein but not defined, and defined in the Indian Contract 
Act, 1872 (9 of 1872), have the  meanings respectively assigned to them in that Act. 
3. Savings.—Except as otherwise provided herein, nothing in this Act shall be deemed— 
(a) to deprive any person of any right to relief, other than specific performance, which he may have 
under any contract; or 
(b) to affect the operation of the Indian Registration Act, 1908 (16 of 1908), on documents. 
4. Specific relief to be granted only for enforcing individual civil rights and not for enforcing 
penal laws.—Specific relief can be  granted only for the purpose of enforcing individual civil rights and 
not for the mere purpose of enforcing a penal law.

India Code  has been developed using open source software “DSpace”. It has 
deployed SOLR search engine through which one can b rowse, perform simple 
search and advance search with filter facility. 
 
1. BROWSE 
 
Allows you to go through a list of items in some specified order . One can browse 
by Community and Collection, Short title, Act number, Act year, Ministry etc. 
 
 
 
Fig 1: Browse Menu  
 
 
For example: following is the screen shot of Browsing through “Ministry”

2. SIMPLE SEARCH 
 
One can type any single word or group of words or phrases which are searched as 
free text word(s) in metadata as well in full text documents. It may locate those 
documents wherever these words or phrases may occur in the metadata and full text 
documents. As a default, SOLR search engine uses ‘AND ’ Boolean operator, that i s, 
search results contain all of the terms. For Example: 
 
2.1. Case 1: Search on National Waterways Act as keywords 
 
It shows documents containing National AND Waterways AND Act as search term. 
  
 
Fig 3: Search on National Waterways Act as keywords

In this case it will search all the documents containing “National Waterways Act ” 
where these words are occurring together.

However, one can further refine the search by using Boolean operators. 
 
 
3. BROADEN THE SEARCH USING “OR” OPERATOR

For Example: Railways OR Road 
 
Fig 5: Search on Railways OR Road as search terms 
 
 This will search documents that have keywords either Railways OR Road anywhere 
in the documents. 
 

 
4. NARROW DOWN SEARCH USING “AND” OPERATOR

SOLR search engine provides facility to apply search filters to limit the search results 
to specific fielded search criteria. 
 
Filter search has three components such as Field Name, Filter Operators and Field 
Value.

Ministry etc. which can be selected from combo box. 
 
Filter Operators: It provides various  search filter operators such as “Contains” 
“Not Contains” “Equals” “Not Equals” which can be selected from combo box. 
 
Field Value: Users has to type value for the field name. It also provides auto 
completion facility.

12. FUZZY SEARCHES 
 
Fuzzy search is the technique of finding string that match a pattern approximately, 
rather than exactly. One can do a fuzzy search using the tilde “~” symbol at the end 
of the Single word term. 
 
For Example: To search for word similar in spellings to “Role” one can do the fuzzy 
search: role~ 
This search will find terms like rome, rola, rale, pole, gole etc.  
 
Here in this example Nation~ searches words like “National”.
